units.title: When and how Macbeth was written
units.summary: Nobody can prove when Macbeth was written: most scholars say around 1606. It was first printed in the 1623 First Folio, the only early text, so make careful claims about dates and performances.

questions.prompt: Which is the safest way to describe when Macbeth was written?
options: In 1611, at the Globe Theatre
In 1623, when it was first printed
In 1603, the year James became king of England
Probably around 1606; the exact date is not known
questions.explanation: No document records the date. Compliments to King James and the Porter’s jokes about equivocation point to about 1606, so “probably” is the honest word.
questions.misconception: Treating a probable date as a proven one.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth was first printed in the First Folio of 1623.
Dr Simon Forman saw the play at the Globe in April 1611.
A surviving record proves the play was performed before King James in 1606.
The First Folio was printed while Shakespeare was still alive.

questions.explanation: A court performance in 1606 is likely but unproven. Shakespeare died in 1616, 7 years before the Folio appeared.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Holinshed’s Chronicles are published
James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England
The Gunpowder Plot is discovered
Simon Forman sees Macbeth at the Globe
Macbeth is first printed in the First Folio

questions.prompt: Match each name to its link with Macbeth.
pairs: wrote the history Shakespeare used as his main source
left the first eyewitness account of a performance
may have added the scenes with Hecate
is the only early printed text of the play
questions.explanation: Each of these explains something about where the play came from and why some details are uncertain.

questions.prompt: Some editions print “scorch’d the snake” (3.2.15) and others ‘scotch’d’. Why do editions differ like this?
options: Shakespeare wrote 2 different versions of the scene
The Globe and the court used different scripts that both survive
Exam boards choose their own wording
There is only 1 early text, the 1623 Folio, so editors must decide whether some words were misprinted
questions.explanation: With a single early source, editors cannot compare versions. Some keep the Folio’s word; others change it to the one they think was meant.

questions.prompt: The Hecate scenes look like scenes in one of Thomas Middleton’s own plays. What is that play called?
questions.explanation: The RSC notes that the Hecate scenes resemble Middleton’s tragicomedy The Witch, which is why some scholars think he added them. Others disagree.

questions.prompt: The play is unusually short. What does this suggest to the RSC?
options: It was written for children
Several scenes were lost in a fire
The Folio text may have been cut and revised for the theatre
Shakespeare ran out of time to finish it
questions.explanation: Brevity points to theatrical editing and revision, possibly involving Middleton.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Shakespeare wrote Macbeth in 1606 so that it could be performed for King James, who watched its first performance.’ What is the main problem?
options: Nothing: every part of this is proven
Macbeth was written for Queen Elizabeth
It presents likely ideas as certain facts: the date and the court performance are probable, not proven
The first performance was in 1623
questions.explanation: Both claims may be true, but no record proves them. An examiner trusts a careful claim, such as saying it was probably written with James in mind, more than a confident guess.
questions.misconception: Stating probable facts about the play’s origins as certain.

questions.prompt: Which pieces of evidence help date the play to around 1606? Choose 2.
options: The Porter’s jokes about equivocation seem to refer to the plot trials of early 1606
Simon Forman’s account of a performance in 1611
The play contains compliments to King James
The play was printed in 1623
questions.explanation: Forman and the Folio show only that the play existed by 1611 and was printed by 1623. The compliments to James and the equivocation jokes point to the years after 1603 and especially 1606.

questions.prompt: Explain why careful students write that Macbeth was “probably” written around 1606, and why the First Folio matters to anyone studying the play. (4 marks)
questions.model: Nobody recorded when Macbeth was written, so a firm date would be a guess. Most scholars place it around 1606 because the play pays compliments to King James, who became king of England in 1603, and because the Porter’s jokes about an equivocator seem to echo the trials after the Gunpowder Plot. The First Folio of 1623 matters because it is the only early printed text. Every modern edition is based on it, so when a word looks wrong, such as “scorch’d” in 3.2, editors have nothing else to check it against. The Folio’s shortness also suggests the play was cut for performance, perhaps with help from Thomas Middleton.
checklist: Explains that no record gives the date, so “probably” is accurate
Gives evidence for about 1606: compliments to James, equivocation jokes linked to the plot trials
States that the 1623 Folio is the only early text
Explains a consequence: editions differ in some words, line numbers or scene divisions
Mentions the possible cutting or revision (Middleton) as uncertain, not proven
questions.explanation: Credit any 4 accurate, clearly explained points. Avoid claiming the court performance or the Middleton additions as fact.

units.title: King James, Banquo and the Gunpowder Plot
units.summary: James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603 and traced his family to Banquo. The Porter’s equivocator is widely read as a reference to the Gunpowder Plot trials. Use this context only when it explains a moment in the play.

questions.prompt: Whose death in 1603 brought James VI of Scotland to the English throne?
options: King Henry VIII
King Duncan
Mary, Queen of Scots
Queen Elizabeth I
questions.explanation: Elizabeth I died in 1603 and James VI of Scotland became James I of England.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: In Holinshed’s Chronicles, Banquo helps Macbeth kill the king.
In Shakespeare’s play, Banquo helps Macbeth kill Duncan.
King James traced his family line back to Banquo.
The Witches tell Banquo that he himself will be king.

questions.explanation: Shakespeare turns Holinshed’s accomplice into an innocent man. The Witches promise that Banquo’s descendants, not Banquo, will be kings.

questions.prompt: Complete the Third Witch’s promise to Banquo: “Thou shalt get ___, though thou be none:” (1.3.70)
questions.explanation: “Get” means “father”: Banquo will be the ancestor of kings without ruling himself.

questions.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: someone who uses double meanings to avoid telling a direct lie
a Scottish lord, such as the lord of Glamis or Cawdor
questions.explanation: All 4 words matter in the play: Cawdor’s treason, the Porter’s equivocator, and Macduff’s description of the murder as sacrilege.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “What, will the line stretch out to th’ crack of doom?” (4.1.132)
options: The First Witch, at the cauldron
Banquo, at the feast
Macbeth, watching the procession of kings descended from Banquo
Malcolm, at his coronation
questions.explanation: Macbeth is horrified that Banquo’s line of kings seems endless. For an audience whose king claimed descent from Banquo, the line had an extra charge.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Duncan cannot judge who is loyal, which links to the play’s concern with treason?
options: “This castle hath a pleasant seat.” (1.6.1)
“O valiant cousin! worthy gentleman!” (1.2.26)
“There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face:” (1.4.13-14)
“What bloody man is that?” (1.2.1)
questions.explanation: Duncan says this about the traitor Cawdor, just before Macbeth enters. He then gives the same complete trust to the next traitor.

questions.prompt: Put these events from the Gunpowder Plot in order.
items: A search is made of the rooms below the hall where Parliament is to meet
The 8 surviving conspirators are tried
All 8 conspirators have been executed
Henry Garnet is executed in London
questions.explanation: The search was around midnight on 4 November 1605; the 8 were executed by the end of January 1606; Garnet died on 3 May 1606.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The Porter mentions an equivocator. This is because of the Gunpowder Plot. In 1605 Guy Fawkes tried to blow up Parliament. A Jacobean audience would be shocked.’ What would an examiner say?
options: The Porter does not mention an equivocator
The context is bolted on: it retells history but never explains what the Porter’s words add to the scene
This is excellent AO3 because it gives a date
The Gunpowder Plot happened after the play was written, so it cannot be mentioned
questions.explanation: AQA’s 2023 report said such discussions “made answers longer, but did not offer more insight”. A stronger sentence links equivocation to the Witches’ double-meaning prophecies.
questions.misconception: Thinking that historical facts earn AO3 marks on their own.

questions.prompt: Why might Shakespeare have changed Banquo from Holinshed’s accomplice into an innocent man?
options: Because Holinshed’s Banquo did not exist
King James traced his line to Banquo, and an innocent Banquo also gives Macbeth a foil who hears the same prophecy but does not act on it
Because the audience would not accept 2 murderers in 1 play
To make Fleance the hero of the play
questions.explanation: The change does 2 jobs: it avoids showing the king’s ancestor as a murderer, and it lets the audience compare 2 responses to the same temptation.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph explaining how the idea of equivocation links the Porter’s speech in 2.3 to Macbeth’s realisation in 5.5. Use context in no more than 1 sentence. (6 marks)
questions.model: The Porter imagines welcoming to hell “an equivocator, that could swear in both the scales against either scale,” (2.3.8-10), a man whose words point 2 ways at once. In 1606 the word would have recalled the trials that followed the Gunpowder Plot, but in the play it reaches further. The Witches are equivocators too: each of their prophecies is true, but not in the sense Macbeth hears. Only in Act 5, when Birnam Wood seems to move, does he begin “To doubt th’ equivocation of the fiend, / That lies like truth.” (5.5.49-50) The phrase “lies like truth” sums up the danger. The Porter’s joke on the morning after the murder has quietly told the audience what Macbeth learns too late.
checklist: Quotes or refers precisely to the Porter’s equivocator (2.3)
Explains equivocation as words with 2 meanings
Links the idea to the Witches’ prophecies
Uses Macbeth’s own words in 5.5 about the fiend’s equivocation
Keeps context to 1 relevant sentence (the plot trials)
Comments on structure: the joke foreshadows Macbeth’s discovery
questions.explanation: The strongest answers use context to explain the words, then spend most of the paragraph on the play itself.

units.title: Witches: Daemonologie and North Berwick
units.summary: King James took witchcraft seriously: the North Berwick trials of 1590 to 1591 and his book Daemonologie (1597) show it. The play’s Witches echo some details, but they are never fully explained and never force Macbeth to act.

questions.prompt: What was the title of the book about witches that James VI published in 1597?
options: The Witch
Daemonologie
Newes from Scotland
Chronicles of Scotland
questions.explanation: Daemonologie is written as a dialogue about witches and the devil. Newes from Scotland (1591) was a pamphlet about the North Berwick trials.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The North Berwick accused were charged with treason against King James.
Newes from Scotland printed confessions from the North Berwick trials.
Daemonologie was written as a play for the stage.
The Survey of Scottish Witchcraft lists about 400 people accused of witchcraft.

questions.explanation: Daemonologie is a dialogue, not a play, and the Survey lists nearly 4,000 accused.

questions.prompt: Complete the First Witch’s line: “But in a ___ I’ll thither sail,” (1.3.9)
questions.explanation: A sieve is full of holes, so sailing in one is impossible without magic. One of the North Berwick accused confessed to sailing in sieves.

questions.prompt: Match each source to what it contains.
pairs: the claim that witches can raise storms at sea or on land
confessions from the North Berwick trials
the name weird sisters, and doubt about what the women were
a database of nearly 4,000 people accused in Scotland
questions.explanation: These sources show that witchcraft was a real fear, and that Shakespeare’s main source already left the Witches uncertain.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that the Witches can torment people but not destroy them?
options: “Though his bark cannot be lost, / Yet it shall be tempest-tost.” (1.3.25-26)
“All hail, Macbeth! that shalt be king hereafter!” (1.3.53)
“When shall we three meet again?” (1.1.1)
“By the pricking of my thumbs, / Something wicked this way comes.” (4.1.44-45)
questions.explanation: The sailor’s ship cannot be sunk, but it can be battered. The limit on their power matters when we ask how far they control Macbeth.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “The instruments of darkness tell us truths;” (1.3.136)
options: Macbeth
Angus
Ross
Banquo
questions.explanation: Banquo warns that evil powers tell small truths to win trust and then betray. Macbeth ignores the warning.

questions.prompt: How might an audience today respond to the Witches differently from an audience in 1606?
options: There is no difference, because everyone has always believed in witches
A modern audience may not believe in witchcraft, but can still read them as a picture of temptation or of Macbeth’s own thoughts
A modern audience cannot find them frightening at all
A modern audience will think they are comic characters
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners stress how “any audience might respond”. The play never explains the Witches, which keeps them unsettling either way.

questions.prompt: In an Edexcel part (a) answer on the Witches’ extract, a student adds a paragraph on Daemonologie. Why does this earn no marks?
options: Part (a) is marked only for spelling
Part (a) assesses AO2 only, so context is not rewarded there
Edexcel does not allow quotations from King James
Daemonologie was written after the play
questions.explanation: Edexcel’s 2024 feedback noted contextual points in part (a), “which is not assessed”, and in 2025 examiners saw frequent references to James I and Daemonologie in the Witches extract.
questions.misconception: Believing context earns credit in every Shakespeare answer on every board.

questions.prompt: Which details in the play also appear in the North Berwick confessions? Choose 2.
options: Raising a storm against a ship
Brewing a potion in a cauldron at court
Riding through the air on broomsticks
Sailing in a sieve
questions.explanation: The sieve and the storm at sea appear in both, so the play may be echoing the trials. The other 2 details are not in the confessions quoted in Newes from Scotland.

questions.prompt: You are answering an AQA question on how Shakespeare presents the Witches in 1.3. Write a paragraph that analyses their language first and uses context in 1 sentence only. (6 marks)
questions.model: The First Witch’s revenge on the sailor shows both the reach and the limits of the Witches’ power. She will travel “in a sieve” and promises “I will drain him dry as hay:”, and the chant of her lines makes the curse sound like a spell being cast as we listen. Yet she admits “Though his bark cannot be lost, / Yet it shall be tempest-tost.” (1.3.25-26) The rhyme of “lost” and “tost” closes the curse neatly, but the meaning is that she can torment the ship, not sink it. The sieve and the storm also appear in the confessions printed after the North Berwick trials, so an audience in 1606 may have heard a real fear behind the scene. That limit matters: when Macbeth arrives moments later, the Witches offer him words, not force, and what he does with them is his own choice.
checklist: Analyses specific words or sounds in the Witches’ speech (AO2)
Uses precise quotation, such as the bark that “cannot be lost”
Makes a point about the limits of their power
Context in 1 linked sentence (North Berwick sieve and storm)
Links back to Macbeth and the question of choice
questions.explanation: Analysis leads; context supports. A whole paragraph of witch-trial history would be bolted on.

units.title: Kings, order and nature
units.summary: Many believed a king’s authority came from God, so killing Duncan is treated as sacrilege. After the murder nature itself goes wrong, and order returns only with Malcolm. Use these ideas to explain images, not to replace analysis.

questions.prompt: What does the divine right of kings mean?
options: A monarch’s authority comes from God, so no earthly power can judge the king
Kings must ask the Church before going to war
Any brave soldier has the right to become king
Kings are chosen by Parliament every few years
questions.explanation: King James was the best-known defender of this idea.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: In 1610 King James told Parliament that kings are even called gods by God himself.
The Great Chain of Being placed kings below animals.
In 2.4 a falcon is killed by an owl.
Macbeth heals the sick by touch in 4.3.

questions.explanation: Kings were placed high on the ladder, below God and the angels. It is the English King Edward, not Macbeth, who heals the sick.

questions.prompt: Complete Macduff’s words on finding Duncan: “Most sacrilegious murder hath broke ope / The Lord’s ___ temple” (2.3.77-78)
questions.explanation: A king was anointed with holy oil at his coronation, so Duncan’s body is imagined as a temple that has been broken into.

questions.prompt: Match each sign of order or disorder to the scene where it appears.
pairs: Lamentings and strange screams heard in the night air
King Edward healing the sick by touch
Malcolm promising to act “by the grace of Grace”
questions.explanation: Disorder follows the murder in Act 2; images of holy, healing kingship arrive in 4.3 and at the end.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that nature mirrors the killing of a king?
options: “I have almost forgot the taste of fears.” (5.5.11)
“Double, double, toil and trouble;” (4.1.10)
“This castle hath a pleasant seat.” (1.6.1)
“A falcon, towering in her pride of place, / Was by a mousing owl hawk’d at and kill’d.” (2.4.15-16)
questions.explanation: The owl, a lower bird that hunts mice, kills the proud falcon, just as a subject has killed his king.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “’Tis said they eat each other.” (2.4.23-24)
options: Macduff, about Duncan’s sons
Ross, about the Witches
Old Man, about Duncan’s horses
Lennox, about the grooms
questions.explanation: Ross reports that Duncan’s horses broke loose; the Old Man adds the rumour that they ate each other. Ross confirms he saw it.

questions.prompt: Why does Shakespeare place the description of King Edward’s healing touch in 4.3?
options: To give the actors a rest before the battle
To contrast a holy king whose power heals with a tyrant whose power destroys, just before Macduff learns of his family’s murder
Because Edward is about to invade Scotland himself
To show that Malcolm wants to become a doctor
questions.explanation: The contrast sharpens the audience’s idea of good kingship, and the healing image is followed at once by news of Macbeth’s cruelty.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Everyone in Shakespeare’s time believed in the Great Chain of Being.’ Which correction is most accurate?
options: It was one widely held idea, not something everyone believed; anchor it in the play’s own images of disorder
It applies only to Shakespeare’s comedies
Only kings believed in it
The idea was invented in the 20th century
questions.explanation: Treat it as one useful way to read the play’s images, such as the owl and the falcon, rather than a fact about every mind of the period.
questions.misconception: Making sweeping claims about what everyone in the period believed.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses context most effectively?
options: The owl killing the falcon mirrors Macbeth killing his king, a crime against the natural order that many in 1606 believed God had set.
King James was the king when Shakespeare wrote Macbeth.
A Jacobean audience would be shocked by everything in this scene.
In Jacobean times people believed in the Great Chain of Being, which was very important.
questions.explanation: The strongest sentence grows the context out of an image in the play. The others state facts or generalise without explaining anything.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare show that Duncan’s murder throws the natural world out of balance, and how is order restored by the end? Refer to 2 or more moments. (8 marks)
questions.model: On the night of the murder Lennox describes storms and “Lamentings heard i’ th’ air, strange screams of death,” (2.3.63-64) as if the air itself grieves. The next morning Ross and the Old Man list stranger signs. Darkness covers the day: “by the clock ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp.” (2.4.8-9) The verb “strangles” turns the night into a murderer, repeating the crime in the sky. The falcon “by a mousing owl hawk’d at and kill’d” (2.4.16) and Duncan’s horses turning wild show creatures attacking their natural superiors, just as a subject has killed his king. For an audience who saw the king as God’s anointed, this disorder shows that the crime is against heaven as well as Scotland. Order returns only when Macduff hails Malcolm as king, and Malcolm promises to act “by the grace of Grace” (5.8.85), placing his rule under God again.
checklist: Uses the storm and cries reported in 2.3
Analyses an image from 2.4 (darkness by day, the falcon and owl, or the horses)
Explains how the image mirrors regicide (AO2)
Brief, relevant context about kingship or order (AO3)
Shows order restored with Malcolm in 5.8
Uses accurate references throughout
questions.explanation: Top answers analyse the words of each sign, then show the restoration as the end of a pattern.

units.title: History, Holinshed and Shakespeare
units.summary: Shakespeare reshaped history: the real Macbeth killed Duncan in battle and ruled for 17 mostly peaceful years. Comparing play, source and history shows his choices, which is a point about methods. Check whether your board rewards context at all.

questions.prompt: When did the real Macbeth reign as King of Scotland?
questions.explanation: Royal records give 1040 to 1057. He was killed at the Battle of Lumphanan in 1057.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The real Duncan was killed by Macbeth in battle, aged about 39.
Holinshed gives Macbeth 10 years of fair rule before he turns cruel.
In Shakespeare’s play, Macbeth’s reign seems long and peaceful.
The real Macbeth was killed by Macduff.

questions.explanation: The real Macbeth was killed by Duncan’s son Malcolm. In the play, tyranny starts at once and the reign feels like months.

questions.prompt: Match each board to how it treats context (AO3) in the Shakespeare question.
pairs: assessed in part (b) only, 5 of its 20 marks
assessed, with less weight than AO1 and AO2
questions.explanation: Check your board before you revise context. On Eduqas, time spent on it earns nothing.

questions.prompt: Put these in time order.
items: Macbeth kills Duncan in battle and becomes king
Macbeth goes on pilgrimage to Rome
Macbeth is killed at the Battle of Lumphanan
Holinshed’s Chronicles are published
questions.explanation: 1040, 1050, 1057, then 1587, centuries later.

questions.prompt: Shakespeare makes Duncan old and saintly, and has him murdered while a guest in Macbeth’s castle. What does this change achieve?
options: It follows the real history exactly
It makes Duncan the villain of the play
It makes the murder easier to forgive
It makes Macbeth’s crime darker, since he betrays a good king, a kinsman and a guest
questions.explanation: Macbeth himself lists these bonds in 1.7: kinsman, subject and host. The changes deepen his guilt.

questions.prompt: The real Lady Macbeth was a granddaughter of King Kenneth III. What was her name?
questions.explanation: Royal records name her Gruoch; her marriage strengthened Macbeth’s claim to the throne.

questions.prompt: Which change most speeds up Macbeth’s fall in the play?
options: Shakespeare sets the play in England
Shakespeare removes the battle at the start
Shakespeare packs 17 years of history into what feels like a few months
Shakespeare makes Macbeth older than Duncan
questions.explanation: Compression makes the fall from hero to tyrant feel sudden and terrible.

questions.prompt: Which statement about context matches the AQA 2023 examiner report?
options: Context should be a separate paragraph at the end
Every paragraph should end with a sentence about the Jacobean era
Answers without dates cannot pass
Many students write without mentioning the Jacobean era and still reach the highest levels
questions.explanation: The report says many students write about the texts “without mentioning the Elizabethan era, the Jacobean era or the Victorian era” and do very well.
questions.misconception: Thinking dates and historical facts are needed to reach the top levels.

questions.prompt: A student plans to open an Eduqas essay with a paragraph comparing Holinshed with the play. What is the best advice?
options: Add more dates to it
Cut it: Eduqas does not assess AO3 on Shakespeare, so spend the time on the play
Move it to the conclusion
Keep it, because Eduqas rewards history
questions.explanation: Eduqas assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only in this section. In 2025 examiners named unnecessary context as the biggest source of underachievement.

questions.prompt: Choose 1 change Shakespeare made to Holinshed or to history. Explain in a paragraph what it adds to the audience’s view of Macbeth. (6 marks)
questions.model: In Holinshed, Macbeth rules justly for 10 years before turning cruel; in the play, tyranny begins almost at once. Shakespeare cuts the good years so that each crime seems to lead straight to the next. Within a scene of being crowned, Macbeth is plotting Banquo’s death, telling himself “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus.” (3.1.52-53) The compression makes the audience see that the crown brings him no peace at all. A reign of fair rule would have softened the story; removing it turns the play into a study of how one murder breeds others, and makes his fall feel fast and inevitable.
checklist: Names a specific change accurately (Banquo, Duncan, the reign, Lady Macbeth’s role)
Explains what the change does to the audience’s view of Macbeth
Supports the point with a precise reference to the play
Treats the change as a choice by Shakespeare (a method, AO2)
Keeps historical detail brief and relevant
questions.explanation: The comparison earns marks when it explains the play, not when it lists differences.

units.title: Act 1 Scenes 1 to 3: the Witches and the hero
units.summary: The Witches open the play in a storm, the wounded Captain praises Macbeth’s brutal courage, and on the heath the prophecies begin. Macbeth’s asides show that the thought of murder comes to him almost at once.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “So foul and fair a day I have not seen.” (1.3.39)
options: Duncan
Macbeth
Banquo
The First Witch
questions.explanation: These are Macbeth’s first words in the play. They echo the Witches’ “Fair is foul, and foul is fair:” (1.1.12) before he has even met them.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The Witches plan to meet Macbeth on the heath once the battle is over.
When the Witches greet him, Macbeth already knows he has been made Thane of Cawdor.
The Captain tells Duncan that Macbeth cut Macdonwald open and fixed his head on the battlements.
The Witches tell Banquo that he will be king.

questions.explanation: Duncan gives Macbeth the Cawdor title in 1.2, but Macbeth only hears of it from Ross after the Witches have hailed him. Banquo is told his descendants will be kings.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 1 Scenes 1 to 3 in order.
items: The Witches agree to meet again when the battle is done
The wounded Captain describes Macbeth’s courage in battle
Duncan orders Cawdor’s execution and gives his title to Macbeth
The Witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor and future king
Ross brings news that Macbeth is now Thane of Cawdor
questions.explanation: The audience knows about the Cawdor title before Macbeth does, so the Witches’ second greeting comes true in front of us.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s aside: “If chance will have me king, why, chance may ___ me / Without my stir.” (1.3.157-159)
questions.explanation: Macbeth decides, for now, to let chance make him king without any action of his own.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth is first presented as a brutally violent warrior?
options: “Look, how our partner’s rapt.” (1.3.156)
“So foul and fair a day I have not seen.” (1.3.39)
“Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chops,” (1.2.24)
“Come what come may,” (1.3.163)
questions.explanation: The Captain’s image of slicing a man from navel to jaw shows violence that is praised because it serves the king.

questions.prompt: Match each line from Act 1 Scenes 1 to 3 to its speaker.
pairs: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair:” (1.1.12)
“For brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name),” (1.2.18)
“What he hath lost, noble Macbeth hath won.” (1.2.78)
questions.explanation: Duncan’s line about Cawdor also hints that Macbeth may inherit the traitor’s nature along with his title.

questions.prompt: The First Witch plans to sail “in a sieve” (1.3.9) and batter a sailor’s ship with storms. Which piece of context links most closely to this?
options: The First Folio of 1623
The Gunpowder Plot of 1605
King James’s speech to Parliament in 1610
Confessions from the North Berwick witch trials, which describe witches sailing in sieves and raising a storm at sea
questions.explanation: Newes from Scotland (1591) printed these confessions. The play may be echoing the trials of witches accused of treason against James.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘In his aside “If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me / Without my stir” Macbeth decides to grab any chance to murder Duncan.’ What has the student misunderstood?
options: The line means the opposite: for now he will leave it to chance and not act (“Without my stir” means without his own action)
The line is about Malcolm, not Duncan
The line is spoken by Banquo, not Macbeth
Nothing: the line shows his decision to kill
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners in 2023 reported that this line was often misread in this way. Read the whole sentence before analysing a word in it.
questions.misconception: Misreading “chance may crown me / Without my stir” as a decision to murder.

questions.prompt: Why does Shakespeare give Macbeth so many asides in 1.3?
options: To let the audience hear thoughts of murder that he hides from Banquo, Ross and Angus
To explain the plot of the battle
Because Macbeth is talking to the Witches
To show that he is too shy to speak to the lords
questions.explanation: Asides create dramatic irony: we know about the “horrid image” in his mind while the others see only a man lost in thought. Eduqas examiners in 2023 said that responses which ignored the asides struggled.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth in Act 1 Scenes 1 to 3? Write 2 paragraphs, using at least 3 short quotations. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare introduces Macbeth through other people’s words before he appears. The Captain calls him “brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name),” (1.2.18) and describes him slicing Macdonwald “from the nave to the chops,” (1.2.24). This violence is celebrated because it protects the king, so the audience first sees a loyal hero. Yet the Witches have already named him in 1.1, which links him to the supernatural before he has said a word, and his first line, “So foul and fair a day I have not seen.” (1.3.39), unknowingly echoes their chant.

Once the prophecies are spoken, Shakespeare uses asides to show what the hero hides. Macbeth starts at the promise of kingship, and soon admits that the thought of murder makes his “seated heart knock at my ribs,” (1.3.149). The physical image shows his body rebelling against his own idea. For now he chooses to wait: “If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me / Without my stir.” (1.3.157-159) The audience sees a man both tempted and frightened, which makes his later choice to kill more tragic.
checklist: Uses the Captain’s report to show Macbeth’s public reputation (AO1)
Notices that Macbeth is linked to the Witches before he appears (structure, AO2)
Analyses the echo of “foul and fair” or another language choice
Explains the asides and what they reveal
Shows that he is tempted but has not yet decided to act
Uses at least 3 accurate, short quotations
questions.explanation: Credit any well-supported reading. The best answers show both the public hero and the private temptation.

units.title: Act 1 Scenes 4 to 6: an heir, a letter and a welcome
units.summary: Duncan names Malcolm as his heir, which blocks Macbeth’s path. Lady Macbeth reads the letter, calls on spirits to fill her with cruelty, and takes charge of the plan before Duncan arrives at a castle he finds pleasant.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Stars, hide your fires! / Let not light see my black and deep desires.” (1.4.57-58)
options: Malcolm, to Duncan
Macbeth, in an aside
Banquo, to Fleance
Lady Macbeth, alone
questions.explanation: Macbeth speaks this aside straight after Duncan names Malcolm as heir. The darkness imagery that runs through the play begins here.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Malcolm reports that the Thane of Cawdor confessed his treasons before he died.
Duncan names Malcolm Prince of Cumberland.
Lady Macbeth only learns that Duncan is coming when Macbeth arrives.
Duncan admires the pleasant air around Macbeth’s castle.

questions.explanation: A messenger tells Lady Macbeth that “The King comes here tonight.” (1.5.35) before Macbeth arrives, and she calls on the spirits at once.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 1 Scenes 4 to 6 in order.
items: Malcolm reports how Cawdor died
Duncan names Malcolm Prince of Cumberland
Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth’s letter
A messenger announces that the King is coming tonight
Lady Macbeth welcomes Duncan to the castle
questions.explanation: The scenes move fast: the obstacle (Malcolm), the plotter (Lady Macbeth), then the victim walking into the trap.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth’s fear about her husband: “It is too full o’ th’ milk of human ___ / To catch the nearest way.” (1.5.17-18)
questions.explanation: She fears his gentle nature will stop him taking the quickest route, murder, to the crown.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Lady Macbeth teaches her husband to hide his intentions?
options: “The King comes here tonight.” (1.5.35)
“This castle hath a pleasant seat.” (1.6.1)
“my dearest partner of greatness)” (1.5.11)
“look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t.” (1.5.76-78)
questions.explanation: The flower and serpent image sums up the gap between appearance and reality that runs through the play.

questions.prompt: At the end of 1.4 Duncan announces where he will go next, as Macbeth’s guest. Name the place.
questions.explanation: “From hence to Inverness,” (1.4.48) Duncan says, and Macbeth rides ahead to prepare his wife. The visit gives the couple their chance.

questions.prompt: In Holinshed, Duncan is a soft king whose slackness lets rebels grow strong. In the play he is trusting and gracious. What does this change add to 1.4 to 1.6?
options: It makes the plan against him more shocking, because the victim is a good and grateful king
It shows Shakespeare had not read Holinshed
It removes any reason for Malcolm to be heir
It makes Duncan look foolish so the audience supports Macbeth
questions.explanation: A gracious Duncan, praising Macbeth and admiring his castle, sharpens the betrayal and the dramatic irony.

questions.prompt: Duncan says of Cawdor, “He was a gentleman on whom I built / An absolute trust.” (1.4.15-16) Why is this moment ironic?
options: Because Malcolm is the traitor
Because Duncan is speaking to the Witches
Because Cawdor is still alive
Because Macbeth, the next man Duncan will trust completely, enters immediately
questions.explanation: Shakespeare times Macbeth’s entrance so that the audience sees Duncan repeat his mistake.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Before she reads the letter, Lady Macbeth is a gentle, obedient wife, but the letter changes her.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: Correct: Macbeth describes her as gentle in 1.3
Correct: the play shows her gentleness in an earlier scene
There is no evidence: 1.5 is her first appearance, and she is already thinking of murder as she reads
She does not read the letter until Act 2
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners in 2023 noted this claim, “despite this being her first moment in the play”. Build arguments on what the play shows.
questions.misconception: Inventing a gentle Lady Macbeth before her first scene.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth in 1.5? Write a paragraph analysing at least 2 quotations. (6 marks)
questions.model: Lady Macbeth’s first scene shows a woman who has decided on murder before her husband arrives. Reading the letter, she fears his nature is “too full o’ th’ milk of human kindness” (1.5.17); milk suggests softness and nursing, qualities she sees as weakness. When she hears that Duncan is coming she calls on spirits to “unsex me here,” (1.5.48) asking to be emptied of everything she links with womanhood and filled “top-full / Of direst cruelty!” (1.5.49-50) The commands make even the powers of darkness sound like servants. An audience might be shocked by how willingly she invites evil in, yet the fact that she needs supernatural help may also hint that cruelty does not come naturally to her, which prepares for her collapse in Act 5.
checklist: States a clear point about her character in this scene
Analyses “milk of human kindness” or similar imagery
Analyses the invocation to the spirits (“unsex me”, “direst cruelty”)
Comments on her commands or control of the scene
Offers an alternative reading or a link forward to Act 5
questions.explanation: Strong answers notice both her power and the hint that she must call for cruelty because she lacks it.

units.title: Act 1 Scene 7: the decision
units.summary: Alone, Macbeth lists the reasons not to kill Duncan and admits only ambition drives him. He tells his wife they will stop, but she attacks his courage and manhood until he agrees to the plan.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “I dare do all that may become a man; / Who dares do more is none.” (1.7.51-52)
options: Banquo
Duncan
Macbeth
Lady Macbeth
questions.explanation: Macbeth argues that a real man has limits. His wife turns the idea of manhood against him.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth begins the scene alone on stage.
Macbeth has decided to kill Duncan before Lady Macbeth enters.
Lady Macbeth plans to make Duncan’s chamberlains drunk.
Macbeth tells his wife, “We will proceed no further in this business:”.

questions.explanation: The soliloquy ends with Macbeth turning away from the murder. Only his wife’s persuasion changes his mind.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from 1.7 in order.
items: Macbeth lists the reasons not to kill Duncan
Macbeth tells his wife they will go no further
Lady Macbeth attacks his courage and manhood
Lady Macbeth explains the plan to drug the chamberlains
Macbeth agrees to the murder
questions.explanation: The scene turns twice: from murder to refusal, and from refusal back to murder.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s admission: “I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ___,” (1.7.25-27)
questions.explanation: He imagines ambition as a rider who leaps too far and falls on the other side of the horse.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth knows Duncan is a good king?
options: “his virtues / Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued, against / The deep damnation of his taking-off;” (1.7.18-20)
“Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dress’d yourself?” (1.7.39-40)
“We fail? / But screw your courage to the sticking-place,” (1.7.69-70)
“False face must hide what the false heart doth know.” (1.7.95-96)
questions.explanation: Duncan’s virtues will speak like angels against the murder: Macbeth understands the crime fully.

questions.prompt: Match each of Lady Macbeth’s tactics to an example from 1.7.
pairs: “And live a coward in thine own esteem,” (1.7.47)
Shocking him with a violent image
questions.explanation: She combines insult, emotional pressure, horror and practical detail. The plan is what finally wins him over.

questions.prompt: Macbeth fears “The deep damnation of his taking-off;” (1.7.20). Which context best explains why killing Duncan is worse than an ordinary murder?
options: Simon Forman’s visit to the Globe
The North Berwick witch trials
The idea that a king’s authority comes from God, so regicide is a sin as well as a crime
The fact that the play was printed in 1623
questions.explanation: Belief in the divine right of kings makes the murder a sin against heaven. Macbeth’s language of angels and damnation reflects this.

questions.prompt: Gutenberg and Folger print Lady Macbeth’s reply as “We fail?” (1.7.68), but some editions print an exclamation mark. Why does this matter to an essay?
options: It shows the scene is in prose
The exclamation mark means Macbeth speaks the line
It does not matter at all
The question mark can sound scornful (as if failure were unthinkable), while an exclamation can sound like grim acceptance; each changes how we see her
questions.explanation: Punctuation shapes tone. Noticing a choice like this, and saying what each version suggests, is the kind of exploration top answers show.
questions.misconception: Assuming every edition prints identical words and punctuation.

questions.prompt: Why is Lady Macbeth’s attack on Macbeth’s manhood so effective?
options: Because his identity rests on being a brave soldier, so calling him a coward strikes at what he values most
Because Macbeth has never fought in battle
Because she threatens to tell Duncan
Because the Witches told her to
questions.explanation: Macbeth’s reputation, the “Golden opinions” he has won, comes from courage. She turns courage into a test he must pass.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare show Macbeth changing his mind in 1.7? Refer to the soliloquy and to Lady Macbeth’s persuasion. (8 marks)
questions.model:
The soliloquy shows a mind that understands the crime completely. Macbeth wishes the deed could be over “quickly” (1.7.2), then lists the bonds it would break: he is Duncan’s “kinsman and his subject,” (1.7.13) and also his host. Duncan’s virtues “Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued,” (1.7.19) a loud, heavenly image that drowns his own excuses. He admits that only “Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (1.7.27) drives him, and the broken line that follows shows the argument collapsing. When his wife enters he is decisive: “We will proceed no further in this business:” (1.7.34)

Lady Macbeth reverses this in a few speeches. She asks “Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dress’d yourself?” (1.7.39-40), turning his ambition into a borrowed costume, and accuses him of living “a coward in thine own esteem,” (1.7.47). Her image of dashing out her baby’s brains shocks him into silence, and the practical plan gives him something to hold. His final line, “False face must hide what the false heart doth know.” (1.7.95-96), ends in a rhyming couplet that sounds like a vow. The audience watches conscience lose to persuasion within a single scene.
checklist: Explains Macbeth’s reasons against the murder in the soliloquy
Analyses imagery such as the angels or “vaulting ambition”
Notes his decision to stop (“proceed no further”)
Analyses at least 2 of Lady Macbeth’s tactics
Comments on structure or form (soliloquy, broken line, rhyming couplet)
Judges why he changes: persuasion, manhood, ambition
questions.explanation: The best answers show change as a process, with a judgement about what finally tips him.

units.title: Act 2 Scenes 1 and 2: the murder
units.summary: Banquo resists “cursed thoughts” while Macbeth follows a dagger of the mind to Duncan’s room. After the offstage murder, Macbeth is horrified by the blood and cannot go back, so Lady Macbeth returns the daggers herself.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Is this a dagger which I see before me, / The handle toward my hand?” (2.1.44-45)
options: Banquo
Lady Macbeth
Macbeth
Fleance
questions.explanation: Macbeth speaks alone just before the murder. The dagger may be a supernatural sign or a product of his own mind.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Banquo admits that he dreamt of the Witches.
Macbeth tells Banquo that he thinks about the Witches often.
Lady Macbeth says she would have killed Duncan herself if he had not looked like her father asleep.
Macbeth takes the daggers back to Duncan’s room.

questions.explanation: Macbeth claims “I think not of them:” (2.1.27-28). He refuses to go back, so Lady Macbeth returns the daggers.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 2 Scenes 1 and 2 in order.
items: Banquo gives Macbeth a diamond from Duncan for his wife
Macbeth sees a dagger in the air
A bell rings and Macbeth goes to Duncan’s room
Macbeth returns carrying the bloody daggers
Lady Macbeth takes the daggers back
Knocking is heard at the south entry
questions.explanation: The diamond, a gift of thanks, is handed over minutes before the murder: Duncan’s generosity heightens the betrayal.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s question: “Will all great Neptune’s ___ wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79)
questions.explanation: Not even the god of the sea’s whole ocean could clean his hand. Guilt is imagined as larger than the world.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Lady Macbeth dismisses guilt straight after the murder?
options: “A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86)
“Had he not resembled / My father as he slept, I had done’t.” (2.2.16-17)
“Sleep that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care,” (2.2.49)
“Wake Duncan with thy knocking! I would thou couldst!” (2.2.94-95)
questions.explanation: Her “little water” answers his “great Neptune’s ocean”. In 5.1 she will find that her hand cannot be cleaned.

questions.prompt: Match each sound in Act 2 Scenes 1 and 2 to what it means.
pairs: Lady Macbeth’s signal that the way is ready
a bird linked with death, which she calls “the fatal bellman”
Macbeth’s guilt, imagined as a curse on his rest
the outside world arriving, which terrifies the murderers
questions.explanation: The murder happens offstage, so Shakespeare builds horror through sound.

questions.prompt: The real Duncan was killed by Macbeth in battle. Why might Shakespeare have chosen to make Duncan a sleeping guest, killed offstage?
options: Because battle scenes were banned on stage
To make Macbeth seem braver
A sleeping guest is helpless and trusting, so the crime becomes a betrayal; keeping it offstage makes the audience focus on the murderers’ reactions
Because Holinshed says Duncan died of old age
questions.explanation: Comparing history with the play shows a deliberate choice. Shakespeare turns a political killing into the betrayal of a sleeping guest who is also his kinsman.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The audience watches Macbeth stab Duncan in his bed.’ What is wrong?
options: Nothing
The murder happens offstage; we see only Macbeth before and after it
Lady Macbeth commits the murder
Duncan is poisoned
questions.explanation: Shakespeare keeps the act itself hidden, so the audience imagines it through the couple’s broken lines and the noises around them.
questions.misconception: Thinking Duncan’s murder is shown on stage.

questions.prompt: Why can Macbeth not say “Amen” after the murder?
options: He feels cut off from God’s blessing by what he has done, even as he most needs it
He has forgotten the prayer
The grooms are praying too loudly
Lady Macbeth stops him
questions.explanation: He says the word “Stuck in my throat.” (2.2.44) His body refuses the prayer, a sign that he has damned himself.

questions.prompt: Compare the reactions of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth straight after the murder of Duncan. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare shows a couple who react in opposite ways. Macbeth is overwhelmed by what he has done. He returns still holding the daggers, unable to forget that “Amen” stuck in his throat, and he hears a voice crying “Macbeth does murder sleep,” (2.2.48). Sleep, the gentle healer “that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care,” (2.2.49) has become his victim, so he imagines himself cut off from rest for ever. His question “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79) makes his guilt bigger than the sea.

Lady Macbeth is practical. She snaps “Infirm of purpose! / Give me the daggers.” (2.2.68-69) and returns them herself, dismissing the dead as “but as pictures.” (2.2.70) Her answer to his ocean is “A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86). The contrast is sharp, but it is also ironic: the woman who mocks his fears will later wash her hands in her sleep, unable to remove the smell of blood. In this scene she seems the stronger, but the play suggests that guilt delayed is not guilt escaped.
checklist: Analyses Macbeth’s horror (Amen, sleep, the ocean image)
Analyses Lady Macbeth’s control (“Infirm of purpose”, “A little water”)
Uses the contrast between ’great Neptune’s ocean’ and “a little water”
Comments on short lines, questions or the offstage murder (AO2)
Links forward to Act 5 to show the irony
Uses accurate quotations
questions.explanation: Top answers use the contrast to make a point about guilt, not just to list differences.

units.title: Act 2 Scenes 3 and 4: discovery and disorder
units.summary: A drunken Porter jokes about hell’s gate before Macduff discovers Duncan’s body. Macbeth kills the grooms, Duncan’s sons flee, and strange signs in nature follow. Macduff refuses to attend Macbeth’s coronation.

questions.prompt: Who says this, the morning after the murder? “’Twas a rough night.” (2.3.70)
options: Lennox
Macbeth
Macduff
Banquo
questions.explanation: Lennox has just described a night of storms and strange cries. Macbeth’s short reply sounds casual, and the audience knows why the night was so rough.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The Porter pretends to be the gatekeeper of hell.
Macduff is the one who discovers Duncan’s body.
Malcolm flees to Ireland and Donalbain to England.
Macduff travels to Scone to see Macbeth crowned.

questions.explanation: Malcolm goes to England and Donalbain to Ireland. Macduff goes home to Fife instead of Scone, the first sign of opposition.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 2 Scenes 3 and 4 in order.
items: The Porter lets in Macduff and Lennox
Macduff discovers that Duncan has been murdered
Macbeth admits he has killed the grooms
Malcolm and Donalbain decide to flee
Ross and the Old Man describe strange signs in nature
questions.explanation: The comic Porter delays the discovery, so the horror lands harder when it comes.

questions.prompt: Complete Macduff’s cry: “Confusion now hath made his ___!” (2.3.76)
questions.explanation: Destruction is pictured as an artist whose greatest work is the murder of a king.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth’s excuse for killing the grooms is a performance?
options: “There’s daggers in men’s smiles:” (2.3.165)
“Who can be wise, amaz’d, temperate, and furious, / Loyal and neutral, in a moment?” (2.3.127-128)
“In the great hand of God I stand;” (2.3.152)
“’Twas a rough night.” (2.3.70)
questions.explanation: The balanced, rhetorical list sounds rehearsed. Macbeth claims to be overcome by feeling while speaking with great control.

questions.prompt: Match each character to where they go at the end of Act 2.
questions.explanation: The sons’ flight makes them look guilty, which clears the way for Macbeth.

questions.prompt: The Porter welcomes “an equivocator, that could swear in both the scales against either scale,” (2.3.8-10). How is this line most often linked to context?
options: To the trials after the Gunpowder Plot, in which equivocation was an issue
To Simon Forman’s diary
To the North Berwick witch trials
To the First Folio’s printing
questions.explanation: The joke is widely read as a reference to the plot trials of early 1606. In the play it also foreshadows the Witches’ double-meaning prophecies.

questions.prompt: Macduff calls the murder a theft of “The life o’ th’ building.” (2.3.79) Some students think “building” means the castle. What does it refer to?
options: Macbeth’s new palace
The Porter’s gate
The castle walls
Duncan’s life, pictured as the life of a holy temple, the king’s anointed body
questions.explanation: The OCR examiners’ report for 2024 noted this misreading. The line continues Macduff’s image of the king as “The Lord’s anointed temple” (2.3.78).
questions.misconception: Reading “the life o” th’ building’ as a description of the castle.

questions.prompt: Lady Macbeth faints when Macbeth describes killing the grooms. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The text proves she is faking
The text proves she is genuinely overcome
She faints because she is ill
The play does not say; it can be read as real shock or as a distraction to stop Macbeth saying too much, and productions choose differently
questions.explanation: Strong answers present both readings and say which the evidence suggests to them. The stage direction alone does not settle it.

questions.prompt: Why does Shakespeare place the Porter’s comic speech straight before the discovery of the murder? (6 marks)
questions.model: The Porter’s scene gives the audience a moment of release after the tension of 2.2, but the comedy is dark. Drunk and slow to answer the knocking, he pretends to be “porter of hell gate,” (2.3.2) welcoming sinners. Without knowing it, he describes the truth: Macbeth’s castle has become a kind of hell, and a murderer lives inside. His joke about “an equivocator” who “could not equivocate to heaven” (2.3.11) foreshadows the double meanings of the Witches. The delay also stretches the suspense, because the audience knows what Macduff will find while the Porter rambles. When Macduff cries “O horror, horror, horror!” (2.3.73), the contrast with the jokes makes the discovery more shocking.
checklist: Explains the comic relief and release of tension
Shows the irony of the “hell gate” idea
Links the equivocator joke to later events (or briefly to context)
Comments on suspense created by delay
Uses the contrast with Macduff’s discovery
questions.explanation: Credit any reasoned purpose supported by the text.

units.title: Act 3 Scenes 1 and 2: a king without peace
units.summary: King Macbeth fears Banquo and resents the prophecy that Banquo’s children will rule. He hires murderers on his own and keeps the plan from his wife, who finds that the crown has brought no contentment.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Thou hast it now, King, Cawdor, Glamis, all,” (3.1.1)
options: Banquo, alone
Fleance, to Banquo
Macduff, to Ross
Lady Macbeth, to Macbeth
questions.explanation: Banquo’s soliloquy opens Act 3. He suspects Macbeth “play’dst most foully” for the crown, yet says nothing in public.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth checks that Banquo and Fleance will be riding that afternoon.
Macbeth tells his wife the full plan to kill Banquo.
Macbeth persuades the murderers that Banquo is their enemy.
Lady Macbeth says “Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6) in a speech alone.

questions.explanation: Macbeth keeps the plan from his wife: she is to be “innocent of the knowledge” (3.2.51).

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 3 Scenes 1 and 2 in order.
items: Banquo, alone, voices his suspicion of Macbeth
Macbeth invites Banquo to the feast
Macbeth, alone, says being king means nothing unless he is safe
Macbeth hires the murderers
Macbeth tells his wife his mind is full of scorpions
questions.explanation: Act 3 opens with 2 soliloquies, Banquo’s and Macbeth’s, that show each man’s fears of the other.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s line to his wife: “O, full of ___ is my mind, dear wife!” (3.2.41)
questions.explanation: His thoughts sting and poison him from inside. The tender “dear wife” sits beside the horror.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth now plans murder without his wife?
options: “We have scorch’d the snake, not kill’d it.” (3.2.15)
“Thou hast it now, King, Cawdor, Glamis, all,” (3.1.1)
“Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6)
“Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck, / Till thou applaud the deed.” (3.2.51-52)
questions.explanation: He shuts her out with an affectionate pet name. In 1.7 she led; now he does.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to what it shows.
pairs: “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus.” (3.1.52-53)
being king means nothing without safety
“Upon my head they plac’d a fruitless crown,” (3.1.66)
he has no heir to inherit the throne
“We have scorch’d the snake, not kill’d it.” (3.2.15)
the danger is wounded but still alive
“Ay, in the catalogue ye go for men;” (3.1.103)
questions.explanation: Each line shows a king who has gained the crown but not peace.

questions.prompt: Macbeth complains that the Witches gave him a “fruitless crown” and “a barren sceptre”. Which context gives this an extra edge for an audience in 1606?
options: Simon Forman saw the play in 1611
The First Folio was printed in 1623
The play was cut for performance
King James traced his family line back to Banquo, the man whose descendants will inherit
questions.explanation: Macbeth’s bitterness points straight at the prophecy that Banquo’s line will rule, the line James claimed.

questions.prompt: Spot the error: ‘In Act 3 Scene 3, Lady Macbeth says “Naught’s had, all’s spent,” and Macbeth calls her “dearest chuck”.’
options: Both lines are in Act 3 Scene 2; 3.3 is the murder of Banquo
Both lines are spoken by Macbeth
Both lines are in Act 1 Scene 7
There is no error
questions.explanation: Even an examiners’ report once placed these lines in 3.3. Precise references show secure knowledge.
questions.misconception: Misplacing key Act 3 quotations in the wrong scene.

questions.prompt: How does Macbeth persuade the murderers in 3.1?
options: He tells them Banquo is to blame for their misfortunes and questions whether they are real men
He offers them the crown
He threatens to kill their children
He shows them the Witches’ letter
questions.explanation: He uses the tactic his wife used on him: an attack on manhood. The persuaded has become the persuader.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare show the relationship between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth changing in 3.2? (8 marks)
questions.model:
In 3.2 the partnership of Act 1 begins to come apart. Lady Macbeth, alone, admits “Naught’s had, all’s spent, / Where our desire is got without content:” (3.2.6-7). The rhyme of “spent” and “content” sounds final, as if she has added up the cost and found it too high. When Macbeth enters she tries her old practical voice, “what’s done is done.” (3.2.14), but he ignores it: “We have scorch’d the snake, not kill’d it.” (3.2.15)

The biggest change is in who leads. Macbeth now plans Banquo’s murder alone and tells her to be “innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck,” (3.2.51). The pet name sounds loving, yet it also treats her almost as a child to be protected from adult business. In 1.7 she controlled the plan and spoke at length; here he has the long speeches, full of images such as the mind “full of scorpions” (3.2.41), and she is left asking questions. Affection remains, but trust and partnership have gone.
checklist: Analyses Lady Macbeth’s ’Naught’s had’ speech
Shows Macbeth ignoring or overriding her advice
Analyses “dearest chuck” and his secrecy
Compares with 1.5 or 1.7 to show change
Comments on who speaks more or leads the conversation (structure)
Reaches a judgement about what has changed and what remains
questions.explanation: The best answers separate love from partnership: one survives longer than the other.

units.title: Act 3 Scenes 3 and 4: murder and the banquet
units.summary: Banquo is murdered but Fleance escapes. At the banquet only Macbeth sees Banquo’s ghost; Lady Macbeth covers for him and then sends the guests away. Macbeth resolves to visit the Witches, too deep in blood to turn back.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “O, treachery! Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly!” (3.3.25)
options: Lennox
Banquo
The First Murderer
Macbeth
questions.explanation: Banquo’s last words save his son, and with him the prophecy that his descendants will be kings.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: A third murderer joins the 2 that Macbeth hired.
Fleance is killed alongside his father.
Only Macbeth can see the ghost at the banquet.
The ghost at the banquet is Duncan’s.

questions.explanation: Fleance escapes, and the ghost is Banquo’s. The stage directions make both clear.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 3 Scenes 3 and 4 in order.
items: Banquo is killed and Fleance escapes
A murderer reports to Macbeth at the banquet
Banquo’s ghost sits in Macbeth’s place
Lady Macbeth tells the lords he has had such fits since youth
Lady Macbeth sends the guests away
Macbeth decides to visit the Witches
questions.explanation: The banquet should show Macbeth as a confident king; instead his guilt is exposed in public.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s image: “I am in blood / Stepp’d in so far that, should I wade no more, / Returning were as ___ as go o’er.” (3.4.168-170)
questions.explanation: He pictures himself halfway across a river of blood: going back is as hard as going on.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Fleance’s escape leaves Macbeth trapped by fear?
options: “It will have blood, they say, blood will have blood.” (3.4.151)
“But now I am cabin’d, cribb’d, confin’d, bound in / To saucy doubts and fears.” (3.4.26-27)
“Sit, worthy friends. My lord is often thus,” (3.4.64)
“You lack the season of all natures, sleep.” (3.4.173)
questions.explanation: The run of words beginning with c and b sounds like walls closing in, the opposite of the freedom he hoped the murder would buy.

questions.prompt: Which thane does Macbeth notice has stayed away from the feast?
questions.explanation: Macbeth asks what his wife thinks of the fact that “Macduff denies his person” (3.4.159) at his command. He has spies in every house.

questions.prompt: Banquo dies but Fleance escapes. Why might this matter to an audience in 1606?
options: Fleance was a real Jacobean actor
Fleance becomes king at the end of the play
It shows the murderers were paid too little
The escape keeps alive the line of kings that King James claimed as his own ancestry
questions.explanation: The prophecy that Banquo will “get kings” survives with his son. Use this briefly, and only where your board rewards context.

questions.prompt: Eduqas examiners in 2024 found that some students thought the ghost at the banquet was Duncan’s. What would have prevented this mistake?
options: Counting the lines in the extract
Skipping the extract and writing about the whole play
Learning more context
Reading the opening stage direction, which names the Ghost of Banquo
questions.explanation: Stage directions are part of the evidence. Read every one before you plan.
questions.misconception: Misidentifying the ghost because the stage directions were not read.

questions.prompt: At the banquet Lady Macbeth asks, “Are you a man?” (3.4.70) Why does this question work less well than in 1.7?
options: Macbeth has already left the room
Macbeth’s fear now comes from guilt and horror, which taunts about courage cannot fix; she can only cover for him
Macbeth does not hear it
She says it to Lennox
questions.explanation: The weapon that won the argument in 1.7 no longer works. Her power over him is fading.

questions.prompt: Eduqas-style: Look at how Macbeth and Lady Macbeth speak and behave at the banquet. How might an audience respond to this part of the play? (8 marks)
questions.model: An audience is likely to feel tension and dread, because we know what Macbeth sees and his guests do not. When the Ghost takes his seat he cries “Thou canst not say I did it. Never shake / Thy gory locks at me.” (3.4.61-62) The denial gives him away, since nobody has accused him. Lady Macbeth’s reaction is quick and controlled: “Sit, worthy friends. My lord is often thus,” (3.4.64) she lies smoothly, then turns on him privately with “Are you a man?” (3.4.70). We may admire her nerve, yet also notice that her old taunt has lost its power. By the end, Macbeth’s words “It will have blood, they say, blood will have blood.” (3.4.151) sound weary and fatal, and an audience may feel a strange pity for a man trapped in the violence he started.
checklist: Explains dramatic irony: the audience shares Macbeth’s view of the Ghost
Analyses Macbeth’s speech to the Ghost
Analyses Lady Macbeth’s public cover and private challenge
Describes a likely audience response (tension, shock, pity) with reasons
Uses precise quotations from the scene
questions.explanation: Eduqas does not reward context here: focus on how the characters speak and behave.

units.title: Act 3 Scenes 5 and 6: Hecate and the rebellion
units.summary: Hecate plans to destroy Macbeth by making him over-confident. In 3.6 Lennox mocks Macbeth’s version of events with heavy irony, and a Lord reports that Malcolm and Macduff are seeking English help.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “security / Is mortals’ chiefest enemy.” (3.5.32-33)
options: Macbeth
The First Witch
Lennox
Hecate
questions.explanation: “Security” here means over-confidence. Hecate plans to ruin Macbeth by making him feel safe.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Hecate scolds the Witches for dealing with Macbeth without her.
Lennox openly accuses Macbeth of murder in front of the Lord.
Malcolm is living at the court of the English King Edward.
Macduff has gone to England to ask for help against Macbeth.

questions.explanation: Lennox never names Macbeth as the killer. He praises him so heavily that the praise becomes an accusation.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from Act 3 Scenes 5 and 6 in order.
items: Hecate scolds the Witches
Hecate plans to lead Macbeth into false confidence
Lennox speaks with irony about the deaths of Duncan and Banquo
The Lord reports that Malcolm is welcome at the English court
Lennox prays for a swift blessing on Scotland
questions.explanation: The 2 short scenes move from supernatural plotting against Macbeth to human plotting against him.

questions.prompt: Complete Lennox’s prayer: “that a swift blessing / May soon return to this our ___ country / Under a hand accurs’d!” (3.6.53-55)
questions.explanation: The “hand accurs’d” is Macbeth’s. Scotland is now pictured as a suffering body, an image Macduff and Ross will use in 4.3.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Lennox uses irony to criticise Macbeth?
options: “And the right valiant Banquo walk’d too late;” (3.6.6)
“I’ll send my prayers with him.” (3.6.56)
“Of the most pious Edward with such grace” (3.6.31)
“security / Is mortals’ chiefest enemy.” (3.5.32-33)
questions.explanation: Lennox pretends that Banquo’s only mistake was walking out too late at night. The mock-innocent tone tells the Lord what he really thinks.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their part in Act 3 Scenes 5 and 6.
pairs: queen of the witches, who plans Macbeth’s ruin
a Scottish lord who mocks the official story
the holy English king who welcomes Malcolm
a warlike English leader whose help is sought
questions.explanation: Opposition to Macbeth is gathering in Scotland and in England.

questions.prompt: Why do some scholars think 3.5 may not be by Shakespeare?
options: Because the Hecate scenes resemble scenes in Thomas Middleton’s play The Witch, though scholars disagree
Because Hecate is not mentioned in the First Folio
Because it is written in prose
Because it was added in the 20th century
questions.explanation: The RSC suggests Middleton may have added these scenes; the Folger notes the attribution is fiercely disputed. Present it as possible, not proven.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Middleton definitely wrote Hecate’s scenes, so they do not count as part of Macbeth.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: Correct: exam boards exclude them
Hecate’s scenes come from Holinshed
The authorship is disputed, and the scenes are in the only early text, so they are part of the play we study
Hecate’s scenes were written by King James
questions.explanation: Treat uncertain claims as uncertain. Whoever wrote them, Hecate’s plan to make Macbeth over-confident shapes 4.1.
questions.misconception: Presenting a disputed authorship claim as fact.

questions.prompt: Why is 3.6 important to the structure of the play?
options: It shows Macbeth’s coronation
It is the first scene in which the forces against Macbeth start to organise
It explains how Duncan was killed
It is the last time we see the Witches
questions.explanation: From here the counter-movement grows: Macduff in England, Siward’s army, and finally Birnam Wood.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare show opposition to Macbeth growing in 3.6? (6 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare shows opposition beginning quietly and then gathering strength. Lennox cannot speak openly, so he uses irony: he says Duncan “Was pitied of Macbeth” and that “the right valiant Banquo walk’d too late;” (3.6.6), as if night walks, not murder, killed him. The careful tone shows how dangerous honest speech has become under a tyrant. The Lord’s reply is more hopeful. Malcolm is at the court of “the most pious Edward” (3.6.31), and Macduff has gone to ask for help so that Scotland may again have “meat” on its tables and “sleep” at night. These ordinary comforts show what Macbeth’s rule has taken away. The scene ends with prayers for “a swift blessing” on “this our suffering country” (3.6.54), so the language of holiness gathers against him.
checklist: Explains Lennox’s irony with a quotation
Comments on why he must speak indirectly (fear of the tyrant)
Shows the Lord’s news about Malcolm, Edward and Macduff
Notes the images of lost food and sleep
Links to the religious language of blessing against Macbeth
questions.explanation: Strong answers see the scene as a turning point in structure, not only as a report.

units.title: Act 4 Scene 1: the apparitions
units.summary: Macbeth demands answers from the Witches. 3 apparitions give him warnings that sound reassuring, and a show of 8 kings confirms Banquo’s line will rule. Told that Macduff has fled, he orders the murder of Macduff’s family.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “By the pricking of my thumbs, / Something wicked this way comes.” (4.1.44-45)
options: The Second Witch, as Macbeth approaches
The First Apparition
Hecate, to the Witches
Macbeth, entering the cave
questions.explanation: The “wicked” thing coming is Macbeth himself. Even the Witches now describe him as evil.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The first apparition, an armed head, warns Macbeth to beware Macduff.
The third apparition is a bloody child.
Macbeth sees a procession of 8 kings followed by Banquo.
Macbeth decides to fight Macduff himself straight away.

questions.explanation: The bloody child is the second apparition; the third is a crowned child holding a tree. Macbeth sends murderers to Macduff’s castle instead of facing him.

questions.prompt: Put these events from 4.1 in order.
items: The Witches brew their charm
An armed head warns Macbeth to beware Macduff
A bloody child says none of woman born shall harm him
A crowned child with a tree speaks of Birnam Wood
A show of 8 kings appears
Lennox reports that Macduff has fled to England
questions.explanation: Each apparition seems to answer the one before. The kings then destroy the comfort they gave.

questions.prompt: Complete the Second Apparition’s command: “Be bloody, bold, and ___.” (4.1.90)
questions.explanation: The words urge exactly the violence Macbeth is already capable of.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth now acts without thinking?
options: “Double, double, toil and trouble;” (4.1.10)
“How now, you secret, black, and midnight hags!” (4.1.48)
“The very firstlings of my heart shall be / The firstlings of my hand.” (4.1.167-168)
“What, will the line stretch out to th’ crack of doom?” (4.1.132)
questions.explanation: His first impulse will become his first act. In 1.7 he weighed every reason; now he removes thought altogether.

questions.prompt: Match each apparition to its message.
pairs: none of woman born shall harm Macbeth
A crowned child holding a tree
he will not be beaten until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane
questions.explanation: The images also hint at the truth: the bloody child suggests Macduff’s birth, and the tree suggests the branches cut in 5.4.

questions.prompt: In the show of kings the last king carries a glass (a mirror) showing many more. What extra meaning might this have had in 1606?
options: It celebrated the Stuart line, since King James traced his ancestry to Banquo
It showed the audience their own faces
It referred to the Gunpowder Plot
It mocked King James’s appearance
questions.explanation: The procession honours James’s claimed ancestors. Macbeth’s horror at it would have struck the audience in a particular way.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The Witches make Macbeth kill Macduff’s family.’ What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing
Macduff’s family is killed by Banquo
The Witches kill the family themselves
The apparitions only say ‘beware Macduff’; the decision to kill his wife and children is Macbeth’s own
questions.explanation: Nothing in the prophecies mentions Macduff’s family. Blaming the Witches ignores Macbeth’s choice, which is the heart of the tragedy.
questions.misconception: Blaming the Witches for actions Macbeth chooses.

questions.prompt: Why are the apparitions’ messages so dangerous for Macbeth?
options: He cannot hear them clearly
They are true, but in senses he does not expect, so they make him over-confident
They tell him to give up the crown
They are lies
questions.explanation: This is equivocation. It fulfils Hecate’s plan that “security” would be his “chiefest enemy”.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth’s relationship with the supernatural in 4.1? (8 marks)
questions.model: In 1.3 the Witches came to Macbeth; in 4.1 he goes looking for them and gives orders. He greets them as “you secret, black, and midnight hags!” (4.1.48), insulting the powers he depends on, which shows a man who thinks he can command evil. Yet the scene makes him its puppet. The Second Witch announces him as “Something wicked” (4.1.45), so the supernatural now sees him as one of its own. The apparitions tell him to be “bloody, bold, and resolute.” (4.1.90), and he hears only comfort in their riddles. Even the show of kings, which he demanded, turns against him and makes him cry “What, will the line stretch out to th’ crack of doom?” (4.1.132) Finally, after cursing those who “trust them”, he resolves that “The very firstlings of my heart shall be / The firstlings of my hand.” (4.1.167-168) The supernatural has not forced his hand; it has simply let him act on his worst impulses.
checklist: Compares Macbeth’s attitude in 4.1 with 1.3
Analyses his commanding or insulting language
Explains how the apparitions mislead through double meaning
Uses the show of kings and his reaction
Shows his decision to act on impulse and judges who is responsible
questions.explanation: Top answers argue a position on control versus choice.

units.title: Act 4 Scenes 2 and 3: Fife and England
units.summary: At Fife, Lady Macduff feels abandoned and talks with her clever son before murderers kill them. In England Malcolm tests Macduff’s loyalty; then Ross brings the news, and Macduff turns grief into resolve.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “He loves us not: / He wants the natural touch;” (4.2.10-11)
options: Ross, about Macduff
Lady Macduff, about her husband
Lady Macbeth, about Macbeth
The Son, about his father
questions.explanation: She feels Macduff has deserted his family. The play makes the audience weigh his choice against her suffering.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Ross defends Macduff’s flight to his wife and then leaves.
A messenger warns Lady Macduff to flee before the murderers arrive.
Malcolm really is more wicked than Macbeth.
Siward is ready to march with 10,000 men.

questions.explanation: Malcolm’s list of vices is a test of Macduff’s loyalty, which he takes back once Macduff passes.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 4 Scenes 2 and 3 in order.
items: Ross defends Macduff to his wife and leaves
Lady Macduff talks with her son about his father
Murderers kill the son
Malcolm tests Macduff by pretending to be wicked
Ross tells Macduff that his family has been killed
Macduff vows to fight Macbeth himself
questions.explanation: The audience sees the murder before Macduff hears of it, so we watch him learn what we already know.

questions.prompt: Complete Macduff’s question: “All my ___ ones? / Did you say all?” (4.3.255-256)
questions.explanation: The repeated “all” shows him struggling to take in the scale of the loss.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macduff shows a different idea of manhood from Macbeth?
options: “I have done no harm.” (4.2.82)
“But I must also feel it as a man:” (4.3.261)
“Dispute it like a man.” (4.3.259)
“Bleed, bleed, poor country!” (4.3.39)
questions.explanation: Malcolm urges him to fight like a man; Macduff replies that a man must also feel grief. Manhood includes feeling.

questions.prompt: Match each line to its speaker.
pairs: “Alas, poor country, / Almost afraid to know itself!” (4.3.189-190)
“Whither should I fly? / I have done no harm.” (4.2.81-82)
questions.explanation: Scotland is pictured as a wounded body, and the innocent pay for Macbeth’s fears.

questions.prompt: In 4.3 a Doctor reports that King Edward cures the sick by touch, and Malcolm explains: “’Tis call’d the evil:” (4.3.168). How is this best used as context in an essay?
options: As proof that Shakespeare was a doctor
As a contrast between a holy king whose power heals and a tyrant whose power destroys
As the reason Macduff leaves Scotland
As evidence that Malcolm is ill
questions.explanation: Keep it tied to the play’s idea of good kingship. One sentence linking the healing touch to Macbeth’s destruction does more than a paragraph of history.
