questions.prompt: The Eduqas 2025 extract was from 4.2. Examiners found some students misread one name. Which slip did they report?
options: Reading ‘Fife’ as ‘Forres’
Reading ‘Lady Macduff’ as ‘Lady Macbeth’
Reading ‘Ross’ as ‘Banquo’
Reading ‘Son’ as ‘Fleance’
questions.explanation: Slow down on names. Confusing the 2 wives would wreck an answer about the innocence of Macduff’s family.
questions.misconception: Confusing Lady Macduff with Lady Macbeth.

questions.prompt: Why does Malcolm pretend to be worse than Macbeth?
options: To impress King Edward
Because he really is wicked
To test whether Macduff is an honest patriot or a spy sent by Macbeth
He wants Macduff to leave
questions.explanation: After Macbeth’s lies, trust must be tested. Macduff’s despair for Scotland proves his loyalty, which shows Malcolm’s caution as a good quality in a future king.

questions.prompt: Eduqas-style: How might an audience respond to the murder of Lady Macduff and her son in 4.2? Refer to how the characters speak and behave. (8 marks)
questions.model: An audience is likely to feel pity and anger in 4.2 because the victims are so clearly innocent. Lady Macduff’s bitterness at her husband, “He loves us not: / He wants the natural touch;” (4.2.10-11), sounds hurt rather than cruel, and her image of “the poor wren” fighting the owl to protect her young shows the instinct of a mother. Her playful talk with her son adds warmth, so the danger feels worse. When a messenger warns her she asks “Whither should I fly? / I have done no harm.” (4.2.81-82) The short questions show her helplessness, and the audience knows that innocence is no protection in Macbeth’s Scotland. The boy’s death, “He has kill’d me, mother:” (4.2.96-97), is brief and shocking. Many in the audience might feel this is the moment Macbeth loses any remaining sympathy.
checklist: Explains a likely audience response (pity, anger, shock)
Analyses Lady Macduff’s language about her husband
Uses the wren image as a sign of protective love
Comments on the son, the warning and the speed of the murder
Links the scene to how the audience now sees Macbeth
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners in 2025 called the “poor wren” image a key discriminator. Context is not assessed on Eduqas.

units.title: Act 5 Scenes 1 and 2: sleepwalking and desertion
units.summary: A Doctor and a Gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth sleepwalk, washing her hands and speaking in broken prose about the murders. Near Birnam Wood the Scottish lords say Macbeth’s title hangs on him like a giant’s robe.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “she has light by her continually; ’tis her command.” (5.1.24-25)
options: Seyton
The Doctor
Lady Macduff
The Gentlewoman
questions.explanation: The Gentlewoman explains why Lady Macbeth carries a light. The woman who once called on thick night now cannot bear the dark.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Lady Macbeth carries a light because she has light by her continually.
She speaks in verse throughout the sleepwalking scene.
The Gentlewoman refuses to repeat what Lady Macbeth has said, because she has no witness.
The Scottish lords plan to meet Malcolm’s army near Birnam Wood.

questions.explanation: Lady Macbeth speaks in broken prose. The Gentlewoman’s caution shows how dangerous it is to repeat secrets.

questions.prompt: Put these lines from the sleepwalking scene in the order Lady Macbeth says them.
items: “Out, damned spot! out, I say!”
“who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?”
“The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now?”
“all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.”
“What’s done cannot be undone.”
questions.explanation: Her mind jumps between murders: Duncan, Lady Macduff, then back to the blood that will not wash away.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth’s words: “Out, damned ___! out, I say!” (5.1.37)
questions.explanation: She rubs at a bloodstain only she can see, the guilt she once said a little water would clear.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth’s title does not fit him?
options: “now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant’s robe / Upon a dwarfish thief.” (5.2.23-25)
“Hell is murky!” (5.1.38)
“More needs she the divine than the physician.” (5.1.78)
“What’s done cannot be undone.” (5.1.71)
questions.explanation: The clothing image shows a man too small for the role he stole. It recalls the “borrow’d robes” of 1.3.

questions.prompt: Match each line from 5.1 to the earlier scene it echoes.
pairs: “Here’s the smell of the blood still:”
2.2, where she said a little water would clear them
3.2, where she said what is done is done
“Fie, my lord, fie! a soldier, and afeard?”
“The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now?”
questions.explanation: The scene replays her past in fragments, which shows guilt surfacing in sleep.

questions.prompt: In Holinshed, Macbeth’s wife is very ambitious and urges him on, but the source gives her little else. What does this tell us about the sleepwalking scene?
options: It is Shakespeare’s own addition, so her guilt and collapse are his choice
It is copied directly from Holinshed
It was written by Middleton
It comes from the history of the real Gruoch
questions.explanation: Comparing source and play shows Shakespeare giving Lady Macbeth a conscience and a tragic end.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Lady Macbeth kills herself on stage at the end of the sleepwalking scene.’ What is wrong?
options: Nothing
5.1 is her last appearance; her death is reported in 5.5, and Malcolm says only that it is thought she took her own life
She dies in 2.2
Macbeth kills her
questions.explanation: Her death happens offstage. Malcolm’s words “as ’tis thought” (5.8.83) mean her suicide is rumoured, not shown.
questions.misconception: Thinking Lady Macbeth’s death, or her suicide, is shown on stage.

questions.prompt: Why does Shakespeare give Lady Macbeth prose in the sleepwalking scene?
options: Because the scene is comic
Because she is a servant
Because the Doctor cannot understand verse
The broken prose shows a mind that has lost the control she once had in verse
questions.explanation: In Acts 1 and 2 she shaped every line; now her words come in fragments, jumping from one memory to another.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth’s guilt in 5.1? (8 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare shows guilt escaping from Lady Macbeth when she can no longer control it. She now has “light by her continually” (5.1.24-25), which is striking from the woman who once called on “thick night” to hide the murder. Her hands are the centre of the scene. “Out, damned spot! out, I say!” (5.1.37) turns her into someone giving orders to a stain that will not obey. Her earlier claim that “A little water clears us of this deed:” is reversed: “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.” (5.1.53-55) The word “little” returns, but now it shows how small and helpless she has become. Her broken prose jumps from Duncan’s blood to Lady Macduff, “The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now?” (5.1.44-45), which reveals guilt for a murder she did not plan. The Doctor’s verdict, “More needs she the divine than the physician.” (5.1.78), suggests her sickness is of the soul. An audience may feel pity as well as judgement.
checklist: Analyses the light and the reversal of the darkness imagery
Analyses the hand-washing and the “spot”
Links “little hand” to “a little water” in 2.2
Comments on the broken prose and the jumps between memories
Uses the Doctor’s view or the audience response (pity or judgement)
Uses precise quotations
questions.explanation: Strong answers show how the scene echoes Act 2, so guilt is presented as delayed, not avoided.

units.title: Act 5 Scenes 3 to 5: despair at Dunsinane
units.summary: Macbeth swings between defiance and despair as his followers desert him. Malcolm’s soldiers cut branches from Birnam Wood. When Seyton reports the Queen’s death, Macbeth reflects that life signifies nothing.

questions.prompt: Who says this, and to whom? “The devil damn thee black, thou cream-fac’d loon!” (5.3.12)
options: Malcolm, to a soldier
Seyton, to a messenger
Macbeth, to a frightened servant
Macduff, to Macbeth
questions.explanation: Macbeth turns his own fear into abuse of the servant who brings news of the English army.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth tells the Doctor to throw physic to the dogs.
Macbeth asks the Doctor whether he can cure a mind diseased.
Malcolm orders each soldier to cut down a branch and carry it.
When he hears that Birnam Wood is moving, Macbeth decides to stay inside the castle.

questions.explanation: He says “Arm, arm, and out!” and goes out to fight, choosing to die “with harness on our back”.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 5 Scenes 3 to 5 in order.
items: Macbeth insults the servant who brings news of the English army
Macbeth asks the Doctor to cure his wife’s troubled mind
Malcolm orders his soldiers to carry branches from Birnam Wood
Seyton reports that the Queen is dead
A Messenger reports that the wood seems to be moving
questions.explanation: Hope and despair alternate scene by scene, and the short scenes speed up the pace.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s image: “Life’s but a walking ___; a poor player,” (5.5.27)
questions.explanation: Life is pictured as a shadow and a bad actor, insubstantial and soon forgotten.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth knows what his crimes have cost him?
options: “I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d.” (5.3.38)
“As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends,” (5.3.29)
“Hang those that talk of fear.” (5.3.43)
“Throw physic to the dogs, I’ll none of it.” (5.3.58)
questions.explanation: He lists what should come with old age and admits he cannot have it.

questions.prompt: Match each line to the mood it shows.
pairs: “I have almost forgot the taste of fears.” (5.5.11)
“At least we’ll die with harness on our back.” (5.5.59)
questions.explanation: Macbeth’s moods swing quickly, which keeps both his courage and his emptiness in view.

questions.prompt: Holinshed gives Macbeth 10 years of just rule, and the real Macbeth’s reign was mostly peaceful. In 5.3 Macbeth admits he has lost “honour, love, obedience, troops of friends”. What does Shakespeare’s change add?
options: It makes Malcolm the villain
It shows Macbeth was always popular
Nothing: the play follows the history
Removing the good years makes his isolation the direct result of his crimes, which sharpens the tragedy
questions.explanation: Compression links each crime to its cost. By Act 5 the tyranny has emptied his life.

questions.prompt: AQA examiners in 2023 found that many students treated the 5.3 extract as Macbeth the fighter. What did they miss?
options: The comic tone of the scene
The Witches’ role in 5.3
Lady Macbeth’s speech in 5.3
Macbeth’s wider sense of despair at this point in the play
questions.explanation: The examiners said students should think carefully about where the extract comes from. His bravado sits beside lines such as “I have liv’d long enough:”.
questions.misconception: Reading an extract without placing it in the play.

questions.prompt: Which reading of “She should have died hereafter.” (5.5.20) is best supported by the speech that follows?
options: Her death has come at a time with no room to grieve; it leads him to feel that all time, and life itself, is meaningless
He thinks she is only pretending
Macbeth is relieved she is dead
He blames Seyton for her death
questions.explanation: “Hereafter” can mean later, when there would be time to grieve. The “Tomorrow” speech that follows supports a reading of exhaustion and emptiness.

questions.prompt: Explore how Shakespeare presents Macbeth’s state of mind in the “Tomorrow” soliloquy (5.5). (8 marks)
questions.model: The soliloquy shows a man for whom life has lost its meaning. The repetition of “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow,” (5.5.22) drags across the line, and the image of time that “Creeps in this petty pace” (5.5.23) makes the future feel slow and small. Life becomes theatre: “a poor player, / That struts and frets his hour upon the stage, / And then is heard no more:” (5.5.27-29). For a man who once acted out the part of a loyal subject and then of a king, the image is bitterly apt. The speech ends on a broken line, “Signifying nothing.” (5.5.31), as if the verse itself runs out. The trigger is his wife’s death, reported by Seyton, yet he does not mourn her directly. An audience may pity him, but may also see that his numbness is the result of his own choices: the man whose hair stood on end at a thought of murder now hears a cry of women without fear.
checklist: Analyses the repetition of “tomorrow” and the slow pace of time
Analyses the theatre image (player, stage)
Comments on form: soliloquy, broken final line
Links to Lady Macbeth’s reported death
Contrasts with his earlier fear or conscience
Offers a judgement on sympathy
questions.explanation: The best answers combine close analysis with a sense of where the speech sits in his fall.

units.title: Act 5 Scenes 6 to 8: the final battle
units.summary: Macbeth fights on, kills Young Siward and trusts the last prophecy until Macduff reveals his birth. In the Folio, Macbeth is killed on stage; Macduff brings in his head and hails Malcolm as king. Lady Macbeth’s death is reported, and her suicide is only rumoured.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Macduff was from his mother’s womb / Untimely ripp’d.” (5.8.19-20)
options: Malcolm, to Siward
Macduff, to Macbeth
Macbeth, to Macduff
Ross, to Malcolm
questions.explanation: Macduff was born by a cut from his mother’s womb, so he is not “of woman born” in the sense the prophecy meant.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth kills Young Siward.
Macbeth refuses to kill himself on his own sword.
Lady Macbeth’s death is shown on stage in Act 5.
In the Folio, Macbeth is killed on stage.

questions.explanation: Lady Macbeth dies offstage. Folger, following the Folio, has Macbeth slain on stage before Macduff returns with the head; some editions only show them leave fighting.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Act 5 Scenes 6 to 8 in order.
items: Malcolm’s soldiers throw down their branches
Macbeth kills Young Siward
Macbeth boasts that he bears a charmed life
Macduff reveals how he was born
Macduff brings in Macbeth’s head
Malcolm invites everyone to his coronation at Scone
questions.explanation: The final prophecy collapses moments before the fight that ends the play.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s boast: “I bear a ___ life, which must not yield / To one of woman born.” (5.8.15-16)
questions.explanation: He believes magic protects him. Macduff’s reply turns the boast into dramatic irony.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Malcolm’s final verdict on the Macbeths is one-sided?
options: “They have tied me to a stake. I cannot fly,” (5.7.1)
“this dead butcher, and his fiend-like queen,” (5.8.82)
“Turn, hell-hound, turn!” (5.8.4)
“Hail, King of Scotland!” (5.8.70)
questions.explanation: Malcolm’s labels leave out the conscience and suffering the audience has seen in both characters.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their fate at the end of the play.
pairs: killed by Macbeth in single combat
reported dead; her suicide is only rumoured
questions.explanation: The deaths come in quick succession, and Lady Macbeth’s is only reported.

questions.prompt: The real Macbeth was killed at the Battle of Lumphanan in 1057 by Duncan’s son Malcolm. In Holinshed, Macduff chases him and kills him. Why does it matter that Shakespeare follows Holinshed here?
options: It makes Malcolm a coward
It gives the final fight to the man whose family Macbeth murdered, so the ending feels like justice
It removes Macduff from the play
It means the play ends in England
questions.explanation: Macduff’s personal loss gives the climax its force. The history shows the choice was a dramatic one.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘At the end of the play Lady Macbeth stabs herself in front of Macbeth.’ Which correction is accurate?
options: Correct
She is still alive at the end
She is killed by Macduff
Her death happens offstage; Seyton reports it in 5.5, and Malcolm says she took her own life only “as ’tis thought”
questions.explanation: Malcolm says: “Who, as ’tis thought, by self and violent hands / Took off her life;” (5.8.83-84). The suicide is a report, not something the audience sees.
questions.misconception: Presenting Lady Macbeth’s suicide as fact or as shown on stage.

questions.prompt: Why might Shakespeare end the play with Macduff carrying Macbeth’s head?
options: To echo the start, when Macbeth fixed Macdonwald’s head on the battlements, so the traitor’s fate returns to him
Because Macbeth asked for it
Because the Witches predicted it
To show Macduff is the new king
questions.explanation: The structure comes full circle. The hero who beheaded a rebel is now displayed as a traitor.

questions.prompt: How far does the ending of the play restore order? Consider Macbeth’s death and Malcolm’s final speech. (8 marks)
questions.model: The ending restores order to a large extent, but Shakespeare leaves some questions open. Macbeth’s last stand has courage: he refuses to “play the Roman fool” (5.8.1) and, even after learning Macduff’s birth, will not yield, crying “lay on, Macduff;” (5.8.38). The audience may feel a flicker of the old admiration. Macduff then enters with “Th’ usurper’s cursed head:” (5.8.66), an image that echoes Macdonwald’s head in 1.2, and hails Malcolm as king. Malcolm’s speech sounds orderly: he rewards his thanes and promises to act “in measure, time, and place.” (5.8.86), the rhyming couplet giving a sense of completion. Yet his verdict on “this dead butcher, and his fiend-like queen,” (5.8.82) flattens characters the audience has watched suffer, and Lady Macbeth’s death is left uncertain, “as ’tis thought”. Order returns to Scotland, but the audience knows more than the new king says.
checklist: Uses Macbeth’s final defiance and judges its effect
Analyses the head as an echo of 1.2 (structure)
Analyses Malcolm’s language of order (measure, time, place; rhyme)
Questions Malcolm’s one-sided verdict
Presents Lady Macbeth’s death as reported and rumoured
Reaches a clear judgement on “how far”
questions.explanation: A “how far” answer needs a clear position with evidence on both sides.

units.title: Macbeth (1): from hero to murderer
units.summary: Macbeth begins as a celebrated warrior, but the thought of murder comes to him almost as soon as the Witches speak. Track his conscience, his ambition and his wife’s influence through Acts 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: Who says this about Macbeth? “O valiant cousin! worthy gentleman!” (1.2.26)
options: Banquo
Duncan
Ross
Malcolm
questions.explanation: Duncan praises Macbeth after the Captain’s report. “Cousin” reminds us they are related, which makes the later murder a betrayal of family.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The Captain calls him “brave Macbeth”.
Macbeth’s letter calls his wife “my dearest partner of greatness”.
In 1.7 Macbeth hesitates mainly because he is afraid of the Witches.
Macbeth kills Duncan’s grooms the morning after the murder.

questions.explanation: In 1.7 he weighs judgement, his duties as kinsman, subject and host, and Duncan’s goodness. The Witches are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of Macbeth’s path in Acts 1 and 2 in order.
items: The Captain praises his courage in battle
In an aside he is terrified by a “horrid image” of murder
He asks the stars to hide his “black and deep desires”
He tells his wife they will proceed no further
He sees a dagger leading him to Duncan’s room
He cannot say “Amen” after the murder
questions.explanation: The order shows a man who is tempted early, resists, and then acts against his own conscience.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s aside: “Stars, hide your fires! / Let not light see my black and deep ___.” (1.4.57-58)
questions.explanation: The desires are his own. This line matters whenever you discuss how far his wife is to blame.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth’s conscience is working before the murder?
options: “For brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name),” (1.2.18)
“’Twas a rough night.” (2.3.70)
“Who can be wise, amaz’d, temperate, and furious,” (2.3.127)
“why do I yield to that suggestion / Whose horrid image doth unfix my hair,” (1.3.147-148)
questions.explanation: His body reacts with horror: hair standing on end. Conscience and ambition are both present from the start.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to what it shows about Macbeth.
pairs: “I have bought / Golden opinions from all sorts of people,” (1.7.35-36)
“My thought, whose murder yet is but fantastical,” (1.3.152)
the murder is still only imagined
“A dagger of the mind, a false creation,” (2.1.50)
his mind is overheated by what he plans
“To know my deed, ’twere best not know myself.” (2.2.93)
he cannot live with the man he has become
questions.explanation: Each quotation marks a different point on his path from temptation to guilt.

questions.prompt: In Holinshed, Banquo helps Macbeth kill the king. In the play, Banquo hears the same prophecy but does nothing. How does this change affect our view of Macbeth?
options: It makes Macbeth’s choice look entirely his own, since another man faces the same temptation and resists
It shows the prophecy forces Macbeth to act
It makes Banquo the real villain
It has no effect on Macbeth
questions.explanation: Banquo becomes a foil. The comparison makes Macbeth’s responsibility clearer.

questions.prompt: A student argues: ‘Macbeth is a good man who is forced into murder by his wife.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: It is wrong because the Witches order the murder
It is wrong because Lady Macbeth never speaks to him about Duncan
Fully correct: he has no thoughts of murder before she speaks
It ignores the evidence that Macbeth imagines murder in 1.3 and admits his “black and deep desires” in 1.4, before he sees her
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners in 2024 criticised answers that blamed almost everything on Lady Macbeth and ignored Macbeth’s own early thoughts.
questions.misconception: Blaming Lady Macbeth for everything Macbeth does.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Macbeth at the start of the play is most precise?
options: He is a hero whose violence is praised because it serves the king, and whose thoughts turn to murder almost at once
He is a coward praised by mistake
He is already a known traitor
He is a gentle man who dislikes fighting
questions.explanation: Precision matters: the play presents both the public hero and the private temptation.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth’s change from hero to murderer in Acts 1 and 2? (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare first shows Macbeth through other people’s praise. The Captain calls him “brave Macbeth” and Duncan greets him as “O valiant cousin! worthy gentleman!” (1.2.26), so the audience meets a loyal warrior. Yet as soon as the Witches speak, his asides reveal a different man. He is horrified by the “horrid image” (1.3.148) of murder, and by 1.4 he asks the stars to hide “my black and deep desires.” (1.4.58) The possessive “my” matters: these desires belong to him.

Shakespeare also shows him resisting. In 1.7 he lists every reason against the deed and tells his wife “We will proceed no further in this business:” (1.7.34). It is her persuasion, and his fear of being thought a coward, that tips him. After the murder the hero has gone. He cannot say “Amen”, he fears that every noise appals him, and he admits “To know my deed, ’twere best not know myself.” (2.2.93) The change is quick, but Shakespeare shows that it was prepared in Macbeth’s own thoughts from the first act.
checklist: Uses others’ praise to show his heroic reputation
Analyses the asides and “black and deep desires”
Shows his resistance in 1.7
Explains the role of Lady Macbeth without blaming her for everything
Analyses his guilt after the murder
Shapes the answer as a change across Acts 1 and 2
questions.explanation: A strong answer has a clear line of argument about why he changes.

units.title: Macbeth (2): tyrant and tragic hero
units.summary: As king, Macbeth kills to feel safe: Banquo, then Macduff’s family. By Act 5 he has lost friends, fear and meaning, yet he dies fighting. Weigh the “dead butcher” against the tragic hero.

questions.prompt: Who says this about Macbeth? “Those he commands move only in command, / Nothing in love:” (5.2.22-23)
options: Macduff
Lennox
Malcolm
Angus
questions.explanation: Angus describes a king obeyed through fear. Compare Duncan, whose thanes loved him.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth hires murderers to kill Banquo and Fleance.
Macbeth orders the killing of Macduff’s wife and children.
At the end Macbeth surrenders to Malcolm.
Even after Birnam Wood moves, Macbeth still trusts that no man of woman born can harm him.

questions.explanation: He refuses to “kiss the ground before young Malcolm’s feet” and fights to the death.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Macbeth’s reign in order.
items: Banquo is murdered
Banquo’s ghost appears at the banquet
Macbeth visits the Witches
Macduff’s family is murdered
Macbeth hears of his wife’s death
Macduff kills Macbeth
questions.explanation: Each murder leads to the next. Shakespeare shows violence growing from insecurity.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s line: “Things bad begun make strong themselves by ___.” (3.2.62)
questions.explanation: He believes more evil will secure what evil began. The rhyming couplet makes it sound like a rule he lives by.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that by Act 5 Macbeth has lost the capacity to feel fear?
options: “Our fears in Banquo / Stick deep,” (3.1.53-54)
“I have almost forgot the taste of fears.” (5.5.11)
“But now I am cabin’d, cribb’d, confin’d,” (3.4.26)
“O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!” (3.2.41)
questions.explanation: Fear once filled his mind; now it has almost gone. The numbness is a kind of punishment.

questions.prompt: Match each description of Macbeth to the character who uses it.
questions.explanation: By Act 5 everyone names him a villain. The audience has seen more of him than they have.

questions.prompt: Macduff displays “Th’ usurper’s cursed head:” (5.8.66). Which context explains why the word usurper carries such weight?
options: The belief that a rightful king’s authority comes from God, so a man who seizes the crown by murder has no true right to it
The North Berwick witch trials
The Globe Theatre’s location
The fact that Macbeth was first printed in 1623
questions.explanation: King James argued that kings rule by divine right. A usurper breaks the order God is believed to have set.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘By the end Macbeth is a pure monster with no human feeling left.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: It is too simple: he grieves for the “honour, love, obedience, troops of friends” he has lost, reflects on life’s meaning and still shows courage
It is wrong because he becomes kind again
Correct: there is no sign of feeling in Act 5
It is wrong because he never kills anyone after Act 2
questions.explanation: Shakespeare keeps Macbeth complex to the end. That complexity is why he can be called a tragic hero.
questions.misconception: Reducing Macbeth in Act 5 to a one-dimensional monster.

questions.prompt: Which reading of Macbeth’s final fight is best supported by the text?
options: He fights because Lady Macbeth told him to
He fights because he believes he will win
He does not fight at all
He fights knowing he will lose, refusing to yield or to die “the Roman fool”: a last flash of the courage he showed in 1.2
questions.explanation: After Macduff’s revelation he knows the prophecy has failed, yet says “lay on, Macduff;” (5.8.38).

questions.prompt: Malcolm calls Macbeth “this dead butcher” (5.8.82). How far do you agree with this view of Macbeth in Acts 3 to 5? (8 marks)
questions.model:
Malcolm’s verdict is supported by much of what Macbeth does after becoming king. He hires murderers for Banquo, telling himself “Things bad begun make strong themselves by ill.” (3.2.62), and after the apparitions he decides that “The very firstlings of my heart shall be / The firstlings of my hand.” (4.1.167-168) The murder of Macduff’s wife and children has no purpose except fear, and here “butcher” seems exact.

Yet the audience sees more than Malcolm does. Macbeth suffers: his mind is “full of scorpions” (3.2.41), and in 5.3 he mourns the “honour, love, obedience, troops of friends,” (5.3.29) he will never have. The “Tomorrow” speech shows a man who understands the emptiness he has made. At the end he refuses to yield, fighting with the courage that first made him a hero. So “butcher” describes his actions, but not his whole self; Shakespeare asks us to judge him and also to see what has been lost.
checklist: Takes a clear position on “how far”
Uses evidence of violence in Acts 3 and 4 (Banquo, Macduff’s family)
Uses evidence of suffering or self-awareness (scorpions, 5.3, “Tomorrow”)
Considers the final fight and courage
Notes that the verdict is Malcolm’s, not necessarily Shakespeare’s
Uses accurate references
questions.explanation: The best answers keep both views in play and decide between them.

units.title: Lady Macbeth (1): power and persuasion
units.summary: Lady Macbeth decides on murder the moment she reads the letter. She calls on spirits for cruelty, controls the plan and the murder night, and uses her husband’s pride in his courage against him.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Leave all the rest to me.” (1.5.86)
options: Hecate
Lady Macbeth
Macbeth
Lady Macduff
questions.explanation: Her last line in 1.5 shows her taking charge of the plan.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Lady Macbeth calls on spirits to fill her with cruelty before Macbeth returns.
She plans to make Duncan’s chamberlains drunk.
She stabs Duncan herself.
She takes the daggers back to Duncan’s room.

questions.explanation: She says she would have killed Duncan had he not resembled her father as he slept. Macbeth commits the murder.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from Acts 1 and 2 in order.
items: She reads Macbeth’s letter
She calls on spirits to unsex her
She tells Macbeth to look like the innocent flower
She attacks his courage when he wants to stop
She takes the daggers from him
questions.explanation: Her control grows scene by scene until the murder night.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth’s command: “Come, you spirits / That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me ___,” (1.5.47-48)
questions.explanation: She asks to be stripped of what she links with womanhood so that nothing can stop her.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Lady Macbeth takes control of the plan?
options: “Out, damned spot! out, I say!” (5.1.37)
“Leave all the rest to me.” (1.5.86)
“My hands are of your color, but I shame” (2.2.82)
“Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6)
questions.explanation: A short, plain line, and the planning is hers. Later quotations show her losing that control.

questions.prompt: Match each method to an example of Lady Macbeth’s language.
pairs: Command to the powers of darkness
“Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dress’d yourself?” (1.7.39-40)
“look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t.” (1.5.76-78)
questions.explanation: Naming the method is the first step; the marks come from explaining what each does to Macbeth and the audience.

questions.prompt: James VI’s Daemonologie claimed that women were the “frailer” sex. How could an AQA answer use this briefly?
options: To prove that Lady Macbeth is a witch
To suggest that Lady Macbeth’s strength in Act 1 would have seemed especially unsettling, in 1 linked sentence
As a separate paragraph at the end of the essay
To show that every Jacobean woman was weak
questions.explanation: AQA rewards context woven into an argument. Avoid sweeping claims about what all women were like.

questions.prompt: A student argues that Lady Macbeth’s line “I have given suck,” (1.7.62) proves she lost a baby before the play, and builds the whole essay on this. What would an examiner say?
options: This is the best possible argument
The line proves she has living children
The line is spoken by Lady Macduff
The play never explains the child; Eduqas examiners in 2024 said arguments resting on a lost baby tended to lead to underachievement
questions.explanation: Stay with what the text shows: the image is designed to shock Macbeth into action.
questions.misconception: Building an argument on events the play does not show.

questions.prompt: Lady Macbeth calls on spirits to give her cruelty. Which reading of this is most thoughtful?
options: Her need to call for cruelty may suggest it does not come naturally, which prepares for her collapse in Act 5
She is joking
She is already a witch
She is talking to the Witches in person
questions.explanation: Strong answers notice what her words imply about her as well as what they ask for.

questions.prompt: AQA-style: How far does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth as a powerful woman in Acts 1 and 2? (8 marks)
questions.model:
In Acts 1 and 2 Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as powerful to a great extent, though there are hints of the limits of that power. She decides on murder before her husband returns and commands the spirits, “Come, you spirits / That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here,” (1.5.47-48), as if the forces of darkness must obey her. She controls Macbeth too: when he says they will stop, she asks “Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dress’d yourself?” (1.7.39-40) and turns his courage into the test he must pass. On the murder night she is the one who acts, snapping “Infirm of purpose! / Give me the daggers.” (2.2.68-69)

Yet her power has gaps. She needs drink to make her “bold” (2.2.2), and she could not kill Duncan because he “resembled / My father as he slept,” (2.2.16-17). Her strength depends on her husband doing the deed. So she is powerful in will and words, but the play quietly shows that she cannot act against her own feelings, which prepares for her breakdown.
checklist: Takes a clear position on “how far”
Analyses her invocation of the spirits
Analyses her persuasion in 1.7
Shows her control on the murder night
Explores limits: drink, her father’s likeness
Context, if used, is brief and linked (AQA)
questions.explanation: A powerful-woman question rewards answers that weigh strength against limits.

units.title: Lady Macbeth (2): guilt and interpretations
units.summary: After the murder Lady Macbeth is shut out of her husband’s plans, covers for him at the banquet, and finally relives the murders in her sleep. Her death is reported offstage, and Malcolm says she killed herself only “as ’tis thought”.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Naught’s had, all’s spent, / Where our desire is got without content:” (3.2.6-7)
options: Macbeth, to the murderers
Lady Macbeth, alone
Lady Macduff, to her son
Banquo, alone
questions.explanation: Alone at the start of 3.2, she admits the crown has brought no contentment.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth does not tell her about his plan to kill Banquo.
At the banquet she sends the guests away when Macbeth sees the Ghost again.
In 5.1 she speaks in verse.
Her death is shown on stage.

questions.explanation: She speaks in broken prose in 5.1, and her death is reported by Seyton in 5.5.

questions.prompt: Put these moments in order.
items: She says “Naught’s had, all’s spent”
She covers for Macbeth at the banquet
She tells him he lacks the season of all natures, sleep
She sleepwalks, watched by the Doctor and Gentlewoman
Seyton reports that the Queen is dead
Malcolm calls her a fiend-like queen
questions.explanation: Her decline is gradual: shut out, protective, exhausted, then broken.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth’s words in 5.1: “all the perfumes of ___ will not sweeten this little hand.” (5.1.53-55)
questions.explanation: The richest perfumes in the world cannot cover the smell of guilt.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that her guilt includes a murder she did not plan?
options: “A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86)
“Are you a man?” (3.4.70)
“Leave all the rest to me.” (1.5.86)
“The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now?” (5.1.44-45)
questions.explanation: Macbeth kept her “innocent of the knowledge”, yet Lady Macduff’s death haunts her too.

questions.prompt: Match each view of Lady Macbeth to a piece of evidence that supports it.
pairs: she calls on spirits to fill her with direst cruelty
she could not kill Duncan because he looked like her father
She is shut out by her husband
he calls her dearest chuck but hides Banquo’s murder
she washes her hands in her sleep
questions.explanation: Strong answers hold more than one view and weigh the evidence.

questions.prompt: Holinshed’s account of Macbeth’s wife says she was very ambitious and urged him on, and gives her little else. What does the comparison suggest?
options: Shakespeare added her guilt, decline and sleepwalking, so her tragic arc is his invention
Holinshed makes her the main character
Holinshed shows her death on stage
Shakespeare copied her sleepwalking from Holinshed
questions.explanation: Giving her a conscience and a fall is one of Shakespeare’s biggest choices.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Shakespeare tells us Lady Macbeth is a “fiend-like queen”.’ What is the problem?
options: It is Malcolm’s judgement, spoken by her enemy at the end; it is not necessarily Shakespeare’s view
The phrase is not in the play
The phrase describes Hecate
The phrase is from Holinshed
questions.explanation: Always say who speaks a line. The audience has seen her suffering, which Malcolm has not.
questions.misconception: Treating a character’s judgement as the author’s verdict.

questions.prompt: OCR’s 2024 discursive question asked how far Shakespeare encourages pity for Lady Macbeth, using at least 2 moments. Which plan is strongest?
options: Write only about Macbeth’s guilt
Contrast her cruelty in 1.5 with her isolation in 3.2 and her suffering in 5.1, then decide how far pity outweighs judgement
List every quotation by Lady Macbeth
Retell the whole plot from 1.5 to 5.5
questions.explanation: The discursive question needs a few moments explored in depth and a clear judgement.

questions.prompt: To what extent does Shakespeare encourage the audience to feel pity for Lady Macbeth? Explore at least 2 moments. (8 marks)
questions.model:
At first Shakespeare gives the audience little reason to pity Lady Macbeth. She calls on spirits to fill her “top-full / Of direst cruelty!” (1.5.49-50) and mocks her husband’s fears. Yet pity grows as her power fades. In 3.2 she sits alone and admits “Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6), and then hears her husband call her “dearest chuck” while he hides Banquo’s murder from her. The woman who led the plan has been shut out of it.

By 5.1 pity is strong. She carries a light and rubs her hands, crying “Out, damned spot!” (5.1.37); her broken prose jumps from Duncan to “The Thane of Fife had a wife.” (5.1.44), guilt for a murder she never planned. Her death is only reported, and Malcolm says she took her own life “as ’tis thought” (5.8.83), so even her end is left to rumour. An audience may still judge her for Act 1, but Shakespeare makes her suffering so private and so human that pity outweighs judgement by the end.
checklist: Takes a clear position on “to what extent”
Uses Act 1 evidence of cruelty to show the case against pity
Analyses her isolation in 3.2
Analyses the sleepwalking scene
Presents her death as reported and her suicide as rumoured
Explores at least 2 moments in depth
questions.explanation: OCR rewards a sustained, personal judgement backed by close analysis.

units.title: Banquo and Fleance
units.summary: Banquo hears a prophecy too, but he distrusts the Witches and prays against “cursed thoughts”. He suspects Macbeth yet stays silent. His murder and Fleance’s escape keep the prophecy of his descendants alive.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Merciful powers, / Restrain in me the cursed thoughts that nature / Gives way to in repose!” (2.1.9-11)
options: Fleance
Macbeth
Duncan
Banquo
questions.explanation: Banquo is tempted in his dreams, but he prays against it. Macbeth follows a dagger instead.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Banquo notices that Macbeth starts with fear at the Witches’ greeting.
Banquo tells Duncan about the Witches’ prophecy.
In 3.1 Banquo suspects that Macbeth played foully for the crown.
Fleance escapes from the murderers.

questions.explanation: Banquo keeps his suspicion to himself, which can be read as caution or as a quiet failure to act.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from Banquo’s part in order.
items: He questions whether the Witches are women
He warns that instruments of darkness tell truths to betray
He admits he dreamt of the Witches
He suspects Macbeth in a soliloquy
He is killed and Fleance escapes
His ghost appears at the banquet
questions.explanation: Banquo moves from questioning to warning to suspicion, and his presence continues after death.

questions.prompt: Complete Banquo’s words to the Witches: “You should be women, / And yet your ___ forbid me to interpret / That you are so.” (1.3.47-49)
questions.explanation: From the first meeting Banquo notices that the Witches are not what they seem.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Banquo is wary of the Witches from the start?
options: “In the great hand of God I stand;” (2.3.152)
“There’s husbandry in heaven;” (2.1.6)
“O, treachery! Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly!” (3.3.25)
“And oftentimes to win us to our harm, / The instruments of darkness tell us truths;” (1.3.135-136)
questions.explanation: He understands at once what Macbeth learns only in Act 5: small truths can lead to great harm.

questions.prompt: Match each moment to Banquo’s response.
pairs: he challenges them and questions what they are
he notices it and points it out to the others
His dream of the Witches in 2.1
he prays to be spared cursed thoughts
he suspects foul play but keeps silent
questions.explanation: Banquo is a foil: each response contrasts with what Macbeth does.

questions.prompt: King James traced his family line back to Banquo. In Holinshed, Banquo helps kill the king. Why might this context matter to the way Shakespeare writes Banquo?
options: It shows that Banquo was a real Scottish king
It explains why Banquo dies in Act 1
It may explain why Banquo becomes innocent in the play, as the ancestor of the reigning king
It proves Shakespeare met King James
questions.explanation: Present the link as a likely reason, not a certainty, and use it in 1 sentence.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Banquo is perfectly good and has no flaws.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: Banquo murders Duncan
Banquo works with the Witches
It overlooks that he suspects Macbeth yet says nothing, and hopes the prophecies may also be his oracles
Correct
questions.explanation: In 3.1 he asks, “May they not be my oracles as well,” (3.1.9). He is tempted, but he does not act.
questions.misconception: Treating Banquo as flawless rather than tempted but restrained.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2018 question asked about the attitudes of Macbeth and Banquo towards the supernatural. Why is a comparison of the 2 men rewarding?
options: Because they both see the dagger
Because they react to the same prophecy in opposite ways, which shows that the choice is Macbeth’s
Because they never meet
Because Banquo is the main character
questions.explanation: Examiners describe contrasts and foils as a very rewarding area.

questions.prompt: Compare the attitudes of Macbeth and Banquo towards the supernatural. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Both men hear the Witches’ prophecies, but Shakespeare makes their attitudes opposite. Banquo is sceptical from the start. He notices that the Witches “should be women, / And yet your beards forbid me to interpret / That you are so.” (1.3.47-49), and when the first prophecy comes true he warns that “The instruments of darkness tell us truths;” (1.3.136) in order to betray. Macbeth, by contrast, is “rapt”, and his asides show that he takes the prophecy as a promise: “Two truths are told,” (1.3.140).

The contrast continues. Banquo dreams of the Witches but prays to be spared “the cursed thoughts that nature / Gives way to in repose!” (2.1.10-11); Macbeth follows a dagger to Duncan’s room. Yet Banquo is not untouched: in 3.1 he wonders whether the prophecies may be his oracles too. Shakespeare shows that the supernatural tempts both men equally. What differs is the choice each makes, which places responsibility on Macbeth.
checklist: Compares their first reactions in 1.3
Analyses Banquo’s warning about “instruments of darkness”
Uses Macbeth’s asides, such as “Two truths are told,”
Contrasts Banquo’s prayer in 2.1 with the dagger
Notes Banquo’s own temptation in 3.1
Reaches a judgement about choice and responsibility
questions.explanation: Comparison should run through the answer, not sit in 2 separate halves.

units.title: The Witches and Hecate
units.summary: The Witches speak in riddles, chants and paradoxes. They tell truths that mislead, but never order Macbeth to kill. Hecate, who may be a later addition, plans to destroy him through over-confidence.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “All hail, Macbeth! that shalt be king hereafter!” (1.3.53)
options: Banquo
Hecate
The Third Witch
The First Witch
questions.explanation: The Third Witch gives the greatest prophecy last, building to a climax.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The Witches tell Macbeth that he must murder Duncan.
The First Witch hails Banquo as “Lesser than Macbeth, and greater.”
Hecate appears in 3.5.
The Witches vanish in 1.3 when Macbeth asks them to stay.

questions.explanation: The Witches never mention murder. That idea comes from Macbeth.

questions.prompt: Put these appearances of the supernatural in order.
items: The Witches meet in thunder and lightning
The Witches hail Macbeth and Banquo on the heath
Hecate scolds the Witches
The apparitions appear from the cauldron
questions.explanation: 1.1, 1.3, 3.5 and 4.1. The Witches appear far less than students often think.

questions.prompt: Complete the Witches’ chant: “Double, double, toil and ___; / Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble.” (4.1.10-11)
questions.explanation: The short, rhyming lines in a falling rhythm set the Witches apart from the human characters’ blank verse.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that the Witches speak in riddles that are hard to interpret?
options: “Look, how our partner’s rapt.” (1.3.156)
“Lesser than Macbeth, and greater.” (1.3.68)
“This castle hath a pleasant seat.” (1.6.1)
“Thou hast it now, King, Cawdor, Glamis, all,” (3.1.1)
questions.explanation: Banquo will be lower than Macbeth in rank but greater in goodness or in descendants. The riddle has more than one meaning.

questions.prompt: Match each line to the language feature it shows best.
pairs: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair:” (1.1.12)
“Though his bark cannot be lost, / Yet it shall be tempest-tost.” (1.3.25-26)
questions.explanation: Identify the feature, then say what it does: confusion, ritual, double meaning, the sound of a spell.

questions.prompt: Holinshed calls the women the weird sisters and suggests they might be goddesses of destiny or fairies. What does Shakespeare do with this uncertainty?
options: He makes them definitely goddesses
He keeps it: his Witches are never fully explained
He cuts them from the play
He removes it by making them ordinary village women
questions.explanation: The uncertainty lets each audience decide how much power they have, which is why they still unsettle.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The Witches control Macbeth like a puppet and make him kill Duncan.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: The Witches kill Duncan themselves
The Witches tell Lady Macbeth to kill Duncan
Correct
The Witches only speak; they never tell him to kill, and Banquo hears prophecies too but does not act
questions.explanation: Weighing what the Witches do against what they do not do leads to a more precise argument.
questions.misconception: Claiming the Witches force Macbeth to murder.

questions.prompt: Edexcel’s 2025 feedback on the Witches extract said similes and repetition were often only identified. Which comment would earn more AO2 credit?
options: The Witches use lots of techniques.
The repetition in “Double, double” sounds like a chant being cast, so the audience hears the spell take shape as it is spoken.
This is a simile because it uses “like”.
There is repetition in this extract.
questions.explanation: Stronger answers explain the effect of the method. The examiners also praised discussion of the rhythm of the Witches’ lines.

questions.prompt: Edexcel part (a)-style: Explore how Shakespeare presents the Witches in 1.3. Refer closely to language, form and structure. (8 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare presents the Witches as powerful but limited. Their language sounds like ritual: the First Witch’s revenge on the sailor ends in a rhyme, “Though his bark cannot be lost, / Yet it shall be tempest-tost.” (1.3.25-26), which closes the curse like a spell. Yet the meaning admits a limit: they can torment, not destroy. Their greetings to Macbeth build in a structured pattern, Glamis, Cawdor, then “All hail, Macbeth! that shalt be king hereafter!” (1.3.53), so the most dangerous promise comes last and lands hardest. To Banquo they speak in riddles, “Lesser than Macbeth, and greater.” (1.3.68), so their words need interpreting, and interpretation is where the danger lies. Banquo notices that they look like women yet have beards, so their very appearance is a paradox. Finally they vanish, leaving Macbeth to decide what to do with their words.
checklist: Analyses the rhyme or rhythm of their speech (form)
Analyses the order of the greetings (structure)
Analyses riddles or paradox (language)
Uses Banquo’s view of their appearance
Comments on the limits of their power
No context: part (a) assesses AO2 only
questions.explanation: Edexcel part (a) rewards analysis of language, form and structure together; context earns nothing there.

units.title: Duncan and Malcolm
units.summary: Duncan is a generous, trusting king whose trust is betrayed; Malcolm is cautious and tests loyalty before he trusts. Between them stands the tyrant, and the contrast defines good kingship.

questions.prompt: Who says this to Macbeth? “I have begun to plant thee, and will labour / To make thee full of growing.” (1.4.32-33)
options: Malcolm
Banquo
Duncan
Ross
questions.explanation: Duncan’s image of planting and growth makes kingship a kind of care. Macbeth’s reign is full of barren images instead.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Duncan names Malcolm as his heir.
Malcolm flees to England after the murder.
Malcolm really is more wicked than Macbeth, as he tells Macduff.
Malcolm orders his soldiers to carry branches from Birnam Wood.

questions.explanation: Malcolm’s confession of vices is a test. His later orders show practical leadership.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from Malcolm’s part in order.
items: He reports how Cawdor died
Duncan names him Prince of Cumberland
He flees to England
He tests Macduff’s loyalty
He orders the branches to be cut
He invites all to his coronation at Scone
questions.explanation: Malcolm grows from a young prince into a cautious, capable king.

questions.prompt: Complete Malcolm’s list: “the king-becoming graces, / As justice, verity, temp’rance, ___,” (4.3.107-108)
questions.explanation: The list sets out the qualities a good king needs, all of which Macbeth lacks.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Duncan rewards loyalty generously?
options: “Dispute it like a man.” (4.3.259)
“This tyrant, whose sole name blisters our tongues,” (4.3.14)
“I have begun to plant thee, and will labour / To make thee full of growing.” (1.4.32-33)
“There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face:” (1.4.13-14)
questions.explanation: The planting image promises growth and future reward.

questions.prompt: Match each image or quality to the king it describes.
questions.explanation: Fertile and holy images belong to good kings; barren ones to the usurper.

questions.prompt: In Holinshed, Duncan is a soft king whose slackness lets rebels flourish; the real Duncan was about 39 and died in battle. What does Shakespeare gain by making Duncan old, gracious and trusting?
options: The murder becomes the destruction of a good king, so Macbeth’s crime is darker
It makes Malcolm unnecessary
It follows Holinshed exactly
Duncan becomes a weak villain
questions.explanation: Every change to Duncan makes the regicide more shocking.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘After Duncan dies, Malcolm becomes king straight away.’ What is wrong?
options: Banquo becomes king
Donalbain becomes king
Malcolm flees, Macbeth is crowned at Scone, and Malcolm becomes king only at the end of the play
Nothing
questions.explanation: Malcolm’s flight makes him look guilty and lets Macbeth take the throne.
questions.misconception: Misremembering the succession after Duncan’s murder.

questions.prompt: Why is Malcolm’s caution in 4.3 a good quality in a king?
options: It shows he trusts nobody ever again
It shows he wants Macduff to leave
It shows he has learned from his father’s misplaced trust and will test loyalty before giving it
It shows he is a coward
questions.explanation: Duncan said there is no art to read the mind in the face. Malcolm finds a way to test what lies behind it.

questions.prompt: Compare how Shakespeare presents Duncan and Malcolm as kings, and how each contrasts with Macbeth. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare uses Duncan and Malcolm to frame Macbeth with images of rightful kingship. Duncan rules through generosity: he promises Macbeth “I have begun to plant thee, and will labour / To make thee full of growing.” (1.4.32-33). His weakness is trust. Of the traitor Cawdor he admits “There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face:” (1.4.13-14), and then trusts Macbeth just as completely. Malcolm learns from this. In 4.3 he tests Macduff before trusting him, and lists the “king-becoming graces” (4.3.107) a ruler needs. He ends the play promising to act “by the grace of Grace” (5.8.85).

Macbeth stands between them as the opposite. Where Duncan plants, Macbeth complains of a “fruitless crown” (3.1.66); where Malcolm’s subjects follow willingly, Macbeth’s “move only in command, / Nothing in love:” (5.2.22-23). The contrast suggests that true kingship depends on care and legitimacy, which murder can never supply.
checklist: Analyses Duncan’s generosity (planting image)
Shows Duncan’s misplaced trust
Shows Malcolm’s caution and the king-becoming graces
Contrasts both with Macbeth’s barren or fearful rule
Brief, relevant context on rightful kingship (optional)
Clear comparison throughout
questions.explanation: Organise the answer around qualities of kingship, not character by character.

units.title: Macduff and Lady Macduff
units.summary: Macduff discovers the murder, refuses to attend the coronation and leaves for England. His wife and children pay the price. His grief shows a manhood that includes feeling, and he becomes the man who kills Macbeth.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “O horror, horror, horror! / Tongue nor heart cannot conceive nor name thee!” (2.3.73-74)
options: Macbeth
Macduff
Banquo
Lennox
questions.explanation: Macduff’s discovery of Duncan’s body is the first time we hear his voice at full strength.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macduff does not go to Scone for Macbeth’s coronation.
Lady Macduff understands and accepts why her husband has left.
Macduff was born by being cut from his mother’s womb.
Macduff kills Macbeth.

questions.explanation: Lady Macduff feels betrayed: “He loves us not:” (4.2.10).

questions.prompt: Put these moments from the Macduffs’ story in order.
items: Macduff discovers Duncan’s body
Macduff goes to Fife instead of Scone
Lady Macduff tells her son his father is dead
Murderers attack Macduff’s family
Ross tells Macduff the news in England
Macduff reveals how he was born
questions.explanation: Macduff’s family suffers in the gap between his decision to leave and his return.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macduff’s image: “for the poor ___, / The most diminutive of birds, will fight, / Her young ones in her nest, against the owl.” (4.2.11-13)
questions.explanation: Even the smallest bird protects its young, so she implies her husband has failed his.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macduff puts Scotland before himself?
options: “Tyrant, show thy face!” (5.7.19)
“Turn, hell-hound, turn!” (5.8.4)
“O horror, horror, horror!” (2.3.73)
“Bleed, bleed, poor country!” (4.3.39)
questions.explanation: In 4.3 Macduff despairs for Scotland as a wounded body, which convinces Malcolm he is loyal.

questions.prompt: Match each line to who says it.
pairs: “But I must also feel it as a man:” (4.3.261)
“Be this the whetstone of your sword.” (4.3.268)
questions.explanation: Malcolm wants grief turned into anger; Macduff insists on feeling it first.

questions.prompt: In Holinshed, Macduff pursues Macbeth and kills him; the real Macbeth was killed by Duncan’s son Malcolm. Why does it suit the play for Macduff to kill Macbeth?
options: Holinshed’s Malcolm dies first
Macduff is the rightful king
The man whose family was murdered brings justice, which gives the climax personal force
Malcolm is too young to fight
questions.explanation: Shakespeare follows his source here because it ties the ending to the play’s moral pattern.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Macduff is supernatural because he was not born of a woman.’ Which correction is accurate?
options: Macduff was born in England
Macduff is one of the apparitions
He is fully human; he was born by being cut from his mother’s womb, and the prophecy depends on a double meaning of ‘born’
Correct
questions.explanation: The prophecy equivocates. Macbeth hears a promise that no man can harm him, but the words hide an exception.
questions.misconception: Misunderstanding the “none of woman born” prophecy.

questions.prompt: Edexcel examiners in 2024 praised answers that treated Macduff and Macbeth as foils. Which pair of moments shows the contrast most clearly?
options: Both men fighting Norway in 1.2
Both men visiting the Witches
Macbeth ordering the murder of a family in 4.1, and Macduff grieving for his family in 4.3
Macduff at the Porter’s gate, and Macbeth at the banquet
questions.explanation: One man destroys families; the other mourns one. The contrast shapes the audience’s sympathies before the final fight.

questions.prompt: Explore how Shakespeare presents Macduff as a foil to Macbeth. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare sets Macduff against Macbeth in what each man feels and does. Macduff’s response to Duncan’s murder is pure horror: “O horror, horror, horror! / Tongue nor heart cannot conceive nor name thee!” (2.3.73-74). Macbeth, who committed it, delivers a polished speech. Macduff refuses to attend the coronation, and in England his despair, “Bleed, bleed, poor country!” (4.3.39), shows he cares for Scotland more than for power.

The sharpest contrast is in their idea of manhood. Macbeth tells the murderers that real men will kill; Macduff, hearing of his family’s murder, insists “But I must also feel it as a man:” (4.3.261). Grief is part of being a man, not a weakness. In the final fight Macduff calls Macbeth “hell-hound” (5.8.4) and reveals that he was “from his mother’s womb / Untimely ripp’d.” (5.8.19-20) The man who feels defeats the man who has forgotten the taste of fears.
checklist: Contrasts their reactions to Duncan’s death
Uses Macduff’s loyalty to Scotland
Analyses “feel it as a man” against Macbeth’s view of manhood
Uses the final confrontation
Makes a clear point about what the contrast shows
Uses precise quotations
questions.explanation: Foil answers work best when each paragraph puts the 2 men side by side.

units.title: Other characters
units.summary: The smaller parts do important work: the Captain builds Macbeth’s reputation, the Porter adds dark comedy, Ross and Lennox report Scotland’s suffering, the Doctor and Gentlewoman witness guilt, and the Siwards show a soldier’s death.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “If a man were porter of hell gate, he should have old turning the key.” (2.3.1-3)
options: Macduff
The Porter
The Old Man
Lennox
questions.explanation: The Porter imagines he guards the gate of hell. Without knowing it, he describes Macbeth’s castle.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Ross brings Macduff the news that his family has been killed.
Young Siward kills Macbeth.
The Old Man talks with Ross about unnatural events after the murder.
Seyton tells Macbeth that the Queen is dead.

questions.explanation: Macbeth kills Young Siward. Macduff kills Macbeth.

questions.prompt: Put these appearances of minor characters in the order they come.
items: The Captain reports the battle
The Porter answers the knocking
The Old Man describes strange signs
Lennox speaks with irony about Macbeth
The Gentlewoman shows the Doctor the sleepwalking
questions.explanation: 1.2, 2.3, 2.4, 3.6, 5.1: the minor characters often show us how Scotland sees events.

questions.prompt: Complete the Old Man’s report: “A falcon, towering in her pride of ___, / Was by a mousing owl hawk’d at and kill’d.” (2.4.15-16)
questions.explanation: The falcon’s high place is like a king’s. The owl’s attack mirrors the regicide.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that minor characters show Scotland’s suffering under Macbeth?
options: “If a man were porter of hell gate,” (2.3.1-2)
“The Queen, my lord, is dead.” (5.5.19)
“Alas, poor country, / Almost afraid to know itself!” (4.3.189-190)
“What bloody man is that?” (1.2.1)
questions.explanation: Ross pictures Scotland as too frightened even to look at itself.

questions.prompt: Match each minor character to the job they do in the play.
pairs: builds Macbeth’s reputation as a warrior
adds dark comedy before the discovery
questions.explanation: Minor characters often act as witnesses, so the audience sees events from outside the Macbeths’ world.

questions.prompt: The wounded soldier in 1.2 is called ‘Captain’ in the Folger and Gutenberg texts but ‘Sergeant’ in some other editions. What does this tell you about the First Folio text?
options: Holinshed calls him a sergeant
They are 2 different characters
The First Folio uses both names, so editors choose
Shakespeare changed his mind in 1611
questions.explanation: With only 1 early text, small inconsistencies remain. Use “Captain” and be aware of “Sergeant”.

questions.prompt: AQA examiners in 2019 found that some students said Macbeth was described as “merciless” in the Captain’s speech. What had they misread?
options: The word describes Duncan
The word describes the rebel Macdonwald, not Macbeth
The word describes the King of Norway
The word is not in the speech
questions.explanation: Gutenberg reads “The merciless Macdonwald” (1.2.11). Check who each description belongs to.
questions.misconception: Giving a description of one character to another.

questions.prompt: When Siward learns his son died with his wounds on the front, he says “Why then, God’s soldier be he!” (5.8.55). Why might Shakespeare include this reaction?
options: To contrast a soldier’s acceptance of death with Macduff’s open grief, giving different pictures of manhood
To make Siward the new king
To show the Witches were right about Siward
To show Siward did not love his son
questions.explanation: Siward and Macduff respond to losing sons in different ways; the play lets both stand.

questions.prompt: Choose 1 minor character. Explain what they add to the play, using at least 2 references. (6 marks)
questions.model: The Porter adds a dark comedy that sharpens the horror of the murder. He staggers to the gate imagining he is “porter of hell gate,” (2.3.2), welcoming sinners such as “an equivocator, that could swear in both the scales against either scale,” (2.3.8-10). The joke is unknowingly true: Macbeth’s castle has become a kind of hell, and the idea of saying 2 things at once looks forward to the Witches’ prophecies. His slow, rambling prose also delays the discovery, so the audience waits in suspense while Macduff knocks. When Macduff finds the body, the switch from jokes to “O horror, horror, horror!” (2.3.73) makes the shock greater. A small part shapes the mood of a whole scene.
checklist: Identifies a clear function for the character
Uses at least 2 accurate references
Explains the effect on the audience
Links the character to a theme or to the main plot
Comments on language or form (prose, irony)
questions.explanation: Any minor character can earn full marks if their function is explained with evidence.

units.title: Ambition
units.summary: Ambition drives the tragedy, but Shakespeare shows it as a force that overreaches and destroys itself. Compare Macbeth’s ambition with his wife’s, and with Banquo’s restraint.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Thriftless ambition, that will ravin up / Thine own life’s means!” (2.4.40-41)
options: Ross
Lady Macbeth
Banquo
Macbeth
questions.explanation: Ross is speaking of Malcolm and Donalbain, who are suspected of paying the grooms. The audience knows the “thriftless ambition” is Macbeth’s.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Lady Macbeth says her husband is “not without ambition”.
Banquo shows no ambition of any kind.
Macbeth describes his ambition as “vaulting”.
Ross blames Duncan’s sons for “thriftless ambition”.

questions.explanation: Banquo wonders whether the prophecies may be his “oracles as well”. He is tempted but does not act.

questions.prompt: Put these signs of Macbeth’s ambition in order.
items: He sees “Two truths” as prologues to “the imperial theme”
He calls the Prince of Cumberland a step he must o’erleap
He admits that only “Vaulting ambition” spurs him
He complains of a “fruitless crown”
He finds his title hangs loose “like a giant’s robe”
questions.explanation: The order traces ambition from excitement to emptiness.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth’s judgement: “Thou wouldst be great; / Art not without ___, but without / The illness should attend it.” (1.5.18-20)
questions.explanation: “Illness” here means the ruthlessness ambition needs. She thinks he wants greatness without the wickedness it takes.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that ambition destroys itself?
options: “my dearest partner of greatness)” (1.5.11)
“Thou wouldst be great;” (1.5.18)
“Two truths are told,” (1.3.140)
“Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (1.7.27)
questions.explanation: The rider who leaps too high falls on the other side: Macbeth predicts his own fall in his own image.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their relationship with ambition.
pairs: acts on ambition against his own conscience
wants greatness for her husband and fears his kindness
is tempted by the prophecy but does nothing to make it happen
pretends to vices to test Macduff, then shows the graces of a good king
questions.explanation: Shakespeare explores ambition by giving several characters the same temptation and different responses.

questions.prompt: In Holinshed, Macbeth’s wife is described as very ambitious and burning with desire to be called queen. In the play, what is different about Lady Macbeth’s ambition?
options: She has no ambition at all
She wants Banquo to be king
She speaks almost entirely about greatness for her husband, not about being queen herself
She wants to be queen instead of him
questions.explanation: Her words focus on him: “Thou wouldst be great;” and the “golden round” that should crown him.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Ross says “Thriftless ambition” because he knows Macbeth killed Duncan.’ What is wrong?
options: Ross is speaking about Banquo
Ross is speaking about Duncan’s sons, who are suspected; the irony is that the audience knows the ambition is Macbeth’s
The line is spoken by Macbeth
Nothing
questions.explanation: Check who a line refers to before using it. Here the dramatic irony is the point.
questions.misconception: Misreading who a description refers to.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2017 report discussed the ambition of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth at the start of the play. Which comparison is most accurate?
options: Neither has any ambition at the start
Lady Macbeth’s ambition only appears in Act 5
Macbeth’s ambition is stronger and he has no doubts
Lady Macbeth’s ambition is open and immediate, while Macbeth’s is mixed with fear and conscience
questions.explanation: Her mind is made up as she reads the letter; his asides show desire tangled with horror.

questions.prompt: AQA-style: Starting with Macbeth’s soliloquy in 1.7, explore how far Shakespeare presents Macbeth as an ambitious character. (8 marks)
questions.model:
In the 1.7 soliloquy Shakespeare presents ambition as the only force pushing Macbeth towards murder, but not the strongest force in his mind. He lists the bonds against the deed, kinsman, subject and host, and imagines Duncan’s virtues pleading “like angels, trumpet-tongued,” (1.7.19). Against all this he admits “I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (1.7.25-27). The image of a rider jumping so hard he falls shows that he already sees ambition as self-destructive.

Elsewhere, ambition is clearly present. In 1.3 he treats the prophecies as “happy prologues to the swelling act / Of the imperial theme.” (1.3.141-142), and in 1.4 he calls Malcolm a step he must “fall down, or else o’erleap,” (1.4.56). Yet it takes his wife to turn ambition into action, and once king he is driven by fear more than desire. So Macbeth is ambitious to a great extent at the start, but ambition alone does not explain what he becomes.
checklist: Analyses the “vaulting ambition” image
Shows the reasons against murder that ambition must overcome
Uses the wider play (1.3 asides, 1.4 “o’erleap”, or Act 3 fear)
Considers other forces: Lady Macbeth, fear, the prophecies
Reaches a clear judgement on “how far”
Context, if used, is brief and linked
questions.explanation: AQA asked this in June 2025. A strong answer weighs ambition against other motives.

units.title: Power and kingship
units.summary: The play compares kings: generous Duncan, holy Edward, cautious Malcolm and the tyrant Macbeth. Macbeth gains the crown but never security or love, because his power has no legitimacy.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “This tyrant, whose sole name blisters our tongues, / Was once thought honest:” (4.3.14-15)
options: Macduff
Ross
Malcolm
Lennox
questions.explanation: Malcolm reminds Macduff that Macbeth once seemed honest, which is why he must test Macduff.
