statements.s: Macbeth is crowned at Scone.
Malcolm lists the “king-becoming graces” a good ruler needs.
Macbeth’s thanes follow him out of love.
The English King Edward is described as healing the sick by touch.

questions.explanation: Angus says those Macbeth commands “move only in command, / Nothing in love:” (5.2.22-23).

questions.prompt: Put these moments about power and kingship in order.
items: Duncan names Malcolm as his heir
Macbeth is crowned
Macbeth fears Banquo’s royal line
Malcolm tests Macduff in England
Macduff hails Malcolm as King of Scotland
questions.explanation: The crown passes from Duncan to Macbeth and finally to Malcolm, the rightful heir.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s line: “To be thus is nothing, / But to be ___ thus.” (3.1.52-53)
questions.explanation: Being king means nothing to him without safety, so the crown leads straight to more murder.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth’s power rests on fear, not loyalty?
options: “I have begun to plant thee,” (1.4.32)
“the king-becoming graces,” (4.3.107)
“Those he commands move only in command, / Nothing in love:” (5.2.22-23)
“Hail, King of Scotland!” (5.8.70)
questions.explanation: Obedience without love is weak; it melts away as Malcolm’s army approaches.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of power to an example from the play.
pairs: Macbeth cutting through the rebels in 1.2
Lady Macbeth overturning her husband’s decision in 1.7
questions.explanation: Edexcel’s 2023 mark scheme suggested answers on power could range across physical, supernatural and persuasive power.

questions.prompt: In 1610 King James told Parliament that “kings are not only God’s lieutenants upon earth and sit upon God’s throne”. How does this context help explain Macbeth’s insecurity?
options: It proves Macbeth was a good king
If kingship comes from God, a crown taken by murder has no true authority, so Macbeth can never feel secure
It shows James admired Macbeth
It means Malcolm has no right to rule
questions.explanation: The idea of divine right explains why a usurper’s power feels hollow and why Malcolm’s return restores order.

questions.prompt: In an Edexcel part (b) answer on power elsewhere in the play, a student spends a paragraph on the printed extract. What is the problem?
options: Part (b) is about language only
None
Part (b) asks about the rest of the play, so material from the extract earns nothing there
Part (b) must only use the extract
questions.explanation: Part (a) uses the extract; part (b) must use other moments, with context.
questions.misconception: Using the extract in Edexcel part (b).

questions.prompt: Why does Shakespeare include Malcolm’s false confession of vices in 4.3?
options: To make Macduff the king
To prove Malcolm is unfit to rule
To define good kingship by its opposite and show Malcolm’s caution
To delay the battle for no reason
questions.explanation: The list of vices is followed by the “king-becoming graces”, so the audience hears both sides of the definition.

questions.prompt: Edexcel part (b)-style: Explain the importance of power elsewhere in the play. Refer to context. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Power matters because the play asks what makes it legitimate. Duncan’s power is generous; he rewards Macbeth with titles and promises “I have begun to plant thee,” (1.4.32). Macbeth takes the crown by murder, but finds it empty: “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus.” (3.1.52-53) He keeps power only through more killing, and by Act 5 his followers “move only in command, / Nothing in love:” (5.2.22-23).

Context sharpens this. King James argued that kings ruled by divine right, as God’s lieutenants on earth, so an audience in 1606 might see a usurper’s power as unnatural and doomed. Shakespeare reinforces this with King Edward, whose touch heals the sick in 4.3, and with Malcolm’s list of the “king-becoming graces” (4.3.107). Power gained through murder destroys the man who holds it; power that serves others is restored when Malcolm promises to act “by the grace of Grace” (5.8.85).
checklist: Uses moments from across the play, not the extract
Contrasts Duncan’s generosity with Macbeth’s insecurity
Shows Macbeth’s power depending on fear
Uses Edward or Malcolm as models of good power
Integrates context on kingship (AO3)
Explains why power is important to the play’s meaning
questions.explanation: Edexcel part (b) is marked for AO1 and AO3; weave context into the argument.

units.title: The supernatural
units.summary: Witches, a floating dagger, a ghost and apparitions: Shakespeare never settles whether the supernatural is outside Macbeth or inside his mind. It tempts and misleads, but it never forces him.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Infected be the air whereon they ride; / And damn’d all those that trust them!” (4.1.157-158)
options: Lennox, in 3.6
Macbeth, after the Witches vanish in 4.1
Banquo, in 1.3
Hecate, in 3.5
questions.explanation: Macbeth curses anyone who trusts the Witches, without noticing that he is cursing himself.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Macbeth sees a dagger in the air before the murder.
Everyone at the banquet sees Banquo’s ghost.
The apparitions appear in 4.1.
Lady Macbeth meets the Witches.

questions.explanation: Only Macbeth sees the Ghost. Lady Macbeth never meets the Witches; she learns of them from the letter.

questions.prompt: Put these supernatural moments in order.
items: The Witches meet in thunder and lightning
The Witches hail Macbeth
Macbeth sees a dagger
Macbeth hears a voice cry “Sleep no more”
Banquo’s ghost appears
The apparitions speak
questions.explanation: As the play goes on, more of the supernatural is seen by Macbeth alone.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s question: “A dagger of the mind, a false ___, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?” (2.1.50-51)
questions.explanation: Macbeth himself offers a psychological explanation for what he sees.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that the supernatural may come from Macbeth’s own mind?
options: “Double, double, toil and trouble;” (4.1.10)
“When shall we three meet again?” (1.1.1)
“By the pricking of my thumbs,” (4.1.44)
“A dagger of the mind, a false creation,” (2.1.50)
questions.explanation: The phrase “of the mind” locates the dagger inside him. The Witches’ scenes, seen by others, are harder to explain this way.

questions.prompt: Match each supernatural moment to a possible explanation.
pairs: guilt made visible to the guilty man alone
truths with double meanings that breed over-confidence
small truths told to win trust and then betray
questions.explanation: Strong answers keep more than one explanation open, as the play does.

questions.prompt: Folger’s introduction notes King James’s belief in a connection between treason and witchcraft. How could this be used briefly in an AQA answer on the Witches?
options: To give a full history of witch trials
To replace analysis of the Witches’ language
To prove that Shakespeare believed in witches
To note that the Witches tempt a subject towards killing his king, joining the 2 crimes James most feared
questions.explanation: One linked sentence adds AO3. A paragraph of history would be bolted on.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Lady Macbeth is a witch because she calls on spirits.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: She is Hecate in disguise
Correct
She calls on spirits, but the play never presents her as a witch; the scene shows her inviting evil into herself
She never calls on spirits
questions.explanation: Precise readings avoid labels the play does not support.
questions.misconception: Labelling Lady Macbeth a witch.

questions.prompt: Which opening thesis on the supernatural is strongest?
options: The supernatural is in the play a lot.
In this essay I will talk about the Witches.
Witches were real in Jacobean times.
Shakespeare uses the supernatural to tempt and mislead Macbeth, but never to force him, so the tragedy remains one of choice.
questions.explanation: A thesis answers the question in a sentence that the essay can then prove.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare use the supernatural to explore Macbeth’s mind? Refer to at least 2 moments. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare uses the supernatural as a mirror for Macbeth’s thoughts. When the Witches hail him as future king, he starts, and soon admits that the “horrid image” of murder makes his heart knock at his ribs. The prophecy has said nothing about killing; the idea is his. Before the murder he sees a dagger and asks whether it is “A dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?” (2.1.50-51) The dagger leads him “the way that I was going;” (2.1.54), so the vision only shows a path he has already chosen.

At the banquet the supernatural becomes guilt made visible. Banquo’s ghost appears to Macbeth alone, and his cry “Never shake / Thy gory locks at me.” (3.4.61-62) reveals what he is hiding to the whole court. In each case the audience cannot be sure whether the vision is real, but it always shows something true about Macbeth’s mind: his desire, his intent, his guilt.
checklist: Uses the first prophecy and Macbeth’s reaction
Analyses the dagger speech
Analyses the ghost at the banquet
Explains how the supernatural reveals desire, intention or guilt
Keeps both real and psychological readings open
Uses precise quotations
questions.explanation: The best answers use the supernatural to say something about character, not just list events.

units.title: Fate and free will
units.summary: The Witches predict, but Macbeth chooses. He tries to wait for chance, then to force fate, then to fight it. Weigh the prophecies against his choices.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Come what come may, / Time and the hour runs through the roughest day.” (1.3.163-164)
options: Banquo
Macbeth
Duncan
Ross
questions.explanation: At the end of 1.3 Macbeth decides, for now, to let time take its course.

questions.prompt: True or false?

Macbeth first says that chance may crown him without his own action.
Banquo hears a prophecy but does nothing to make it come true.
Macbeth tries to stop the prophecy about Banquo’s heirs by having Fleance killed.

questions.explanation: The prophecy says only that he will be king. Murder is never mentioned.

questions.prompt: Put these stages in Macbeth’s response to fate in order.
items: He decides to leave it to chance
He chooses to kill Duncan
He tries to destroy Banquo’s line
He demands more answers from the Witches
He fights on after the last prophecy fails
questions.explanation: He moves from waiting for fate, to forcing it, to defying it.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s complaint: “Upon my head they plac’d a fruitless ___,” (3.1.66)
questions.explanation: He feels fate has cheated him: he is king, but Banquo’s line will inherit.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth tries to fight against fate?
options: “If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me” (1.3.157-158)
“Come what come may,” (1.3.163)
“Two truths are told,” (1.3.140)
“Rather than so, come, fate, into the list,” (3.1.76)
questions.explanation: He challenges fate to single combat rather than accept that Banquo’s children will rule.

questions.prompt: Match each prophecy to how it comes true.
pairs: Duncan gives Macbeth the title after Cawdor’s treason
Macbeth murders Duncan and is crowned
Fleance escapes and the show of kings appears
Until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane
soldiers carry branches cut from the wood
questions.explanation: Only 1 prophecy, the crown, comes true through Macbeth’s own crime.

questions.prompt: Holinshed suggests the weird sisters might be goddesses of destiny. How does this context relate to the play’s question of fate?
options: It raises the possibility that the future is fixed, which Shakespeare keeps open by never explaining the Witches
It shows the Witches are ordinary women
It proves Macbeth has no choice
It has no link to fate
questions.explanation: The play keeps the uncertainty, so the audience must weigh destiny against choice.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The Witches tell Macbeth to kill Banquo.’ What is wrong?
options: The Witches only say Banquo will get kings; the decision to kill him is Macbeth’s own
Lady Macbeth plans Banquo’s murder
Hecate tells him to kill Banquo
Nothing
questions.explanation: Macbeth plans Banquo’s murder alone and keeps it from his wife.
questions.misconception: Attributing Macbeth’s choices to the Witches.

questions.prompt: Which argument about fate and free will is most balanced?
options: Fate plays no part in the play at all
Lady Macbeth controls fate
The prophecies set the goal, but Macbeth chooses the means; when he tries to change fate, as with Fleance, he fails
Macbeth has no choice because the Witches predicted everything
questions.explanation: A balanced argument admits the power of the prophecies and the weight of Macbeth’s decisions.

questions.prompt: Is Macbeth a victim of fate or the author of his own downfall? Refer to at least 2 moments. (8 marks)
questions.model:
The prophecies shape what Macbeth wants, but the play shows that he chooses how to get it. In 1.3 he could wait: “If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me / Without my stir.” (1.3.157-159) Banquo hears a prophecy too and does nothing. Macbeth instead chooses murder, against the reasons he lists in 1.7, so the first and greatest crime is his own.

Later he tries to control fate rather than accept it. He resents the “fruitless crown” (3.1.66) and arranges Banquo’s and Fleance’s deaths, even challenging fate to fight: “come, fate, into the list,” (3.1.76). Fleance escapes, and the show of kings confirms the prophecy. Here fate seems stronger than his will. Yet the final prophecies only mislead him because he wants to believe them. Macbeth is not a puppet; he is a man whose choices make him easy prey for the words that tempt him.
checklist: Takes a clear position
Uses the “chance” aside and his choice to murder
Uses Banquo as a comparison
Shows Macbeth trying to fight fate (Banquo, Fleance)
Considers how the final prophecies mislead him
Uses precise quotations
questions.explanation: Answers that weigh both sides and decide earn the higher marks.

units.title: Guilt and conscience
units.summary: Macbeth’s guilt arrives at once, in visions, voices and sleeplessness; his wife’s is held back until it breaks out in her sleep. Blood, water and sleep carry the theme through the play.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Canst thou not minister to a mind diseas’d,” (5.3.50)
options: Macbeth, to the Doctor
The Gentlewoman, to the Doctor
Malcolm, to Macduff
Lady Macbeth, to Macbeth
questions.explanation: Macbeth asks the Doctor to cure his wife, but the words describe his own mind too.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: After the murder Macbeth says he could not say “Amen”.
Lady Macbeth shows no sign of discontent until the sleepwalking scene.
At the banquet Macbeth sees the Ghost of the man he had murdered.
The Doctor says Lady Macbeth needs a priest more than a physician.

questions.explanation: In 3.2 she already admits “Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6).

questions.prompt: Put these signs of guilt in order.
items: Macbeth cannot say “Amen”
Macbeth fears that all great Neptune’s ocean cannot wash his hand
Macbeth’s mind is full of scorpions
Banquo’s ghost appears to Macbeth
Lady Macbeth sleepwalks
questions.explanation: Guilt moves from Macbeth to his wife as the play goes on.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s words after the banquet: “It will have blood, they say, blood will have ___.” (3.4.151)
questions.explanation: The repetition makes violence sound like a law that cannot be escaped.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Lady Macbeth’s guilt surfaces only when she cannot control it?
options: “That which hath made them drunk hath made me bold:” (2.2.1-2)
“Leave all the rest to me.” (1.5.86)
“who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?” (5.1.41-42)
“Are you a man?” (3.4.70)
questions.explanation: Asleep, she relives the horror she hid while awake.

questions.prompt: Match each symbol of guilt to a moment where it appears.
pairs: her claim that a little water clears them
a voice crying that Macbeth shall sleep no more
the light she keeps by her continually
questions.explanation: Each symbol returns, changed, in Act 5: the blood will not wash off and sleep brings no rest.

questions.prompt: After the murder Macbeth cannot say “Amen”. How does belief in the divine right of kings help explain his feeling?
options: It shows the grooms were guilty
It means Macbeth will become a priest
It shows that kings had to say Amen
Killing God’s anointed king is a sin against heaven, so he feels cut off from God’s blessing
questions.explanation: Macduff calls the murder sacrilege. Macbeth’s guilt is religious as well as personal.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Lady Macbeth feels no guilt at all until Act 5.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: She never feels guilty
Correct
She feels guilty only in Act 1
Not quite: she could not kill Duncan because he looked like her father, and in 3.2 she admits their desire has brought no content
questions.explanation: Her guilt is held back, not absent. Tracing early signs makes an answer more precise.
questions.misconception: Thinking Lady Macbeth’s guilt appears from nowhere in 5.1.

questions.prompt: How does the presentation of guilt differ between the 2 Macbeths?
options: Only Macbeth feels guilty
Only Lady Macbeth feels guilty
They feel exactly the same at the same time
His guilt is immediate and imaginative; hers is suppressed and returns later, uncontrolled, in sleep
questions.explanation: The structure crosses their paths: he grows numb as she breaks down.

questions.prompt: Explore how Shakespeare presents guilt in the play. Refer to both Macbeth and Lady Macbeth. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare presents guilt as a punishment that cannot be escaped. Macbeth feels it the moment the deed is done. He cannot say “Amen”, and imagines a voice crying “Macbeth does murder sleep,” (2.2.48), cutting him off from rest. His question “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79) makes guilt larger than the sea. As king, guilt becomes fear: his mind is “full of scorpions” (3.2.41), and Banquo’s ghost exposes him in public.

Lady Macbeth seems free of guilt at first, insisting that “A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86). Yet Shakespeare reverses this. In 5.1 she rubs her hands in her sleep, crying “Out, damned spot! out, I say!” (5.1.37), and finds that no perfume can sweeten “this little hand.” The word “little” returns to mock her earlier confidence. Through the images of blood and sleep, Shakespeare suggests guilt may be delayed but never avoided.
checklist: Analyses Macbeth’s immediate guilt (Amen, sleep, ocean)
Shows guilt turning to fear in Act 3
Analyses Lady Macbeth’s early denial
Analyses the sleepwalking scene
Tracks a symbol (blood, water, sleep) across the play
Makes a clear overall point
questions.explanation: Linking moments through a symbol is a strong way to show structure.

units.title: Appearance and reality
units.summary: From “Fair is foul” onwards, nothing in Macbeth is what it seems: friendly faces hide murder, prophecies hide traps, and even Malcolm pretends. The theme links to equivocation and to the play’s clothing images.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Your face, my thane, is as a book where men / May read strange matters.” (1.5.73-74)
options: Macduff, to Malcolm
Duncan, to Macbeth
Banquo, to Macbeth
Lady Macbeth, to Macbeth
questions.explanation: She warns him that his face gives away his thoughts and teaches him to hide them.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Lady Macbeth welcomes Duncan with elaborate courtesy.
Malcolm’s list of his own vices in 4.3 is true.
Macbeth pretends to be outraged when Duncan’s body is found.
Donalbain warns that there are daggers in men’s smiles.

questions.explanation: Malcolm pretends to be wicked to test Macduff. It is a deception used for good.

questions.prompt: Put these deceptions in order.
items: The Witches’ truths that lead to harm
Lady Macbeth’s welcome to Duncan
Macbeth’s display of grief and fury after the murder
Macbeth’s friendly invitation to Banquo
Malcolm’s false confession to Macduff
questions.explanation: Deception spreads from the Witches to the Macbeths, and finally is turned against tyranny by Malcolm.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s couplet: “False face must hide what the false ___ doth know.” (1.7.95-96)
questions.explanation: The repeated “false” and the rhyme make deception sound like a vow.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that friendly appearances hide danger after the murder?
options: “This castle hath a pleasant seat.” (1.6.1)
“Fair is foul, and foul is fair:” (1.1.12)
“So foul and fair a day I have not seen.” (1.3.39)
“There’s daggers in men’s smiles:” (2.3.165)
questions.explanation: Donalbain sees that smiles may hide murderers, so he and Malcolm flee.

questions.prompt: Match each character to the way they deceive.
pairs: plays the gracious hostess to Duncan
invites Banquo to the feast while planning his death
pretends to be worse than Macbeth
questions.explanation: Not all deception is evil: Malcolm’s protects Scotland.

questions.prompt: Macbeth finally sees “th’ equivocation of the fiend, / That lies like truth.” (5.5.49-50) Which context is most often linked to equivocation in the play?
options: The publication of Holinshed in 1587
The building of the Globe
Simon Forman’s diary
The Gunpowder Plot trials of early 1606, in which equivocation was an issue
questions.explanation: The Porter’s “equivocator” is widely read as a reference to the trials. In the play, equivocation is the Witches’ method.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Malcolm is shown to be a liar and a bad king because he lies to Macduff.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: Malcolm’s lies come true
His lie is a test of loyalty, quickly withdrawn; it shows caution, unlike Duncan’s trust in appearances
Malcolm never speaks to Macduff
Correct
questions.explanation: The play explores when appearances must be tested, not only when they deceive.
questions.misconception: Treating all deception in the play as equally evil.

questions.prompt: Why is “Fair is foul, and foul is fair:” (1.1.12) a strong starting point for an essay on appearance and reality?
options: It tells the audience the weather
The paradox announces a world where good and evil look alike, which the rest of the play explores
It explains the plot of Act 5
It is Macbeth’s first line
questions.explanation: Macbeth’s first line echoes it, linking him to the Witches’ world of confusion.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare explore the gap between appearance and reality? Refer to at least 2 moments. (8 marks)
questions.model:
From the Witches’ paradox “Fair is foul, and foul is fair:” (1.1.12), Shakespeare builds a world where nothing can be trusted. Duncan admits “There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face:” (1.4.13-14), and at once trusts Macbeth, whose aside asks the stars to hide his “black and deep desires.” Lady Macbeth makes deception a method, telling her husband to “look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t.” (1.5.76-78) The image of a snake beneath a flower suggests danger hidden inside beauty.

The theme is completed by equivocation. The apparitions tell Macbeth truths that sound like safety, and only in Act 5 does he see “th’ equivocation of the fiend, / That lies like truth.” (5.5.49-50) Even good characters must deceive: Malcolm pretends to be wicked to test Macduff. Shakespeare suggests that in a world corrupted by one murder, appearances must be tested before they can be trusted.
checklist: Uses “Fair is foul” or a similar paradox
Analyses Duncan’s misplaced trust
Analyses the flower and serpent image
Explains equivocation and the prophecies
Considers Malcolm’s deception as a contrast
Makes an overall point about trust
questions.explanation: Answers that link deception to the play’s structure earn the higher marks.

units.title: Gender and masculinity
units.summary: Characters argue about what a man is: daring, limited, ruthless or feeling. Lady Macbeth rejects what she links with womanhood, while Lady Macduff shows protective love. Use context only where your board rewards it.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “When you durst do it, then you were a man;” (1.7.56)
options: Malcolm
Lady Macbeth
Macbeth
Lady Macduff
questions.explanation: She defines manhood as daring to act, and so makes murder a test of masculinity.

questions.prompt: True or false?

Macbeth tells the murderers they are men only in name, as a list of dogs.
Macduff says a man should never show grief.
Lady Macbeth asks the spirits to unsex her.

questions.explanation: Macduff insists “But I must also feel it as a man:” (4.3.261).

questions.prompt: Put these statements about manhood in order.
items: Macbeth: a man dares only what becomes a man
Lady Macbeth: when you dared it you were a man
Macbeth to the murderers: in the catalogue you go for men
Lady Macbeth at the banquet: are you a man?
Macduff: I must also feel it as a man
questions.explanation: The debate about manhood runs from 1.7 to 4.3 and ends with a different answer.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s praise of his wife: “Bring forth men-children only; / For thy undaunted ___ should compose / Nothing but males.” (1.7.83-85)
questions.explanation: “Mettle” means spirit or courage, with a pun on “metal”. He sees her courage as masculine.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Lady Macbeth links womanhood with weakness?
options: “A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86)
“Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6)
“Leave all the rest to me.” (1.5.86)
“Come to my woman’s breasts, / And take my milk for gall,” (1.5.54-55)
questions.explanation: She wants her milk, a symbol of nurture, turned to bitter poison.

questions.prompt: Match each speaker to their idea of what a man is.
pairs: a man dares to do what he has sworn
a man knows the limits of what is right
a man will kill when told his enemy wronged him
a man must feel grief as well as fight
questions.explanation: The play tests several definitions and seems to favour Macduff’s.

questions.prompt: Daemonologie claimed women were the “frailer” sex, and the AQA 2017 report warned against sweeping claims such as “All Elizabethan women were...”. How should this context be used?
options: Briefly, to sharpen a point about how unsettling Lady Macbeth’s strength might seem, and only on boards that reward AO3
On every board, including Eduqas
To prove all women in 1606 were weak
As a long paragraph about Jacobean women
questions.explanation: Context should explain the play, not replace it. On Eduqas it earns nothing at all.

questions.prompt: Eduqas examiners in 2025 named one problem as the biggest source of underachievement. What was it?
options: Writing about Act 3
Using too many short quotations
Planning for too long
Sweeping, unnecessary comments on gender in Jacobean society, even though context is not assessed
questions.explanation: On Eduqas, analyse how characters speak and behave; leave Jacobean gender out.
questions.misconception: Adding gender context on a board that does not assess AO3.

questions.prompt: Why is Lady Macduff an important contrast to Lady Macbeth?
options: She is more ambitious than Lady Macbeth
She helps Macbeth
She is a protective mother, like the “poor wren”, which shows the nurturing role Lady Macbeth rejects
She is a witch
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners in 2025 said the “poor wren” image was a key discriminator for higher bands.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare present ideas about what it means to be a man? (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare stages a debate about manhood. In 1.7 Macbeth argues for limits: “I dare do all that may become a man; / Who dares do more is none.” (1.7.51-52) Lady Macbeth overturns this, insisting “When you durst do it, then you were a man;” (1.7.56), so that courage means killing. Macbeth learns her lesson and uses it on the murderers, telling them that “in the catalogue ye go for men;” (3.1.103), like dogs listed by breed.

The play does not leave this definition unchallenged. When Macduff hears that his family has been murdered, Malcolm urges “Dispute it like a man.” (4.3.259), and Macduff replies “But I must also feel it as a man:” (4.3.261). Feeling becomes part of manhood, not a betrayal of it. The man who feels kills the man who has forgotten fear, which suggests that Shakespeare favours Macduff’s idea over Lady Macbeth’s.
checklist: Analyses Macbeth’s view in 1.7
Analyses Lady Macbeth’s challenge
Shows Macbeth using manhood on the murderers
Analyses Macduff’s “feel it as a man”
Reaches a judgement about which view the play favours
Context brief and relevant, or absent for Eduqas
questions.explanation: Show the debate developing, not a list of quotations.

units.title: Order and disorder
units.summary: Duncan’s murder breaks the natural order: darkness by day, a falcon killed by an owl, horses turning wild. Disorder spreads through Scotland under the tyrant until Malcolm restores rightful rule.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Unnatural deeds / Do breed unnatural troubles:” (5.1.75-76)
options: The Old Man
The Doctor
Lennox
Ross
questions.explanation: The Doctor links Lady Macbeth’s sleepwalking to the crimes behind it.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: After the murder it is dark during the day.
In 2.4 a falcon kills an owl.
Lennox reports strange screams and lamenting in the air on the night of the murder.
Malcolm promises to act “in measure, time, and place”.

questions.explanation: The owl, a lower bird, kills the falcon, just as a subject kills his king.

questions.prompt: Put these moments of disorder and order in order.
items: Strange screams are heard on the night of the murder
Darkness covers the day and a falcon is killed
Scotland is described as a suffering country
King Edward’s healing touch is described
Malcolm is hailed as king
questions.explanation: Disorder spreads, then images of healing and rightful rule return.

questions.prompt: Complete Ross’s description: “by the clock ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling ___.” (2.4.8-9)
questions.explanation: The “travelling lamp” is the sun, strangled by night as Duncan was murdered.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that the murder is a crime against the whole natural order?
options: “Hail, King of Scotland!” (5.8.70)
“’Twas a rough night.” (2.3.70)
“I have done the deed.” (2.2.19)
“Confusion now hath made his masterpiece!” (2.3.76)
questions.explanation: Chaos itself has created its greatest work: the destruction of a king.

questions.prompt: Match each sign to what it suggests.
pairs: the light of rightful rule put out
creatures rebelling against the order that tamed them
Malcolm’s rhyming couplet at the end
questions.explanation: Shakespeare uses nature to show the scale of the crime.

questions.prompt: Many people in the period thought of the universe as an ordered ladder, the Great Chain of Being. How does this idea help explain the falcon and the owl?
options: It shows owls were thought to be royal
It proves Shakespeare studied birds
It shows nature is always peaceful
A lower creature destroying a higher one mirrors a subject killing his king, breaking the order everything was thought to belong to
questions.explanation: Present the Great Chain as one widely held idea, not as something everyone believed.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘In 2.4 the falcon represents Macbeth and the owl represents Duncan.’ What is wrong?
options: Nothing
It is the other way round: the proud, high-flying falcon is like the king, and the mousing owl that kills it is like Macbeth
The falcon represents Banquo
Neither bird is mentioned
questions.explanation: Check the direction of the image: the lower bird destroys the higher, as the subject destroys the king.
questions.misconception: Reversing the falcon and owl image.

questions.prompt: How does Malcolm’s final speech help to restore order?
options: He praises Macbeth
He leaves Scotland for England
He rewards the thanes, invites all to his coronation and ends with a rhyming couplet promising measure, time and place
He gives the crown to Macduff
questions.explanation: Ceremony and the closed sound of rhyme suggest harmony returning.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare show the murder of Duncan throwing Scotland into disorder? (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare shows disorder beginning in nature on the night of the murder. Lennox describes chimneys blown down and “Lamentings heard i’ th’ air, strange screams of death,” (2.3.63-64) as if the world itself is grieving. Macduff’s “Confusion now hath made his masterpiece!” (2.3.76) presents chaos as an artist and the murder as its greatest work. The next day the signs grow stranger: night “strangles the travelling lamp.” (2.4.9), and a falcon is “by a mousing owl hawk’d at and kill’d.” (2.4.16) The verb “strangles” repeats the crime in the sky.

Disorder then spreads to Scotland’s people. Under the tyrant, Ross describes a country “Almost afraid to know itself!” (4.3.190), and Lennox prays for a blessing on “this our suffering country” (3.6.54). For an audience who saw the king as placed by God, these images show that the crime has damaged everything. Only when Malcolm promises to act “in measure, time, and place.” (5.8.86) does the play return to harmony.
checklist: Analyses the storm and cries on the night of the murder
Analyses “Confusion now hath made his masterpiece”
Analyses darkness by day or the falcon and owl
Shows disorder spreading to Scotland (Ross, Lennox)
Brief context on kingship or order
Shows order restored by Malcolm
questions.explanation: Strong answers trace a pattern: order broken, disorder spreading, order restored.

units.title: Violence
units.summary: Violence is praised in battle at the start and condemned as murder later. It moves from reported to offstage to on stage, and ends where it began, with a severed head. Ask how the play judges each act.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d.” (5.3.38)
options: The Captain
Macbeth
Macduff
Young Siward
questions.explanation: In 5.3 Macbeth’s language returns to the battlefield. AQA examiners in 2023 praised pairing ’hack’d’ with “unseam’d” from 1.2.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The Captain describes Macbeth cutting Macdonwald from the navel to the jaw.
Duncan’s murder is shown on stage.
Banquo’s murder is shown on stage.
Macduff’s son is killed on stage.

questions.explanation: Duncan’s murder happens offstage; later murders are shown, as violence becomes more open.

questions.prompt: Put these violent acts in order.
items: Macbeth kills Macdonwald in battle
Macbeth murders Duncan
Macbeth kills the grooms
Murderers kill Banquo
Murderers kill Macduff’s son
Macduff kills Macbeth
questions.explanation: Violence escalates from public battle to private murder to the killing of children.

questions.prompt: Complete the Captain’s report: “Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chops, / And fix’d his head upon our ___.” (1.2.24-25)
questions.explanation: The play begins and ends with a head displayed, which links the hero and the tyrant.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth’s violence becomes pointless cruelty?
options: “For brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name),” (1.2.18)
“I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d.” (5.3.38)
“give to th’ edge o’ th’ sword / His wife, his babes,” (4.1.172-173)
“They have tied me to a stake. I cannot fly,” (5.7.1)
questions.explanation: Macduff has escaped, so killing his family achieves nothing except terror.

questions.prompt: Match each violent act to how it is staged.
pairs: reported by the Captain and praised
shown on stage in the dark
followed by his head carried on stage
questions.explanation: How violence is staged shapes how the audience judges it.

questions.prompt: The real Duncan was killed by Macbeth in battle, where killing a rival openly was common. Why might Shakespeare have turned this into a secret murder of a sleeping guest?
options: To follow Holinshed exactly
To make the act a betrayal rather than a battle, so it is judged as murder, not warfare
Because battles could not be described on stage
To make Macbeth seem braver
questions.explanation: The change separates praised violence (1.2) from condemned violence (2.2).

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2019 question asked how far Macbeth is presented as a violent character. Examiners noted that some answers focused on Lady Macbeth instead. What went wrong?
options: They wrote about Act 1
They reproduced a prepared essay instead of answering the question on Macbeth’s violence
They used too many quotations
They mentioned the Captain
questions.explanation: Use what you know, but reshape it to fit the exact words of the question.
questions.misconception: Writing a prepared essay rather than answering the question set.

questions.prompt: Is violence ever presented as good in the play?
options: No, all violence is condemned equally
Yes, when it defends the rightful king, as in 1.2 and Macduff’s final fight; the play judges violence by its purpose
Only the Witches’ violence is good
Only offstage violence is good
questions.explanation: The same act, killing, is praised or condemned depending on who it serves.

questions.prompt: Edexcel part (b)-style: Explain the importance of violence elsewhere in the play (not in 5.8). Refer to context. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Violence matters because the play asks when killing is honourable and when it is murder. At the start, Macbeth’s brutality is praised: the Captain describes how he “unseam’d him from the nave to the chops,” (1.2.24), and Duncan calls him “worthy gentleman!” This violence defends the king, so it earns honour. Duncan’s murder reverses this. It happens offstage to a sleeping guest, and Macbeth fears “The deep damnation of his taking-off;” (1.7.20). For an audience who believed kings ruled by God’s will, killing a king was a sin as well as a crime.

After this, violence spreads and loses purpose. Macbeth admits “blood will have blood.” (3.4.151) and orders the deaths of Macduff’s “wife, his babes,” (4.1.173) even though Macduff has escaped. The violence that once protected Scotland now destroys it, which shows how far Macbeth has fallen.
checklist: Uses moments from elsewhere in the play, not 5.8
Contrasts praised violence in 1.2 with the murder of Duncan
Shows violence escalating (Banquo, Macduff’s family)
Integrates context on kingship or regicide (AO3)
Explains why violence is important to the play’s meaning
Uses accurate references
questions.explanation: Edexcel’s 2024 part (b) asked about violence elsewhere; extract material earns nothing in part (b).

units.title: Form: tragedy and the tragic hero
units.summary: Macbeth is a tragedy: a great man falls through a flaw and ends in death, and order returns. Use tragedy as a lens to explain how moments create pity and fear, not as a label.

questions.prompt: Which description of a tragedy fits Macbeth best?
options: A play with no deaths at all
A play that ends with marriages and celebration
A serious play that traces the fall of a great person and ends in death
A play that mocks the faults of ordinary people
questions.explanation: Tragedy follows the fall of a high-status figure. Macbeth moves from praised general to slain tyrant.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: A tragic hero is usually a person of high status.
Macbeth’s story ends in his death.
Lady Macbeth has a soliloquy of self-knowledge like Macbeth’s “Tomorrow” speech.
Order is restored at the end of the play.

questions.explanation: Lady Macbeth dies offstage without a speech of self-knowledge, which is why critics debate whether she is tragic.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of tragedy to how it appears in Macbeth.
pairs: a great general and the King’s cousin
the ambition he names as his only spur
his sense in 5.3 that he has lived long enough
Malcolm hailed as king at the end
questions.explanation: Knowing the conventions lets you explain why Shakespeare shapes the story as he does.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s image of his life in 5.3: “I have liv’d long enough: my way of life / Is fall’n into the sere, the yellow ___;” (5.3.26-27)
questions.explanation: Autumn imagery: his life has withered. This is the self-knowledge that marks a tragic hero.

questions.prompt: Why does a tragic hero need qualities the audience admires?
options: So that the audience wants him to win
So that the play becomes a comedy
So that the fall feels like the loss of something good, creating pity rather than satisfaction
Because all characters must be admirable
questions.explanation: If Macbeth were simply evil, his death would only satisfy. His courage and conscience make it tragic.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that Macbeth gains self-knowledge?
options: “For brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name),” (1.2.18)
“To know my deed, ’twere best not know myself.” (2.2.93)
“Come what come may,” (1.3.163)
“Hang those that talk of fear.” (5.3.43)
questions.explanation: Straight after the murder he understands what he has made of himself.

questions.prompt: What is the term, from Greek, for a tragic hero’s fatal flaw?
questions.explanation: Hamartia is often translated as a fatal flaw or error. In Macbeth it is usually identified as ambition.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the idea of tragedy most effectively?
options: Tragedy is a genre and Macbeth is in it.
When Macbeth sees that his life has fallen “into the sere, the yellow leaf”, the audience pities the waste of the brave soldier of Act 1, which is the tragic effect.
Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic hero because he is brave.
Macbeth is a tragedy because it is sad.
questions.explanation: Use tragedy as a lens on a specific moment, not as a label.
questions.misconception: Labelling Macbeth a tragic hero without explaining how a moment creates pity or fear.

questions.prompt: What makes Macbeth unusual as a tragedy?
options: Nobody dies
The tragic hero is also the villain: a good man chooses evil and watches himself become a tyrant
The ending is happy for Macbeth
The hero is a servant
questions.explanation: This is why critics disagree so sharply about how much sympathy Macbeth deserves.

questions.prompt: Is Lady Macbeth a tragic figure? Argue your view with evidence from at least 2 moments. (8 marks)
questions.model: Lady Macbeth has a tragic shape even though she lacks some features of a tragic hero. At first she seems all-powerful, commanding spirits to fill her “top-full / Of direst cruelty!” (1.5.49-50) and taking control of the murder night. Her fall begins quietly: in 3.2 she admits “Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6), and her husband shuts her out of his plans. In 5.1 her controlled verse has collapsed into broken prose, and she cannot clean the imagined blood from “this little hand.” (5.1.54-55) This is suffering of a deeply tragic kind. However, she has no speech of self-knowledge to match her husband’s, and her death is only reported, with Malcolm adding that she died by her own hand “as ’tis thought”. I would argue she is tragic in her fall but not a tragic hero in the full sense, because the play denies her the moment of understanding it gives him.
checklist: Takes a clear position
Uses her power in Act 1 as the height from which she falls
Uses 3.2 or the banquet to show decline
Analyses the sleepwalking scene
Considers what she lacks (self-knowledge speech, onstage death)
Presents her death as reported
questions.explanation: Either view can reach the top mark if it is argued with evidence.

units.title: Structure and stagecraft
units.summary: The play rises to a turning point in Act 3 and then falls fast. Echoes, juxtapositions, offstage deaths and stage effects such as knocking, darkness and a severed head all shape what the audience feels.

questions.prompt: Where does the turning point of the play come?
options: Act 1, when the Witches appear
Act 3, when Fleance escapes and the Ghost appears
Act 5, when Macbeth dies
Act 2, when the Porter speaks
questions.explanation: Macbeth is at the height of his power in Act 3; from Fleance’s escape onwards, things go wrong for him.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Act 5 has 8 scenes, many of them very short.
Duncan’s murder takes place offstage.
4.3 is one of the shortest, fastest scenes in the play.
Thunder and lightning accompany the Witches’ appearances.

questions.explanation: 4.3 is long and slow, making the audience wait for Ross’s news.

questions.prompt: Match each stage effect to where it is used.
pairs: the end of 2.2 and the start of 2.3
questions.explanation: Light and sound tell the story as much as the words do.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of Macbeth’s rise and fall in order.
items: Praised as a hero in battle
Murders Duncan
Crowned king
Loses control at the banquet
Isolated at Dunsinane
Killed by Macduff
questions.explanation: A clear arc: rise in Acts 1 and 2, height in Act 3, fall in Acts 4 and 5.

questions.prompt: What is the main effect of the knocking straight after the murder?
options: It shows the Witches are coming
It is a cue for music
It signals that the battle has started
It breaks the silence and makes the audience jump with the Macbeths, as the outside world arrives
questions.explanation: Macbeth asks “Whence is that knocking?” (2.2.74-75). The sound turns guilt into panic.

questions.prompt: Which pair shows juxtaposition of comedy and horror?
options: Malcolm’s coronation invitation in 5.8
The witty talk between Lady Macduff and her son, just before the murderers arrive
The Witches’ chant in 4.1
Duncan praising Macbeth in 1.4
questions.explanation: The warmth of the conversation makes the sudden violence more shocking.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s cry as the knocking continues: “Wake Duncan with thy ___! I would thou couldst!” (2.2.94-95)
questions.explanation: The scene ends on a wish he cannot have: to undo the murder.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘In every edition, Macbeth’s death happens offstage.’ Which correction is accurate?
options: Correct
In the Folio, which Folger follows, Macbeth is killed on stage; some editions have only “Exeunt fighting”
Macbeth dies in Act 4
Macbeth kills himself on stage
questions.explanation: Edition differences can change staging. Gutenberg has only “Exeunt fighting”, while the Folio stage direction shows him slain.
questions.misconception: Assuming every edition stages the ending the same way.

questions.prompt: Why does Shakespeare use many short scenes in Act 5?
options: To give the Witches more time
To speed up the pace and show Macbeth’s world closing in as the army approaches
To slow the play down
Because the actors were tired
questions.explanation: Cutting between Dunsinane and the advancing army builds tension and lets the audience know more than Macbeth.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare use structure to present Macbeth’s rise and fall? Refer to at least 2 structural choices. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare structures the play as a clear rise and fall. Macbeth is praised before he appears, so his reputation is built by others: the Captain’s “brave Macbeth” (1.2.18) makes his fall from greatness longer. The murder of Duncan is kept offstage, which turns the audience’s attention to its effect on the murderers rather than the act itself.

Echoes shape the fall. The traitor Cawdor’s execution in Act 1 is mirrored by Macbeth’s own treason, and Macdonwald’s head “upon our battlements” (1.2.25) returns as Macbeth’s head carried by Macduff. In Act 5 the pace quickens through short scenes that cut between the castle and the advancing army, so the audience watches the trap close while Macbeth boasts. The structure itself makes the point that the man who rose by violence falls in the same way.
checklist: Explains the rise-and-fall arc
Comments on Macbeth being introduced through others’ praise
Explains the effect of the offstage murder
Uses an echo (Cawdor, the head, hand-washing)
Explains the pace of Act 5
Links structure to meaning
questions.explanation: AQA examiners in 2023 praised answers that explored how Shakespeare structures the introduction of Macbeth.

units.title: Verse, prose and rhyme
units.summary: Nobles usually speak blank verse; the Porter and the sleepwalking Lady Macbeth speak prose; the Witches chant in short rhyming lines; couplets often seal decisions. A change of form is a signal.

questions.prompt: What is blank verse?
options: Verse with no punctuation
Ordinary sentences with no rhythm
Unrhymed lines with a regular rhythm of 10 syllables (iambic pentameter)
Rhyming lines of 4 beats
questions.explanation: Most of the play is in blank verse, the normal voice of the noble characters.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: The Porter speaks in prose.
The Witches often chant in short lines that start on a stressed beat.
Lady Macbeth speaks in verse while sleepwalking.
Rhyming couplets often come at the end of a scene.

questions.explanation: Her broken prose in 5.1 shows a mind out of control.

questions.prompt: Match each example to its form.
pairs: “If a man were porter of hell gate, he should have old turning the key.” (2.3.1-3)
“Hear it not, Duncan, for it is a knell / That summons thee to heaven or to hell.” (2.1.76-77)
“Is this a dagger which I see before me,” (2.1.44)
questions.explanation: Naming the form is the start; explaining its effect earns the marks.

questions.prompt: Complete the couplet that ends 2.1: “Hear it not, Duncan, for it is a knell / That summons thee to heaven or to ___.” (2.1.76-77)
questions.explanation: The rhyme seals the decision as Macbeth goes to commit the murder.

questions.prompt: Why does Shakespeare give the Porter prose?
options: Because the Porter is a king
Because prose is more serious than verse
Because he is a witch
Prose suits his comic, drunken, rambling character and sets him apart from the nobles’ verse
questions.explanation: Prose is the natural voice of comedy and of characters outside the noble world.

questions.prompt: Which of these are rhyming couplets? Choose 2.
options: “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus.” (3.1.52-53)
“Is this a dagger which I see before me,” (2.1.44)
“Away, and mock the time with fairest show: / False face must hide what the false heart doth know.” (1.7.94-96)
“Banquo, thy soul’s flight, / If it find heaven, must find it out tonight.” (3.1.161-162)
questions.explanation: Show/know and flight/tonight rhyme. Both couplets seal a decision to kill.

questions.prompt: What effect do shared verse lines have in the whispered exchanges after the murder in 2.2?
options: They make the scene comic
They create speed and tension, as the couple finish each other’s lines
They show the characters are asleep
They slow the scene down
questions.explanation: Split lines make the dialogue feel urgent and breathless.

questions.prompt: A student calls “cabin’d, cribb’d, confin’d, bound in” (3.4.26) a tricolon. What is wrong?
options: It is a rhyming couplet
It is prose
Nothing
It is a list of 4, not 3; OCR examiners in 2024 warned that tricolon is over-identified, so name a technique only when it fits and explain its effect
questions.explanation: Better: the run of words beginning with c and b sounds like walls closing in on Macbeth.
questions.misconception: Calling any list a tricolon.

questions.prompt: Why does “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow,” (5.5.22) seem to drag?
options: It is spoken by the Witches
The repeated word and commas slow the rhythm, matching the “petty pace” Macbeth describes
It rhymes with the next line
It is written in prose
questions.explanation: Rhythm can enact meaning: the line moves as slowly as the time it describes.

questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare use changes of form to present Lady Macbeth? (6 marks)
questions.model: In Act 1 Lady Macbeth speaks in controlled, commanding blank verse. Her invocation, “Come, you spirits / That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here,” (1.5.47-48), uses the regular rhythm of verse to sound like a ritual she is directing. In 5.1 that control has gone. She speaks only prose, in short, repeated fragments: “Out, damned spot! out, I say!” (5.1.37) Her thoughts jump from Duncan’s blood to Lady Macduff without any connecting logic. The change from verse to prose shows that the woman who once shaped every line now cannot control even her own sentences, so the form itself shows her mind breaking down.
checklist: Identifies blank verse in Act 1 accurately
Analyses an Act 1 example of controlled speech
Identifies prose in 5.1 accurately
Explains the effect of the broken prose
Links the change of form to her loss of control
questions.explanation: OCR examiners in 2024 found some students struggled to comment on blank verse accurately, so be precise with terms.

units.title: Soliloquies, asides and dramatic irony
units.summary: Soliloquies and asides let the audience into Macbeth’s mind, and dramatic irony comes from knowing what other characters do not. Read every “Aside” stage direction before you analyse an extract.

questions.prompt: What is an aside?
options: A stage direction for an exit
A long speech made alone on stage
A song sung by the Witches
A line spoken to the audience, or to one character, that others on stage do not hear
questions.explanation: A soliloquy is spoken alone; an aside is spoken while others are present.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: “If it were done when ’tis done” begins a soliloquy in 1.7.
Banquo has a soliloquy at the start of 3.1.
An aside is heard by everyone on stage.
Macbeth’s “Tomorrow” speech comes in 5.5.

questions.explanation: Others on stage do not hear an aside; that is what creates dramatic irony.

questions.prompt: Match each soliloquy to its opening words.
pairs: “Is this a dagger which I see before me,”
questions.explanation: Knowing where each soliloquy falls lets you track Macbeth’s mind across the play.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s aside in 1.3: “Present fears / Are less than horrible ___.” (1.3.150-151)
questions.explanation: What he imagines frightens him more than any real danger.

questions.prompt: Which line creates dramatic irony because the audience knows what Duncan does not?
options: “O valiant cousin! worthy gentleman!” (1.2.26)
“I have begun to plant thee,” (1.4.32)
“What bloody man is that?” (1.2.1)
“This castle hath a pleasant seat.” (1.6.1)
questions.explanation: Duncan admires the pleasant air of the castle where he will be murdered that night.

questions.prompt: In the 1.3 extract, who does not hear Macbeth’s asides?
options: The audience
Banquo, Ross and Angus
The Witches, who stay on stage
Lady Macbeth, who is on stage
questions.explanation: Banquo can only see that Macbeth is “rapt”; the audience hears the horrid image in his mind.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in Macbeth’s argument in the 1.7 soliloquy in order.
items: He wishes the deed could be done quickly with no consequences
He fears judgement in this life
He lists his duties as kinsman, subject and host
He imagines Duncan’s virtues pleading like angels
He admits only vaulting ambition drives him
questions.explanation: The soliloquy builds a case against murder, then collapses into the admission about ambition.

questions.prompt: Eduqas examiners in 2023 reported that Banquo’s “Cousins, a word, I pray you.” (1.3.139) was often misread. What does it mean?
options: Banquo speaks to his cousin Macbeth about the Witches
Banquo asks Ross and Angus for a quiet word, “I pray you” meaning please
Banquo prays to God
Banquo asks the Witches to return
questions.explanation: “I pray you” is a polite request, not a prayer. Reading the line in context avoids the mistake.
questions.misconception: Reading “I pray you” as a prayer.

questions.prompt: Macbeth says in an aside, “The greatest is behind.” (1.3.126) What does he mean?
options: The greatest prophecy, becoming king, is still to come
Banquo is standing behind him
The battle was the greatest event
The greatest danger is behind him
questions.explanation: “Behind” means still to follow. Eduqas examiners in 2023 listed this line among those often misunderstood.

questions.prompt: Eduqas-style: Look at Macbeth’s asides in 1.3 (from “This supernatural soliciting” to “Come what come may”). How might an audience respond to this part of the play? (8 marks)
questions.model: An audience is likely to feel unease, because the asides let us hear what Macbeth hides from the men beside him. He argues with himself in balanced phrases, “Cannot be ill; cannot be good.” (1.3.144), which show a mind weighing a choice. Then he admits that the idea of murder makes his hair stand on end and his “seated heart knock at my ribs,” (1.3.149). The physical detail makes his fear vivid and shows his conscience is alive. While he speaks, Banquo can only observe “Look, how our partner’s rapt.” (1.3.156), so the audience shares a secret the others do not. Finally Macbeth seems to step back: “If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me / Without my stir.” (1.3.157-159) An audience may feel relief, yet also suspect that the thought, once spoken, will not go away.
checklist: Explains that asides are hidden from the other characters
Analyses the balanced phrasing or the physical reaction
Uses Banquo’s line to show what the others see
Describes a likely audience response with reasons
Reads “chance may crown me / Without my stir” correctly
No context needed (Eduqas)
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners in 2023 said that answers which ignored or misunderstood the asides struggled.

units.title: Imagery and motifs (1): blood and sleep
units.summary: Blood moves from honour to guilt to madness; sleep moves from peace to torment. Show how a motif changes across the play, and you have a reason to move from the extract to other moments.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “What bloody man is that?” (1.2.1)
options: Duncan
Banquo
Macbeth
Malcolm
questions.explanation: The first line of 1.2. Here blood means honour: the Captain’s wounds prove his courage.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: In 1.2 blood is a sign of honour and courage.
Lady Macbeth asks the spirits to make her blood thick.
Macbeth envies Duncan because Duncan sleeps well in his grave.
By the end, sleep has become a comfort to both Macbeths.

questions.explanation: Sleep is lost: Macbeth “shall sleep no more” and Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep.

questions.prompt: Put these blood images in the order they appear.
items: The bleeding Captain reports the battle
Lady Macbeth asks the spirits to make thick her blood
Macbeth asks if Neptune’s ocean can wash his hand
Macbeth says blood will have blood
Lady Macbeth cries out at the damned spot
questions.explanation: Honour, then cruelty, guilt, more murder, and finally madness.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s description of sleep: “Sleep that knits up the ravell’d ___ of care,” (2.2.49)
questions.explanation: A “sleave” is a tangle of silk thread. Some editions print “sleeve”; the image is the same.

questions.prompt: How does the meaning of blood change between 1.2 and 2.2?
options: It does not change
From guilt to honour
From a sign of illness to a sign of health
From a sign of honour in battle to a sign of guilt that cannot be washed away
questions.explanation: Tracking this change gives you a ready-made argument about Macbeth’s fall.

questions.prompt: Match each sleep image to what it shows.
pairs: “Sleep that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care,” (2.2.49)
sleep as a healer of worry
“After life’s fitful fever he sleeps well;” (3.2.26)
only the dead can rest now
“You lack the season of all natures, sleep.” (3.4.173)
sleep keeps nature fresh, and they have lost it
even asleep, she finds no rest
questions.explanation: Sleep is the reward of innocence that the Macbeths destroy for themselves.

questions.prompt: Lady Macbeth says “You lack the season of all natures, sleep.” (3.4.173) What does “season” mean here?
options: A sports season
A reason
Seasoning, like the salt that keeps food fresh
A time of year
questions.explanation: Sleep preserves and refreshes every living thing, as salt preserves food.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Blood always stands for guilt in Macbeth.’ Which comment is most accurate?
options: Blood never appears in the play
Correct
Not always: in 1.2 the Captain’s blood stands for honour, and the change to guilt is the point to analyse
Blood stands only for the Witches
questions.explanation: Showing how an image changes is what examiners reward.
questions.misconception: Treating a motif as having one fixed meaning.

questions.prompt: Why does Macbeth’s “Macbeth does murder sleep” image matter for the rest of the play?
options: It is a joke
It shows Macbeth is tired after the battle
It means Duncan was awake when killed
It predicts the sleeplessness that torments both Macbeths, ending in Lady Macbeth’s sleepwalking
questions.explanation: By killing a sleeping man, Macbeth kills his own peace; the motif runs to 5.1.

questions.prompt: Track the blood motif from Act 1 to Act 5. How does Shakespeare use it to show change? (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare uses blood to measure Macbeth’s fall. In 1.2 Duncan greets the wounded Captain with “What bloody man is that?” (1.2.1), and blood is a badge of honour earned in the king’s service. In 1.5 Lady Macbeth asks the spirits to “make thick my blood,” (1.5.50) so that pity cannot flow through her; blood now stands for human feeling she wants to destroy.

After the murder it becomes guilt. Macbeth asks whether “all great Neptune’s ocean” could “wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79), an image that makes his crime larger than the sea. By 3.4 it has become a law: “blood will have blood.” (3.4.151) Finally Lady Macbeth, who said a little water would clear them, rubs at a spot that will not go: “Out, damned spot!” (5.1.37). The motif moves from honour to guilt to madness, so tracking it shows the moral collapse of both characters.
checklist: Uses the Captain’s blood as honour (1.2)
Uses Lady Macbeth’s “make thick my blood” (1.5)
Analyses the ocean image (2.2)
Uses “blood will have blood” (3.4)
Uses the sleepwalking scene (5.1)
Explains the change the motif shows
questions.explanation: A motif essay is strongest when each step shows a new meaning.

units.title: Imagery and motifs (2): darkness, clothing, nature
units.summary: Darkness hides crime and light exposes it; borrowed and oversized clothes show a stolen title; predators hunt innocent creatures; children stand for the future Macbeth cannot control; Scotland is sick until Malcolm heals it.

questions.prompt: Which image does Macbeth use when he hears he is Thane of Cawdor?
options: Borrowed robes
A scorpion
A naked new-born babe
A giant’s robe
questions.explanation: “why do you dress me / In borrow’d robes?” (1.3.114-115) begins the clothing image.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Both Macbeth and Lady Macbeth call on darkness to hide their crimes.
Angus compares Macbeth’s title to a giant’s robe on a dwarfish thief.
Macbeth calls Banquo and Fleance a “poor wren”.
Pity is imagined as a naked new-born babe.

questions.explanation: Lady Macduff uses the “poor wren” image for a mother bird defending her young.

questions.prompt: Match each term to an example.
pairs: “O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!” (3.2.41)
questions.explanation: Use terms accurately, then say what the image does.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s question: “why do you dress me / In borrow’d ___?” (1.3.114-115)
questions.explanation: His titles are like someone else’s clothes. By Act 5 the clothes are far too big.

questions.prompt: Edexcel’s 2025 part (b) asked about symbols elsewhere in the play. Which were rewarded, according to the examiners?
options: Only the Witches’ cauldron
Only colours
Blood, the dagger, Banquo’s ghost, water, clothing, animals and birds, and even characters as symbols
Only the dagger
questions.explanation: Some candidates struggled to know what they could discuss. A wide range was accepted.

questions.prompt: Which images involve children or babies? Choose 2.
options: “Bring forth men-children only;” (1.7.83)
“like a giant’s robe” (5.2.24)
“And pity, like a naked new-born babe,” (1.7.21)
“Bleed, bleed, poor country!” (4.3.39)
questions.explanation: Children stand for the future, and for the heirs Macbeth cannot control.

questions.prompt: Ross calls Macduff’s murdered family “these murder’d deer,” (4.3.242). What does the image suggest?
options: Food for a feast
Macduff is a hunter
Innocent creatures hunted and slaughtered for sport
Wild animals that deserved death
questions.explanation: Like the falcon and the wren, the deer are innocent victims of a predator.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The simile “full of scorpions is my mind” shows Macbeth is troubled.’ What is wrong?
options: It is a metaphor, not a simile (there is no “like” or “as”), and the comment needs to explain what the stinging image suggests
It is personification
Nothing
The line is Lady Macbeth’s
questions.explanation: Accurate terms and developed explanation both matter.
questions.misconception: Confusing metaphor and simile.

questions.prompt: Macbeth’s titles are compared to borrowed robes and to a giant’s robe. What does this imagery suggest about his rule?
options: Because Duncan gives him new clothes
Because he wears a crown in every scene
Because Macbeth is a tailor
Because his titles never fit: they are borrowed in 1.3 and hang loose like a giant’s robe on a thief in 5.2
questions.explanation: The image shows a man who has stolen a role too big for him.

questions.prompt: Edexcel part (b)-style: Explain the importance of symbols elsewhere in the play. You may choose any symbols. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Symbols carry the play’s ideas from scene to scene. Clothing shows that Macbeth’s power never fits. When he is told he is Thane of Cawdor he asks “why do you dress me / In borrow’d robes?” (1.3.114-115), and by Act 5 Angus says his title hangs “like a giant’s robe / Upon a dwarfish thief.” (5.2.24-25) The robe has not changed size; Macbeth has shrunk into the thief he is.

Light and darkness work in the same way. Both Macbeths call on night to hide their crimes, Macbeth with “Stars, hide your fires!” (1.4.57), but in 5.1 Lady Macbeth must have “light by her continually” (5.1.24-25). The darkness she once welcomed has become unbearable. In a play written for an audience who believed kingship came from God, these symbols suggest that stolen power and hidden crimes cannot stay hidden for long.
checklist: Chooses symbols from outside any given extract
Analyses clothing (borrowed robes, giant’s robe)
Analyses light and darkness
Shows how each symbol changes through the play
Integrates context briefly (AO3 in part b)
Explains why symbols matter to the play’s meaning
questions.explanation: Edexcel part (b) is marked for AO1 and AO3, so link context to your argument.

units.title: Key quotations: ambition, power and kingship
units.summary: Learn short, flexible quotations on ambition and power, each with its speaker and reference. Pair early lines with later ones to show change, and pick the single word you would analyse.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s aside: “Two truths are told, / As happy prologues to the swelling act / Of the imperial ___.” (1.3.140-142)
questions.explanation: Theatre imagery: the prophecies feel like the prologue to a grand play about kingship.

questions.prompt: In which scene does Lady Macbeth say “Naught’s had, all’s spent,”?
questions.explanation: It opens 3.2, spoken alone: the first sign that the crown has brought no contentment.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to its speaker.
pairs: “Thriftless ambition, that will ravin up / Thine own life’s means!” (2.4.40-41)
“I have begun to plant thee, and will labour / To make thee full of growing.” (1.4.32-33)
“now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him,” (5.2.23-24)
questions.explanation: Knowing who speaks is part of knowing a quotation.

questions.prompt: Put these quotations in the order they appear in the play.
items: “Two truths are told,”
“Stars, hide your fires!”
“Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself”
“To be thus is nothing,”
“I have liv’d long enough:”
questions.explanation: 1.3, 1.4, 1.7, 3.1, 5.3: together they trace ambition from excitement to emptiness.

questions.prompt: In “Upon my head they plac’d a fruitless crown,” (3.1.66), which single word gives you the most to analyse?
options: upon
fruitless
head
they
questions.explanation: “Fruitless” suggests a barren tree with no heirs, against Duncan’s planting and Banquo’s line of kings.

questions.prompt: Complete Malcolm’s promise: “by the grace of Grace, / We will perform in measure, time, and ___.” (5.8.85-86)
questions.explanation: The rhyming couplet, grace and place, gives a sense of order restored.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that stolen power brings fear instead of security?
options: “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus.” (3.1.52-53)
“Two truths are told,” (1.3.140)
“I have begun to plant thee,” (1.4.32)
“Thou wouldst be great;” (1.5.18)
questions.explanation: Being king is “nothing” to Macbeth without safety, which drives him to more murder.

questions.prompt: A student can only remember Macbeth’s motive as ‘ambition that jumps too high’ and analyses the word ‘jumps’. What would OCR examiners say?
options: The answer must be left blank
Misquotation is not penalised as such, but analysis of words that are not Shakespeare’s own cannot be credited; paraphrase instead and analyse words you are sure of
Full marks for the analysis
Only AO4 marks are affected
questions.explanation: If unsure of the wording, paraphrase it and put your analysis into the ideas, or choose a quotation you know exactly.
questions.misconception: Analysing misremembered words as if they were Shakespeare’s.

questions.prompt: Which sentence embeds a quotation most effectively?
options: In 1.7 there is a quotation about ambition.
Macbeth feels ambitious. “Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (1.7.27). This shows ambition.
Ambition is a theme in the play and Macbeth has it.
Macbeth sees his ambition as a rider whose leap is so “Vaulting” that it “o’erleaps itself” (1.7.27), predicting his own fall.
questions.explanation: Short quotations woven into your own sentence let you analyse exact words.

questions.prompt: Using at least 2 quotations, write a paragraph on how Shakespeare presents ambition as self-destructive. (6 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare presents ambition as a force that destroys the person it drives. Macbeth himself imagines it as a rider: he has no spur “but only / Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (1.7.26-27). The image is of a leap so eager that the rider falls on the other side, so he predicts his own fall before he acts. Once he is king, ambition brings no reward. He complains that the Witches “plac’d a fruitless crown” (3.1.66) upon his head; the word “fruitless” turns the crown into a barren tree with no heirs. By Act 5 his life has fallen “into the sere, the yellow leaf;” (5.3.27). The images move from a leap upwards to a withered leaf, which shows ambition consuming the man it promised to raise.
checklist: States a clear point about ambition
Uses at least 2 accurate quotations with references
Analyses specific words or images
Shows change across the play
Embeds quotations smoothly
questions.explanation: Pairing an early and a late quotation is an efficient way to show change.

units.title: Key quotations: the supernatural, fate and free will
units.summary: Learn quotations on the Witches, visions and choice. Pair Banquo’s early warning with Macbeth’s late realisation, and use “We will proceed no further” as proof that Macbeth could stop.

questions.prompt: Complete the Third Witch’s prophecy: “All hail, Macbeth! that shalt be king ___!” (1.3.53)
questions.explanation: “Hereafter” is vague about how and when, which leaves room for Macbeth’s own choices.

questions.prompt: True or false?
