“Thou shalt get kings, though thou be none:” is spoken to Macbeth.
“A dagger of the mind” comes from 2.1.
Macbeth says “come, fate, into the list”.

questions.explanation: “Thou shalt get kings” is the Third Witch’s prophecy to Banquo.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to what it shows.
pairs: “You should be women, / And yet your beards forbid me to interpret / That you are so.” (1.3.47-49)
“This supernatural soliciting / Cannot be ill; cannot be good.” (1.3.143-144)
“none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth.” (4.1.91-92)
an equivocal promise that breeds false confidence
“We will proceed no further in this business:” (1.7.34)
proof that Macbeth is free to stop
questions.explanation: Each quotation fits more than one essay; the comment shows how to use it.

questions.prompt: Put these quotations in the order they appear.
items: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair:”
“The instruments of darkness tell us truths;”
“Rather than so, come, fate, into the list,”
“By the pricking of my thumbs,”
“That palter with us in a double sense;”

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s realisation: “And be these juggling fiends no more believ’d, / That palter with us in a double ___;” (5.8.23-24)
questions.explanation: Too late, he sees that the prophecies had double meanings.

questions.prompt: Which later quotation pairs best with Banquo’s warning “The instruments of darkness tell us truths;” (1.3.136)?
options: “To doubt th’ equivocation of the fiend, / That lies like truth.” (5.5.49-50)
“Thou shalt get kings, though thou be none:” (1.3.70)
“Double, double, toil and trouble;” (4.1.10)
“When shall we three meet again?” (1.1.1)
questions.explanation: Banquo saw in 1.3 what Macbeth sees only in 5.5: truth used to deceive.

questions.prompt: In “That palter with us in a double sense;” (5.8.24), what does “palter” suggest?
options: To fight bravely
To deal deceitfully, using words that shift their meaning
To sing loudly
To heal the sick
questions.explanation: The fiends trick by playing with meanings, which is exactly what equivocation does.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Macbeth says “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” in 1.3.’ What is wrong?
options: It comes from 5.1
Banquo says it
The Witches chant it together in 1.1; Macbeth’s first line, “So foul and fair a day I have not seen.”, echoes it in 1.3
Nothing
questions.explanation: Getting the speaker right lets you make the better point: Macbeth unknowingly echoes the Witches.
questions.misconception: Attributing the Witches’ paradox to Macbeth.

questions.prompt: Which argument does “We will proceed no further in this business:” (1.7.34) support most strongly?
options: Macbeth never thinks about murder
Macbeth has free will: he can decide against the murder, so his later choice is his own
The Witches control Macbeth completely
Lady Macbeth is a witch
questions.explanation: It is the clearest evidence that fate does not force him.

questions.prompt: Using at least 2 quotations, write a paragraph on whether Macbeth is controlled by fate. (6 marks)
questions.model: The prophecies give Macbeth a goal, but the quotations show that he chooses how to reach it. The Third Witch promises only that he “shalt be king hereafter!” (1.3.53), a prophecy silent about murder. Macbeth even considers leaving it to chance, and in 1.7 decides: “We will proceed no further in this business:” (1.7.34). A man controlled by fate could not stop himself like this. Later he tries to fight destiny, crying “come, fate, into the list,” (3.1.76), but fails to destroy Banquo’s line. Only at the end does he see how the Witches deceived him, as “juggling fiends” who “palter with us in a double sense;” (5.8.24). Fate tempts and misleads him; it does not force him.
checklist: Takes a clear position
Uses the vague first prophecy
Uses “We will proceed no further” as evidence of choice
Uses a later quotation on fate or equivocation
Embeds quotations and analyses words
questions.explanation: Judgement plus 2 well-chosen quotations makes a strong paragraph.

units.title: Key quotations: guilt, appearance and reality
units.summary: Learn quotations on conscience and deception. Many work in pairs: Macbeth’s ocean and Lady Macbeth’s perfumes; ’what’s done is done’ and ’what’s done cannot be undone’.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s words to his wife: “And make our faces ___ to our hearts, / Disguising what they are.” (3.2.38-39)
questions.explanation: The King must wear a mask over his true feelings.

questions.prompt: What are “vizards”?
options: Servants
Swords
Wizards
Masks
questions.explanation: Their faces must become masks that hide their hearts.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to its speaker.
pairs: “Canst thou not minister to a mind diseas’d,” (5.3.50)
“More needs she the divine than the physician.” (5.1.78)
“A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86)
questions.explanation: Guilt is seen from inside by the Macbeths and from outside by the Doctor and Gentlewoman.

questions.prompt: Put these quotations in the order they appear.
items: “There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face:”
“This castle hath a pleasant seat.”
“False face must hide what the false heart doth know.”
“There’s daggers in men’s smiles:”
“That lies like truth.”

questions.prompt: Which quotation from 5.1 echoes Macbeth’s “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79)
options: “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.” (5.1.53-55)
“The Thane of Fife had a wife.” (5.1.44)
“More needs she the divine than the physician.” (5.1.78)
“Hell is murky!” (5.1.38)
questions.explanation: Both images say that nothing in the world can clean the guilty hand. Now she feels what he felt.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s aside: “The eye wink at the hand, yet let that be, / Which the eye fears, when it is done, to ___.” (1.4.59-60)
questions.explanation: He wants his eyes to ignore what his hand does: a divided self.

questions.prompt: Which technique is most clearly at work in “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79)?
options: Pun
Hyperbole, exaggeration that makes guilt larger than the sea
Rhyming couplet
Prose
questions.explanation: The exaggeration conveys how overwhelming his guilt feels.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘In 5.1 Lady Macbeth says “what’s done is done.”’ What is wrong?
options: Neither line is in the play
That line is from 3.2; in 5.1 she says “What’s done cannot be undone.”, which reverses its meaning
Macbeth says both lines
Nothing
questions.explanation: The 2 lines make a powerful pair: acceptance in 3.2 becomes despair in 5.1.
questions.misconception: Confusing 2 similar quotations from different scenes.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a quotation about appearance and reality most effectively?
options: Lady Macbeth tells him to hide his thoughts.
“look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t.” This is a quotation.
There is a flower in 1.5.
Lady Macbeth tells her husband to “look like the innocent flower,” but be the snake beneath, an image that hides danger inside beauty.
questions.explanation: Embed a short phrase, then explain the image.

questions.prompt: Using at least 2 quotations, write a paragraph on how Shakespeare presents guilt in both Macbeths. (6 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare shows both Macbeths unable to escape guilt, though it strikes them at different times. Straight after the murder Macbeth asks whether “all great Neptune’s ocean” could “wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79); the hyperbole makes his guilt larger than the sea. His wife answers with confidence, “A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86). Yet in 5.1 she finds that “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.” (5.1.53-55) Her image now matches his: nothing in the world can clean the hand. The echo shows that her guilt was delayed, not avoided, and the word “little” turns from confidence to helplessness.
checklist: Uses the ocean image (2.2)
Uses “A little water” (2.2)
Uses the perfumes of Arabia (5.1)
Explains the echo between the 2 characters
Analyses a specific word (“little”, “all”)
questions.explanation: Learning quotations in pairs makes paragraphs like this easy to build.

units.title: Key quotations: gender and violence
units.summary: Learn quotations on manhood, womanhood and bloodshed. Link Lady Macbeth’s “Are you a man?” with Macduff’s “feel it as a man”, and Macbeth’s ’hack’d’ in 5.3 with ’unseam’d’ in 1.2.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth’s challenge at the banquet: “Are you a ___?” (3.4.70)
questions.explanation: Her old weapon from 1.7, which no longer works on a man haunted by guilt.

questions.prompt: Who says this? “Your castle is surpris’d; your wife and babes / Savagely slaughter’d.” (4.3.240-241)
options: Ross
The Doctor
Lennox
Malcolm
questions.explanation: Ross delivers the news bluntly after a long hesitation.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to its speaker.
pairs: “When you durst do it, then you were a man;” (1.7.56)
“I dare do all that may become a man;” (1.7.51)
“But I must also feel it as a man:” (4.3.261)
questions.explanation: 4 voices, 4 ideas of what a man or a parent should be.

items: “Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chops,”
“When you durst do it, then you were a man;”
“It will have blood, they say, blood will have blood.”
“give to th’ edge o’ th’ sword / His wife, his babes,”
“I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d.”

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macduff’s image: “He wants the natural ___; for the poor wren,” (4.2.11)
questions.explanation: She accuses her husband of lacking the natural instinct to protect his family.

questions.prompt: In “I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d.” (5.3.38), which word could you pair with a word from the Captain’s report in 1.2?
options: “flesh”, which recalls “fled”
“hack’d”, which recalls “unseam’d”
“bones”, which recalls “battlements”
“fight”, which recalls “Fair”
questions.explanation: AQA examiners in 2023 noted that pairing “hacked” with “unseamed” gave students a way into how Macbeth changes.

questions.prompt: Macbeth praises his wife’s “undaunted mettle” in 1.7. Why is “mettle” a rich word to analyse?

It means spirit or courage and puns on “metal”, suggesting she is hard, unbending and fit to produce only male children
It means a medal for bravery
It describes a sword
questions.explanation: Double meanings like this are worth a sentence of analysis.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Lady Macbeth says “Bring forth men-children only;” to show she wants sons.’ What is wrong?
options: Nothing
Lady Macduff says it
Macbeth says it to her, admiring her fierce courage as masculine
Malcolm says it
questions.explanation: Getting the speaker right changes the point: it is his view of her.
questions.misconception: Giving a line to the wrong speaker.

questions.prompt: Which pair of quotations best shows the play questioning Lady Macbeth’s idea of manhood?
options: “Are you a man?” and “Are you a man?”
“Out, damned spot!” and “Hell is murky!”
“When you durst do it, then you were a man;” and “But I must also feel it as a man:”
“Bring forth men-children only;” and “Leave all the rest to me.”
questions.explanation: Daring to kill, set against the right to feel grief: the play gives Macduff the last word.

questions.prompt: Using at least 2 quotations, write a paragraph on how Shakespeare presents violence changing through the play. (6 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare presents violence first as heroic and then as monstrous. The Captain describes how Macbeth “unseam’d him from the nave to the chops,” (1.2.24), and the brutal verb is praised because it serves the king. By Act 4 the same man orders his murderers to “give to th’ edge o’ th’ sword / His wife, his babes,” (4.1.172-173). The violence has lost any purpose; it falls on the innocent because Macduff himself has escaped. In 5.3 Macbeth’s vow, “I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d.” (5.3.38), returns to the battlefield language of Act 1, so the warrior seems to come back. The difference is that this time he fights to defend a stolen crown.

Uses the order to kill Macduff’s family (4.1)
Uses 5.3 ’hack’d’ and links it to 1.2
Explains how the purpose of violence changes

questions.explanation: A pair of echoing words gives an answer a clear structure.

units.summary: Learn quotations on order and disorder, then practise quoting well: keep it short, embed it, use a slash for a verse line break, and paraphrase when you are unsure of the exact words.

Words you have left out
A stage direction
A change of speaker

pairs: “Lamentings heard i’ th’ air, strange screams of death,” (2.3.63-64)
“A falcon, towering in her pride of place,” (2.4.15)
questions.explanation: Disorder is reported by many voices, not just the main characters.

items: “Lamentings heard i’ th’ air,”
“dark night strangles the travelling lamp.”
“You know your own degrees, sit down.”
“Bleed, bleed, poor country!”
“Unnatural deeds / Do breed unnatural troubles:”

‘Stars / hide your fires! Let not light see / my black and deep desires.’

questions.prompt: OCR examiners in 2024 commented on heavy square-bracket edits in quotations. What was the problem?

They are not allowed by the exam board
They are only allowed in prose
questions.explanation: Choose a shorter quotation that fits your sentence instead of rewriting Shakespeare’s words in brackets.
questions.misconception: Over-editing quotations with square brackets.

questions.prompt: Which pair of quotations best shows order collapsing within the banquet scene?
options: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair:” (1.1.12) and “Double, double, toil and trouble;” (4.1.10)
“You know your own degrees, sit down.” (3.4.1) and “Stand not upon the order of your going,” (3.4.146)
“Out, damned spot! out, I say!” (5.1.37) and “Hell is murky!” (5.1.38)
“Bleed, bleed, poor country!” (4.3.39) and “Hail, King of Scotland!” (5.8.70)
questions.explanation: The feast that began with guests seated by rank ends with Lady Macbeth sending them out in any order.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph on how Shakespeare presents disorder after Duncan’s murder, embedding at least 2 short quotations with references. (6 marks)
questions.model: After the murder, Shakespeare shows nature itself falling into disorder. Lennox reports “strange screams of death,” (2.3.63-64) on the night of the killing, as if the air were mourning. The next day Ross describes how “dark night strangles the travelling lamp.” (2.4.9) The personification turns night into a murderer, so the sky repeats Macbeth’s crime against his king. The Old Man adds that a falcon was “by a mousing owl hawk’d at and kill’d.” (2.4.16), a lower bird destroying a higher one. Together these images show that killing a king breaks more than a law: it damages the whole order of things.
checklist: Embeds at least 2 short quotations
Gives accurate references
Analyses a specific image (personification, the falcon and owl)
Explains how disorder mirrors the murder
Keeps quotations short and flowing
questions.explanation: Short, embedded quotations with exact references show secure knowledge.

units.title: The assessment objectives in plain English
units.summary: Every mark comes from 4 assessment objectives: your argument and evidence (AO1), Shakespeare’s methods (AO2), context (AO3) and accurate writing (AO4). The top levels reward a clear, exploratory argument.

questions.prompt: Match each assessment objective to what it means for your Macbeth answer.
pairs: a clear personal argument backed by well-chosen references
how Shakespeare’s language, form and structure create meaning
how the contexts of the play shape its ideas
accurate spelling, punctuation, vocabulary and sentence structure
questions.explanation: AO wording comes from the DfE’s subject content; these are plain-English versions.

questions.prompt: Which assessment objective rewards analysis of language, form and structure?
options: AO4
AO2
AO3
AO1
questions.explanation: AO2 carries the largest share of marks across the qualification: 40 to 45% under DfE rules.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: On all 4 boards, the exam is closed book.
Context (AO3) earns marks in Eduqas’s Shakespeare questions.
Edexcel part (a) assesses AO2 only.
AQA gives AO3 6 of the 30 marks in Section A.

questions.explanation: Eduqas assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 in Section A. Context earns nothing there.

questions.prompt: On AQA Paper 1 Section A, the 30 marks are AO1 12, AO2 12 and AO3 6. How many extra marks are given for AO4?
questions.explanation: AQA adds 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar, so Section A is worth 34 marks in total.

questions.prompt: Put these AQA level descriptions in order, from lowest to highest.
items: Simple, explicit comments, often retelling the story
Supported, relevant comments that identify some methods
Explained, structured comments with some relevant terms
Clear, sustained understanding with clear explanation of effects
Thoughtful, developed response with references woven in
Critical, exploratory argument with judicious references
questions.explanation: The ladder climbs from retelling, to explaining, to exploring.

questions.prompt: Which description belongs to AQA’s Level 6 (26 to 30 marks)?
options: Relevant comments supported by some references
A critical, exploratory, conceptualised argument with judicious references and fine-grained analysis
Simple comments with little reference to the text
Explained comments with some terminology
questions.explanation: Paraphrased from the AQA mark scheme. The leap to the top comes from having a single clear idea about the question.

questions.prompt: Under DfE rules, which assessment objective carries the largest share of GCSE English Literature marks?
questions.explanation: AO2 is the largest; AO1 is close behind. Together they carry most of the marks on every board.

questions.prompt: A student believes that using as many technical terms as possible guarantees high AO2 marks. Which comment is most accurate?
options: AO2 asks for relevant terminology where appropriate; marks come from explaining how methods create meaning
Terms lose marks on every board
AO2 is only about spelling
Correct: terms are counted
questions.explanation: Examiners reward understanding, not vocabulary. A term with no explanation earns little.
questions.misconception: Thinking terminology alone earns AO2 marks.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows the critical style AO1 asks for?
options: Shakespeare presents the dagger as a vision that leads Macbeth “the way that I was going;” (2.1.54), suggesting that the supernatural only confirms a choice he has made.
Macbeth sees a dagger and it is scary.
I really liked the part where Macbeth sees the dagger.
The dagger scene is in Act 2.
questions.explanation: Writing as a critic means making an argued point about how Shakespeare presents something.

questions.prompt: Write 1 paragraph on Macbeth’s ambition that meets AO1, AO2 and AO3 at once, as an AQA answer would. Then label where each AO appears. (6 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare presents Macbeth’s ambition as a force he recognises as dangerous even as he yields to it [AO1]. Alone in 1.7 he admits he has no spur “but only / Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (1.7.26-27); the image of a rider leaping so eagerly that he falls on the other side predicts his own fall [AO2]. For an audience who believed kings ruled by God’s will, this ambition was more than a personal flaw, because it aimed at killing the Lord’s anointed [AO3]. Shakespeare lets Macbeth see the danger clearly, which makes his choice to continue more tragic [AO1].
checklist: Opens with an argued point that answers a question (AO1)
Uses a precise, embedded quotation (AO1)
Analyses an image or method and its effect (AO2)
Includes 1 brief, linked context point (AO3)
Labels each AO accurately
questions.explanation: AQA rewards integration: the best paragraphs combine AOs rather than treating them separately.

units.title: How AQA and Edexcel set the question
units.summary: AQA: 1 extract-based question, 30 marks plus 4 for SPaG, covering the extract and the whole play. Edexcel: part (a) on the extract (AO2 only) and part (b) on a theme elsewhere in the play (AO1 and AO3).

questions.prompt: How many marks is AQA Paper 1 Section A worth in total, including SPaG?
questions.explanation: 30 marks for the response plus 4 for AO4.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: AQA gives 1 question on the play, with no choice.
AQA’s printed extract is roughly 20 to 30 lines long.
Edexcel part (b) should be based mainly on the printed extract.
Edexcel’s Shakespeare section has no AO4 marks.

questions.explanation: Part (b) asks about the theme elsewhere in the play; material from the extract earns nothing there.

questions.prompt: Match each recent question to its board and year.
pairs: Lady Macbeth in 1.7, then power elsewhere
Macduff and Macbeth in 5.8, then violence elsewhere
the Witches in 1.3, then symbols elsewhere
the Captain’s report in 1.2: Macbeth as a violent character
questions.explanation: Recent questions show the range: characters, relationships, themes and even symbols.

questions.prompt: Edexcel part (b) is worth 20 marks: some for AO1 and 5 for AO3. How many marks are for AO1?
questions.explanation: 20 minus 5 = 15. AO1 dominates part (b), but context is required.

questions.prompt: On AQA, what can happen if you write only about the extract and ignore the rest of the play?
options: You lose only the SPaG marks
Nothing
You get extra marks for detail
Your mark can be capped at the top of Level 2
questions.explanation: The question has 2 bullets: the extract and the play as a whole. Cover both.

questions.prompt: Put these AQA questions on Macbeth in date order.
items: Macbeth as a violent character (the Captain’s report)
Macbeth as a male character who changes (5.3)
Lady Macbeth as a strong female character (1.7)
Macbeth as an ambitious character (“If it were done”)
questions.explanation: 2019, 2023, 2024, 2025. Both 2024 and 2025 used extracts from 1.7.

questions.prompt: Paper 1 lasts 1 hour 45 minutes for 2 sections. What does AQA’s 2023 report advise about timing?
options: Give broadly equal time to each section, about 50 minutes each
Spend almost all the time on Shakespeare
There is no advice
Spend 20 minutes on Shakespeare
questions.explanation: The report says “the best approach is to give broadly equal time to each section”.

questions.prompt: In Edexcel part (a), a student writes a paragraph about King James and witchcraft. What is wrong?
options: Part (a) assesses AO2 only, so contextual points are not rewarded there
Nothing
Edexcel bans the word “Jacobean”
Context must go in part (a) only
questions.explanation: Edexcel’s 2024 feedback noted context in part (a), “which is not assessed”. Save context for part (b).
questions.misconception: Putting context into Edexcel part (a).

questions.prompt: AQA questions ask “how far” Shakespeare presents something. Why does this matter?
options: It means you should not use the extract
It invites a judgement: agree, disagree or argue “to some extent”, and say which
It means you must agree completely
It means you must write as much as possible
questions.explanation: A clear judgement gives the essay a thesis to prove.

questions.prompt: AQA-style plan: Starting with an extract from 5.3, explore how far Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a man who has lost everything. Write a thesis and choose 4 moments, at least 2 from beyond the extract. (6 marks)
questions.model:
Thesis: By Act 5 Macbeth has lost almost everything that gave his life meaning, his wife, his friends, his peace and his fear, but Shakespeare leaves him his courage, so the loss is not complete.
Extract (5.3): “I have liv’d long enough: my way of life / Is fall’n into the sere, the yellow leaf;” (5.3.26-27) and the lost “honour, love, obedience, troops of friends,” (5.3.29). Method: autumn imagery and a list of what old age should bring.
Beyond: 1.2 “brave Macbeth” (1.2.18), what he had at the start; 3.2 “full of scorpions is my mind” (3.2.41), the peace he lost; 5.5 “Signifying nothing.” (5.5.31), the meaning he lost; 5.8 “lay on, Macduff;” (5.8.38), the courage he keeps.
Judgement: he has lost everything except the courage he began with, which makes the ending tragic rather than simply just.
checklist: Thesis answers “how far” in 1 or 2 sentences
Uses 2 or more moments from the extract with methods
Uses 2 or more moments from elsewhere, including Act 3 or later
Orders moments to build an argument
Ends with a judgement
questions.explanation: AQA 2023 examiners found that answers starting with a thesis generally did very well.

units.title: How OCR and Eduqas set the question
units.summary: OCR: choose 1 of 2 questions, extract-based or discursive, in about 45 minutes, for 36 marks plus 4 for SPaG. Eduqas: answer both an extract question (15) and a whole-play essay (20 plus 5 for SPaG), with no marks for context.

questions.prompt: How long does the OCR question paper tell you to spend on the Shakespeare section?
options: About 30 minutes
About 45 minutes
About 1 hour 45 minutes
About 20 minutes
questions.explanation: The paper says “You should spend about 45 minutes on this section.”

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: OCR offers a choice between 2 questions on Macbeth.
On Eduqas you answer both the extract question and the essay.
The Eduqas extract question is worth 15 marks.
OCR gives no marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

questions.explanation: OCR adds 4 AO4 marks to the 36 for the response.

questions.prompt: Match each recent question to its board and year.
pairs: extract from 1.3, Macbeth and Banquo after the Cawdor news
extract from 3.4, Banquo’s ghost at the banquet
extract from 4.2, Lady Macduff and Ross
questions.explanation: Eduqas extracts have ranged across Acts 1, 3 and 4, so know the whole play.

questions.prompt: How many marks are given for spelling, punctuation, vocabulary and sentence structure on the Eduqas Shakespeare essay?
questions.explanation: The essay is 20 marks plus 5 for AO4, making 25; with the 15-mark extract question, Section A totals 40.

questions.prompt: OCR prints its extracts from one particular edition. Which?
options: The First Folio facsimile
The Alexander Text (Collins)
Project Gutenberg
The Folger edition
questions.explanation: Wording and line numbers may differ slightly from your own edition, so do not panic over small differences.

questions.prompt: OCR’s discursive question asks you to explore at least how many moments from the play?
options: Every scene
questions.explanation: A few moments analysed closely beat a tour of the whole play.

questions.prompt: How does the Eduqas paper advise you to divide your time on the Shakespeare section?
options: Equal time on both
All the time on the essay
40 minutes on the extract and 20 on the essay
About 20 minutes on the extract and about 40 minutes on the essay
questions.explanation: The essay carries more marks, so it gets more time. Weaker answers spent too long on the extract.

questions.prompt: On Eduqas, a student plans a paragraph on Jacobean attitudes to women for the essay. What would examiners say?
options: It should go in the extract answer instead
Context is not assessed in the Eduqas Shakespeare questions; in 2025 such comments were the biggest source of underachievement
Excellent AO3
It earns SPaG marks
questions.explanation: Eduqas examiners wrote of “the time wasted in offering sweeping and entirely unnecessary contextual comments on gender in Jacobean society”.
questions.misconception: Writing context for Eduqas, which does not assess it.

questions.prompt: The Eduqas extract question asks how an audience might respond. Which audience should you consider?
options: Any audience, including a modern one
Only King James
Only a theatre critic
Only a Jacobean audience
questions.explanation: Eduqas’s 2024 report calls this an invitation to consider “how any audience might respond”.

questions.prompt: OCR discursive-style: Explore how Shakespeare presents horror in Macbeth. Explore at least 2 moments from the play. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Shakespeare creates horror less through what he shows than through how characters react. Duncan’s murder happens offstage, so the horror arrives through Macbeth’s broken lines and bloody hands. He cannot say “Amen”, and asks whether “all great Neptune’s ocean” could “wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” (2.2.78-79). The audience imagines the deed through his terror.

The discovery in 2.3 turns horror outward. After the Porter’s jokes, Macduff’s cry “O horror, horror, horror! / Tongue nor heart cannot conceive nor name thee!” (2.3.73-74) shows language failing in the face of the crime, and his image of “The Lord’s anointed temple” (2.3.78) broken open makes the murder a sacrilege. The juxtaposition with comedy makes the shock sharper. By 4.2 horror falls on the innocent: a child cries “He has kill’d me, mother:” (4.2.96-97). Across the play, Shakespeare moves horror from guilty imagination to open slaughter, so the audience feels the moral world collapsing.
checklist: Focuses on horror throughout, not ambition or character in general
Explores at least 2 moments in depth
Analyses language and dramatic methods (offstage murder, juxtaposition)
Considers audience response
Builds a line of argument across the moments
questions.explanation: OCR examiners in 2024 found some answers drifted to ambition despite its limited relevance to a question on horror.

units.title: Reading the question and planning
units.summary: Read the question twice, underline its key words and decide your answer before you write. A 1-sentence thesis and 4 or 5 well-chosen moments, including Act 3 or 4, keep every paragraph on the question.

questions.prompt: What should you do first when you open the question?
options: Count the lines in the extract
Choose your favourite quotation
Read it twice and underline the key words and the command
Start writing your prepared introduction
questions.explanation: Most lost marks start in the first 5 minutes, when students answer the question they expected rather than the one set.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: AQA’s 2023 report found that answers starting with a thesis generally did very well.
Long, pre-learnt introductions are rewarded by examiners.
For a “how far” question you should take a position.
Your plan should include moments from across the play, not only Act 1.

questions.explanation: Examiners describe pre-learnt openings as “unnecessary preamble”.

questions.prompt: Put these planning steps in order.
items: Read the question twice
Underline the key words and the command
Write a 1-sentence thesis
Choose 4 or 5 moments with a quotation and a method each
Put the moments in an order that builds the argument
questions.explanation: About 5 minutes of planning saves time later.

questions.prompt: Match each command to what it asks for.
pairs: a judgement on the extent of something (AQA)
explain the importance of ... elsewhere in the play
why a theme matters beyond the extract (Edexcel part b)
explore at least 2 moments from the play
close analysis of a few chosen moments (OCR discursive)
questions.explanation: Each board’s wording points to a different kind of answer.

questions.prompt: Which is the best thesis for: explore how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a strong female character?
options: In this essay I will look at Lady Macbeth.
Lady Macbeth is strong in will and words in Act 1, but the play shows that her strength depends on suppressing feelings that return to destroy her.
Lady Macbeth is a character in Macbeth written by Shakespeare.
Lady Macbeth is the eponymous hero’s wife.
questions.explanation: A thesis answers the question and gives the essay a shape.

questions.prompt: In ‘explore how far Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a male character who changes’, which words matter most to underline?
options: explore, Shakespeare
Macbeth, male character, changes, how far
presents, as
a, who
questions.explanation: AQA’s 2023 question used this wording. “Changes” means you must track development across the play.

questions.prompt: You are planning an essay on Macbeth and fear. Which 2 moments would extend your plan beyond Act 1?
options: 3.1: “Our fears in Banquo / Stick deep,” (3.1.53-54)
5.5: “I have almost forgot the taste of fears.” (5.5.11)
1.3: “Present fears / Are less than horrible imaginings.” (1.3.150-151)
1.3: “Look, how our partner’s rapt.” (1.3.156)
questions.explanation: Examiners report that weaker essays stay in the first half; Act 3 moments are a key discriminator.

questions.prompt: A student sees ‘Lady Macbeth’ in a question about horror and writes their prepared essay on her ambition. What is the problem?
options: Lady Macbeth is not in the play
It does not answer the question set; examiners repeatedly report prepared essays drifting from the question
None: any essay on Lady Macbeth will do
Horror questions must be about the Witches
questions.explanation: Use what you know, but reshape it to fit the exact words of the question.
questions.misconception: Writing a prepared essay instead of answering the question.

questions.prompt: OCR’s 2024 report said some discursive answers moved between agreeing and disagreeing at random. What is the best fix?
options: Avoid disagreeing at all
Write more paragraphs
Plan a line of argument first, so each paragraph moves the thesis forward and any counter-point is placed deliberately
Use more quotations
questions.explanation: Planning gives structure; the examiners noted “still little evidence of planning”.

questions.prompt: Write a thesis and a 4-moment plan for: How does Shakespeare present the way Lady Macbeth changes during the play? (6 marks)
questions.model:
Thesis: Lady Macbeth changes from the planner who controls her husband to a woman shut out of his plans and destroyed by guilt she tried to deny; the change shows that her strength depended on silencing her own conscience.
1. 1.5: “unsex me here,” (1.5.48), commands to the spirits; method: imperatives. Point: control and chosen cruelty.
2. 2.2: “A little water clears us of this deed:” (2.2.86); method: contrast with Macbeth’s ocean. Point: denial of guilt.
3. 3.2: “Naught’s had, all’s spent,” (3.2.6) and “dearest chuck” (3.2.51); method: rhyme, pet name. Point: discontent and exclusion.
4. 5.1: “Out, damned spot!” (5.1.37); method: broken prose. Point: guilt returns; control is lost.
Judgement: the change is complete, and the seeds of it are visible in Act 2.
checklist: Thesis answers the question in 1 or 2 sentences
4 moments spread across the play, including Act 3
Each moment has a quotation and a method
Moments are ordered to show change
Ends with a judgement
questions.explanation: Eduqas asked about how Lady Macbeth changes in 2023. A plan like this takes about 5 minutes.

units.title: Using the extract
units.summary: Place the extract, read every stage direction, check who says what, and mark 4 to 6 short phrases to analyse. Zoom in on single words, then zoom out to link the moment to the whole play.

questions.prompt: What should you do first with a printed extract?
options: Start writing straight away
Look for the hardest word
Place it: read the introduction line and work out what has just happened
Copy out the longest speech
questions.explanation: Knowing where the extract sits stops you misreading it.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Stage directions are part of the evidence in an extract.
You can give a line to whichever character suits your argument.
An aside tells you something a character hides from others on stage.
You may use line references from the printed extract.

questions.explanation: Check who speaks every line before you analyse it.

questions.prompt: Match each slip reported by examiners to how to avoid it.
pairs: read every stage direction before you start
Placing the 1.3 extract after the murder
use the introduction line to place the extract
notice what a character hides from others
questions.explanation: All of these slips come from Eduqas reports between 2023 and 2025.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for reading an extract in order.
items: Read the introduction line
Read the stage directions
Check who says what
Mark 4 to 6 short phrases to analyse
Note a link to another moment in the play
questions.explanation: Placing, reading, then selecting: the analysis comes after you know what is happening.

questions.prompt: You are analysing Macduff’s “Bleed, bleed, poor country!” (4.3.39) in a 4.3 extract. Which zoom-out link is strongest?
options: Ross’s “Alas, poor country, / Almost afraid to know itself!” (4.3.189-190), later in the same scene, which develops the image of Scotland suffering
The Witches’ first appearance
Duncan praising the castle
The Porter’s jokes
questions.explanation: A link that develops the same image shows how a moment fits the whole play.

questions.prompt: A line in the extract has the stage direction “Aside”. What does that tell you?
options: The other characters on stage do not hear it, so it reveals hidden thoughts
The character leaves the stage
The line is sung
The line is shouted
questions.explanation: Asides create dramatic irony, which is worth analysing.

questions.prompt: In Edexcel part (a), how should you use the extract?
options: Ignore it and write about the whole play
Summarise the plot of the extract
Use it only for context
Analyse it closely for language, form and structure
questions.explanation: Part (a) is about the extract only; part (b) moves elsewhere.

questions.prompt: AQA examiners in 2019 found students describing Macbeth as “merciless”. What had gone wrong?
options: They used too many quotations
They wrote about Act 5
They gave a description of Macdonwald to Macbeth
They used a word Shakespeare never wrote
questions.explanation: In the Captain’s speech, “The merciless Macdonwald” (1.2.11) is the rebel. Check who each description belongs to.
questions.misconception: Giving one character’s description to another.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2023 extract came from 5.3. Many students wrote only about Macbeth as a fighter. What would have improved their answers?
options: Avoiding quotations from the extract
Writing more about the Witches
Placing the extract in Macbeth’s wider despair at this point in the play
Writing only about Lady Macbeth
questions.explanation: Think about where the extract comes from. His bravado sits next to lines such as “I have liv’d long enough:” (5.3.26).

questions.prompt: Zoom in and zoom out: take Lady Macbeth’s line “Your face, my thane, is as a book where men / May read strange matters.” (1.5.73-74) Analyse the words closely, then link the line to another moment in the play. (6 marks)
questions.model:
Zoom in: Lady Macbeth compares her husband’s face to “a book where men / May read strange matters.” (1.5.73-74) A book is meant to be read, so his face openly displays the thoughts he should hide; “strange matters” hints at murder without naming it. The image shows her already managing him, treating his honesty as a danger.
Zoom out: the warning links to Duncan’s admission that “There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face:” (1.4.13-14). Duncan cannot read faces; Lady Macbeth fears that others can read Macbeth’s. Later, at the banquet, his face and words do betray him in public, so her fear comes true.
checklist: Analyses the book image closely
Comments on “strange matters” or another phrase
Explains what the line shows about Lady Macbeth or Macbeth
Links accurately to another moment (Duncan in 1.4, the banquet)
Explains what the link adds
questions.explanation: One short line can give you a point and a link across the play.

units.title: Writing about Shakespeare’s methods
units.summary: Methods include language, form, structure and stagecraft. Naming a technique is only the start: say what Shakespeare does, how it works, why it matters to the audience, and where else it connects.

questions.prompt: Which of these counts as a “method” for AO2?
options: Only the plot
Only historical context
Language, form, structure and stagecraft
Only metaphors and similes
questions.explanation: Methods include where a moment comes and what happens offstage.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: Placing an event offstage is a structural or dramatic method.
Naming a technique earns full AO2 marks on its own.
A soliloquy is a feature of form.
Knocking at the gate is an example of stagecraft.

questions.explanation: AO2 marks come from explaining effects.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of method to an example.
pairs: the metaphor of a mind “full of scorpions”
Macdonwald’s head in 1.2 echoed by Macbeth’s in 5.8
the knocking at the gate after the murder
questions.explanation: Use the full range, not just language.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of this analysis frame in order.
items: What does Shakespeare do? (a precise quotation)
How does it work? (the method)
Why? (the effect on the audience and the meaning)
Where else? (a link to another moment)
questions.explanation: The frame keeps each point analytical rather than descriptive.

questions.prompt: Which comment on Lady Macbeth’s “Come, thick night,” (1.5.57) is strongest?
options: She commands night itself to arrive, as if the darkness were her servant; the woman who will later need a light by her bed here welcomes the dark.
Shakespeare uses an imperative.
This is a quotation from Act 1.
The imperative shows she wants darkness.
questions.explanation: The best comment explains the effect and links forward to 5.1.

questions.prompt: What did AQA examiners say about labelling word classes?
options: It was often done incorrectly, and using parts of speech as a prism for analysis is generally reductive
It is required by the mark scheme
It is the best way to gain AO2
It earns AO4 marks
questions.explanation: Focus on what the words do, not on their grammatical labels.

questions.prompt: Edexcel’s 2025 feedback on the Witches extract said stronger answers discussed something beyond simile and repetition. What?
options: King James’s handwriting
The trochaic rhythm of the Witches’ lines and the structure of their exchange
The cost of the costumes
The number of lines in the extract
questions.explanation: Form and structure can carry as much meaning as images.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘A Marxist reading shows that Macbeth is about the proletariat.’ What did AQA examiners say about this kind of comment?
options: It is the best way to show AO3
Marxist readings are banned
Theory is required for Level 6
Critical theories that appear poorly understood do not contribute to the student’s own interpretation
questions.explanation: Use everyday, accurate terms and your own interpretation.
questions.misconception: Name-dropping critical theory instead of analysing the play.

questions.prompt: Eduqas examiners in 2025 were frustrated by quotations that were learned but not “mined” for AO2. What does mining a quotation mean?
options: Repeating it twice
Learning it by heart
Analysing its words, images and effects closely
Putting it in bold
questions.explanation: Learning quotations is only half the job; the marks come from analysing them.

questions.prompt: Write a “best” level analysis of Macbeth’s aside “Stars, hide your fires! / Let not light see my black and deep desires.” (1.4.57-58) Use the What, How, Why, Where else frame. (6 marks)
questions.model: What: Straight after Duncan names Malcolm as heir, Macbeth asks the stars to hide their light so that his “black and deep desires.” (1.4.58) stay unseen. How: he speaks in an aside, so the court hears nothing; the lines rhyme, fires and desires, which makes them sound like a spell or vow. Why: the audience learns that ambition has grown into intent, while Duncan, on stage, is praising him; the gap between what we hear and what Duncan sees creates dramatic irony. Where else: Lady Macbeth makes the same request in 1.5, “Come, thick night,” (1.5.57), so both partners call on darkness, and in 5.1 she must keep a light beside her. The darkness they summon becomes the darkness they cannot escape.
checklist: Places the quotation precisely (after Malcolm is named heir)
Explains the aside and the rhyme (form)
Explains the effect on the audience (dramatic irony)
Links to Lady Macbeth’s call for darkness or the light in 5.1
Avoids technique-spotting without explanation
questions.explanation: This frame works for any quotation in any board’s question.

units.title: Embedding quotations and writing accurately
units.summary: Embed short quotations in your own sentences, use a slash for verse line breaks, and paraphrase when unsure. AQA and OCR give 4 marks for accuracy, Eduqas 5 on the essay, and Edexcel none in this section.

questions.prompt: What is an embedded quotation?
options: A quotation in a footnote
A quotation in capital letters
A quotation written on a separate line
A quotation that forms part of your own sentence
questions.explanation: Embedding keeps the argument flowing and focuses attention on the exact words.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: AQA gives 4 marks for AO4 on the Shakespeare question.
OCR gives 4 marks for AO4 on the Shakespeare question.
Eduqas gives its 5 AO4 marks on the extract question.
Edexcel gives no AO4 marks in its Shakespeare section.

questions.explanation: Eduqas’s 5 marks are on the essay only.

questions.prompt: Match each board to the marks for AO4 in its Shakespeare section.
questions.explanation: Accuracy still matters on Edexcel: clear writing helps every other mark.

questions.prompt: Correct the spelling of the underlined word: ‘Macbeth’s first solilloquy comes in 1.7.’
questions.explanation: Soliloquy: s-o-l-i-l-o-q-u-y. Spell key terms and names correctly for AO4.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses “prophecy” and “prophesy” correctly?
options: The Witches prophesy that Macbeth will be king, and the prophesy sets the tragedy in motion.
The Witches prophecy that Macbeth will be king, and the prophecy sets the tragedy in motion.
The Witches prophesy that Macbeth will be king, and the prophecy sets the tragedy in motion.
The Witches prophecy that Macbeth will be king, and the prophesy sets the tragedy in motion.
questions.explanation: Prophecy (with a c) is the noun; prophesy (with an s) is the verb.

questions.prompt: Which sentence embeds and punctuates its quotation correctly?
options: Macbeth fears that not even “all great Neptune’s ocean” (2.2.78) could wash his hand clean, an image that makes his guilt larger than the sea.
Macbeth fears that not even all great Neptune’s ocean could wash his hand clean.
Macbeth fears that not even all great Neptune’s ocean could wash his hand clean (2.2.78).
Macbeth fears that not even “all great Neptune’s ocean (2.2.78) could wash his hand clean.
questions.explanation: Only Shakespeare’s words go inside the quotation marks, and the reference follows them.

questions.prompt: Which sentences use apostrophes correctly? Choose 2.
options: Macbeth’s ambition grows after the prophecy.
Macbeths’ ambition grows after the prophecy.
The Witches’ prophecies mislead him.
The Witche’s prophecies mislead him.
questions.explanation: Singular owner: Macbeth’s. Plural owner ending in s: the Witches’.

questions.prompt: A student copies out 4 full lines of the dagger speech and then writes 1 sentence about it. Which advice is best?
options: Keep doing this: longer quotations score more
Never quote at all
Only quote stage directions
Short is strong: choose up to about 6 words you can analyse closely
questions.explanation: Long quotations take time and leave little room for analysis.
questions.misconception: Thinking longer quotations earn more marks.

questions.prompt: You cannot remember exactly what Macbeth says about life in 5.5. What should you do?
options: Paraphrase: Macbeth compares life to a poor actor who struts on the stage and is then forgotten
Write ‘quote here’
Make up words that sound Shakespearean and put them in quotation marks
Leave a blank space
questions.explanation: Paraphrase earns credit for knowledge. Analysis of words that are not Shakespeare’s cannot be credited.

questions.prompt: Rewrite this paragraph so that its quotation is embedded and analysed: ‘Lady Macbeth is in control. “Infirm of purpose! / Give me the daggers.” (2.2.68-69) This shows she is in control.’ (4 marks)
questions.model: Lady Macbeth seizes control the moment her husband falters, dismissing him as “Infirm of purpose!” (2.2.68). The phrase turns his conscience into a weakness of will, and the short, commanding demand that follows, to “Give me the daggers.” (2.2.69), shows her ready to do what he cannot. In this scene, at least, she is the stronger partner.
checklist: Embeds the quotation in a sentence of the student’s own
Analyses a specific word or phrase (“Infirm of purpose”)
Comments on the command or sentence form
Avoids repeating the point with a weak ending such as ‘this shows she is in control’
questions.explanation: Compare the 2 versions: the second gives the same evidence but does more with it.

units.title: Mistakes examiners keep seeing
units.summary: Examiner reports repeat the same warnings: bolted-on context, prepared essays, no thesis, misreading the extract, technique-spotting, unanalysed quotations, only the first half of the play, and blaming Lady Macbeth for everything.

questions.prompt: Which board’s examiners said in 2025 that unnecessary comments on gender in Jacobean society were the biggest source of underachievement?
options: Eduqas
OCR
Edexcel
AQA
questions.explanation: Eduqas does not assess context in its Shakespeare questions at all.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: AQA’s 2023 report said discussions of the Gunpowder Plot made answers longer without adding insight.
Calling any list of 3 a tricolon impresses OCR examiners.
Eduqas examiners in 2024 criticised answers that blamed almost everything on Lady Macbeth.
Covering Act 3 was a key discriminator in Eduqas answers on Lady Macbeth.

questions.explanation: OCR’s 2024 report said tricolon was over-identified.

questions.prompt: Match each mistake to the report that described it.
pairs: Stock openings such as ‘the eponymous hero’
Context included in part (a), which is not assessed
Answers drifting to ambition in a question on horror
Arguments resting on a lost baby
questions.explanation: Each board’s report tells you what its examiners want to see less of.

questions.prompt: Which of these did examiners report as problems? Choose 2.
options: Starting with a clear thesis
Using short, embedded quotations
Naming a simile or repetition without explaining it
Wording copied from online revision material
questions.explanation: Thesis-led answers and short embedded quotations were praised, not criticised.

questions.prompt: Why do examiners dislike pre-learnt openings with phrases like ‘the eponymous hero’?
options: The phrase is factually wrong
They break the AO4 rules
They are too short
They create unnecessary preamble instead of answering the question
questions.explanation: Start with a thesis that answers the question in 1 or 2 sentences.

questions.prompt: Eduqas examiners in 2024 saw many answers arguing sympathy for Macbeth by blaming his wife. What evidence did those answers ignore?
options: The Porter’s jokes
Macbeth’s own early thoughts of murder and “black and deep desires”, and her absence from the later murders
The number of scenes in Act 5
The weather in 1.1
questions.explanation: A fair judgement weighs Macbeth’s choices as well as her influence.

questions.prompt: AQA’s 2023 report mentioned phrasing copied from online material. What effect did it have?
options: It added nothing and sometimes got in the way of students’ own ideas
It was not noticed
It guaranteed Level 6
It improved AO4 marks
questions.explanation: Your own words, even if simpler, show your own understanding.

questions.prompt: A student builds a whole essay on the claim that Lady Macbeth lost a baby before the play. What did Eduqas examiners in 2024 report about this approach?
options: It earns extra AO3 marks
It is required by the mark scheme
It is the most rewarded reading
It tended to lead to underachievement
questions.explanation: The play does not tell us; stay with what the text shows.
questions.misconception: Building an argument on events the play does not show.

questions.prompt: Which change would most improve an essay that uses only moments from Acts 1 and 2?
options: Quoting the same lines again
Adding a longer introduction
Adding moments from Act 3, such as “dearest chuck” or the banquet
Adding more context about King James
questions.explanation: Eduqas’s 2023 report described Act 3 moments as a key discriminator.

questions.prompt: This paragraph from an AQA answer has 4 problems. Rewrite it to fix them: ‘In this extract Macbeth sees a dagger. In Jacobean times people believed in witches and King James wrote Daemonologie in 1597. This is a metaphor. A Jacobean audience would be scared.’ (6 marks)
questions.model: Shakespeare uses the dagger to show how far Macbeth’s mind has already travelled towards murder. He asks whether it is “A dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?” (2.1.50-51), and the questions show a man unsure whether the vision is real or produced by his own guilty excitement. When he admits it marshals him “the way that I was going;” (2.1.54), the supernatural seems only to confirm a choice he has made. For an audience who took witchcraft seriously, the vision might suggest evil powers at work, yet Shakespeare keeps the explanation open, which makes Macbeth’s responsibility harder to escape.
checklist: Replaces narrative with an argued point
Quotes and analyses the dagger speech instead of mislabelling a technique
Cuts the bolted-on facts and keeps context to 1 linked sentence
Replaces the generalised “Jacobean audience” ending with a specific effect
Links the moment to Macbeth’s choice or the wider play
questions.explanation: The problems were narrative, bolted-on context, mislabelled technique and a stock ending.

units.title: Model answer (1): the extract and the plan
units.summary: Work through an AQA-style question on how the Macbeths’ relationship changes, starting with 3.2. Underline the key words, write a thesis, choose moments before and after the extract, and decide your judgement.

questions.prompt: The question is: Starting with this conversation, explore how far Shakespeare presents the relationship between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth as changing. Which words are the key words?
options: explore, between
starting, with
relationship, changing, how far, this conversation and the whole play
Shakespeare, presents
questions.explanation: “Changing” means you must track development; “how far” asks for a judgement.

questions.prompt: True or false? (about the 3.2 extract)

statements.s: Lady Macbeth asks why her husband keeps alone.
Macbeth says “We have scorch’d the snake, not kill’d it.”
Macbeth tells his wife about his plan to kill Banquo.
Lady Macbeth tells him “You must leave this.”

questions.explanation: He hides the plan: later in the scene she must be “innocent of the knowledge”.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the plan in order.
items: Underline the key words
Write a thesis
Choose moments from the extract
Choose moments from before and after the extract
Decide your judgement on “how far”
questions.explanation: Planning for about 5 minutes gives the essay its spine.

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth’s advice in the extract: “Gently my lord, sleek o’er your rugged ___;” (3.2.30-31)
questions.explanation: She is still concerned with appearances; he is concerned with what lies beneath.

questions.prompt: Which thesis is strongest for this question?
options: The relationship changes from a partnership she leads to one in which he acts alone; in 3.2 affection remains, but the power has already moved to him.
The Macbeths are married and talk in 3.2.
Lady Macbeth is evil and Macbeth is good.
This essay will discuss the relationship.
questions.explanation: It answers “how far” and separates love from partnership, which gives the essay a shape.

questions.prompt: Which moment from before the extract best shows what the relationship was like at the start?
options: The Porter’s speech
The Witches’ chant in 4.1
Macbeth’s letter calling her “my dearest partner of greatness)” (1.5.11)
Malcolm’s coronation
questions.explanation: “Partner” is the key word: in Act 1 they plot as equals, with her in charge.

questions.prompt: In the extract Macbeth says the living must lie “In restless ecstasy.” (3.2.25) What does “ecstasy” mean here?
options: A frenzy of mental torment
Great happiness
A deep sleep
A dance
questions.explanation: Shakespeare’s “ecstasy” means a state of being beside oneself, here with fear and guilt.

questions.prompt: A student writes a brilliant answer on the extract but never mentions the rest of the play. What could happen on AQA?
options: Nothing, if the analysis is detailed
Full marks
The mark can be capped at the top of Level 2 for not covering both the extract and the whole play
Only AO4 marks are lost
questions.explanation: Both bullets in the question must be addressed.
questions.misconception: Thinking extract analysis alone can reach the top levels on AQA.

questions.prompt: Who says this in the extract? “O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!” (3.2.41)
options: Banquo
Macbeth
Lady Macbeth
The Doctor
questions.explanation: The endearment “dear wife” comes from a man who is keeping Banquo’s murder from her, which is the key irony to analyse.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph on how the structure of the 3.2 conversation shows a shift in power between the Macbeths. Use at least 2 quotations from the extract. (6 marks)
questions.model: The shape of the conversation shows who now holds the power. Lady Macbeth begins with questions, “why do you keep alone,” (3.2.10), and short practical advice, but her husband answers with long speeches of his own fears. He moves from “We have scorch’d the snake, not kill’d it.” (3.2.15) into a vivid account of terrible dreams, and she is reduced to brief instructions about appearances. When she tries to close the subject with “You must leave this.” (3.2.40), he overrides her at once. In 1.7 she had the long, persuasive speeches and he fell silent; here the pattern is reversed, which shows that the partnership she led has become one in which he decides and conceals.
checklist: Comments on who speaks more and who asks questions
Uses at least 2 accurate quotations from the extract
Explains how the structure shows power shifting
Compares with 1.7 or 1.5
Reaches a clear point about change
questions.explanation: Structure in a conversation includes length of speeches, questions and who has the last word.

units.title: Model answer (2): the essay
units.summary: A top-band essay answers “how far” in its first sentence, signposts its argument, keeps quotations short, analyses single words, compares with earlier scenes and uses context once, where it helps.

questions.prompt: What does the first sentence of a top-band answer do?
options: Answers the question with a clear thesis
Defines tragedy
Retells the plot of the extract
Gives the date of the play
questions.explanation: AQA examiners found that answers starting with a thesis generally did very well.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: A top answer keeps quotations short enough to analyse word by word.
Context should fill a separate paragraph at the end.
Comparing the extract with earlier scenes helps show change.
Signposting the argument early helps the examiner follow it.

questions.explanation: In a strong answer context appears briefly, where it strengthens a point.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of a model paragraph to the assessment objective it mainly shows.
pairs: A brief link to ideas about women in 1606
questions.explanation: Strong paragraphs combine several AOs.

questions.prompt: Put the paragraphs of the model essay’s argument in order.
items: Thesis: the balance tips in this conversation
The extract: questions, advice ignored, “We”
The extract: who speaks most, and the “dear wife” irony
Before: the partnership of 1.5 and 1.7
After: the banquet and Act 5
Conclusion: love lasts longer than partnership
questions.explanation: Extract first, then backwards and forwards through the play, ending with a judgement.

questions.prompt: Macbeth says “We have scorch’d the snake, not kill’d it.” (3.2.15). Which comment on “We” is strongest?
options: The plural “We” clings to the idea of a shared enterprise, even though he is about to act alone against Banquo.
“We” is a pronoun.
“We” shows they are happy.
“We” means Macbeth and Banquo.
questions.explanation: A single word, analysed in context, can carry a whole point about the relationship.

questions.prompt: Macbeth tells his wife: “Let your remembrance apply to Banquo;” (3.2.34-35). Why is this dramatic irony?
options: Banquo is the king
She has already killed Banquo
He urges her to honour Banquo at the feast while knowing he has arranged Banquo’s murder
Banquo is listening
questions.explanation: He now deceives his own partner, as she once taught him to deceive Duncan.

questions.prompt: Which context sentence is brief and linked to the argument?
options: King James was born in 1566 and became king of England in 1603 after Elizabeth I died.
James’s Daemonologie called women the “frailer” sex; Shakespeare gives the strength to the wife, which makes the later reversal more disturbing.
Jacobean people believed many things about women.
The play was performed at the Globe.
questions.explanation: Context earns marks when it sharpens a point about the play.

questions.prompt: A student adds a whole paragraph on the Gunpowder Plot to an essay on the Macbeths’ relationship. What is the problem?
options: Context is banned on AQA
Nothing: more context means more marks
The plot happened after the play
It is bolted on: it makes the answer longer without adding insight into the relationship
questions.explanation: AQA’s 2023 report made exactly this point about Gunpowder Plot paragraphs.
questions.misconception: Thinking any context improves an answer.

questions.prompt: Why does the model compare the 3.2 conversation with 1.7?
options: Because the question is about 1.7
To show the Witches’ influence
In 1.7 she spoke at length and he fell silent; in 3.2 it is reversed, which turns a detail into evidence of change
To retell 1.7
questions.explanation: Comparison is how you prove change, the key word in the question.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph for the same question using the banquet (3.4) as your moment. Keep quotations short and track the change. (6 marks)
questions.model: At the banquet Lady Macbeth still protects her husband in public, but her power over him is fading. When he sees the Ghost she covers for him smoothly, “My lord is often thus,” (3.4.64), the same quick control she showed on the murder night. In private, though, her old weapon fails. “Are you a man?” (3.4.70) won the argument in 1.7, but now it cannot reach a man tormented by what he sees. By the end of the scene she can only send the guests away and tell him he lacks “the season of all natures, sleep.” (3.4.173) The partnership survives as loyalty, but she no longer leads it, and this is the last time they share the stage.
checklist: Uses the banquet accurately
Analyses her public cover for him
Shows her taunt about manhood failing (compared with 1.7)
Keeps quotations short and embedded
Explains what has changed in the relationship
questions.explanation: Examiners say that covering Act 3 separates stronger answers.

units.title: Model answer (3): the whole play and the verdict
units.summary: The model essay follows the relationship to Act 5, offers 2 readings of “She should have died hereafter”, and ends with a judgement that adds a final idea. Learn to spot what lifts an answer from Level 3 to Level 6.

questions.prompt: Which act do examiners say often separates stronger answers on the Macbeths’ relationship?
options: Act 5 only
Act 3
Act 1
None
questions.explanation: Moments such as “dearest chuck” and the banquet show how the relationship changes after the murder.

questions.prompt: True or false?

statements.s: In Act 5 Macbeth and Lady Macbeth never share the stage.
A strong conclusion simply repeats the introduction.
The model answer offers 2 interpretations of a key line.
The model would sit in AQA’s Level 6.

questions.explanation: A strong conclusion makes a judgement and adds a final idea.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from the model answer in play order.
items: “my dearest partner of greatness”
“Infirm of purpose!”
“dearest chuck”
“Are you a man?”
“She should have died hereafter.”
questions.explanation: 1.5, 2.2, 3.2, 3.4, 5.5: a whole-play path through the relationship.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s response to his wife’s death: “She should have died ___.” (5.5.20)
questions.explanation: “Hereafter” means “later”, and the line can be read more than one way.

questions.prompt: Which pair of readings of “She should have died hereafter.” (5.5.20) does the model use?
options: He does not hear the news; or he misunderstands it
He is glad; or he is joking
She should have died later, when there was time to mourn; or the line signals exhaustion and numbness
He blames Seyton; or he blames Malcolm
questions.explanation: Holding 2 readings together, and using both, is a mark of an exploratory answer.

questions.prompt: What makes a strong conclusion?
options: A clear judgement on the question plus a final idea that grows from the argument
A paragraph of context
A new quotation not yet discussed
A summary of every paragraph
questions.explanation: The model ends: the crime meant to make them partners is the thing that divides them.

questions.prompt: Within which AQA level and mark range would a critical, exploratory, thesis-driven answer like the model sit?
options: Level 3, 11 to 15
Level 4, 16 to 20
Level 5, 21 to 25
Level 6, 26 to 30
questions.explanation: Level 6 asks for a critical, exploratory, conceptualised argument with fine-grained analysis.

questions.prompt: A student ends an essay: ‘In conclusion, as I said at the start, the relationship changes.’ What is the main weakness?
options: It is too long
It uses the word “conclusion”
It mentions the relationship
It repeats the introduction without a judgement on “how far” or a final idea
questions.explanation: Conclusions should decide, not restate.
questions.misconception: Thinking a conclusion should repeat the introduction.

questions.prompt: A Level 3 paragraph says: ‘Macbeth says his mind is full of scorpions. This is a metaphor. It shows he is worried.’ Which revision lifts it most?
options: Add the date of the play
Quote the whole speech
Explain that scorpions sting and poison from inside, so his fear cannot be escaped, and link it to how he now hides Banquo’s murder from his wife
Add the word “metaphor” twice
questions.explanation: Explaining the image and linking it to the question’s focus moves the paragraph up the levels.

questions.prompt: This paragraph would sit around AQA Level 3. Rewrite it so that it analyses methods and tracks change: ‘At the end Macbeth doesn’t care about Lady Macbeth. When she dies he says she should have died hereafter. This shows he doesn’t care. At the start they were close.’ (6 marks)
questions.model: By Act 5 the partners of Act 1 have become strangers. The couple never share the stage, and Lady Macbeth’s death is only reported by Seyton, so the audience sees Macbeth’s response rather than the loss itself. His reply, “She should have died hereafter.” (5.5.20), can mean that she should have died later, when there would be time to grieve, or it may show that he is too exhausted to feel anything. Either reading marks a change from the man who once wrote to his “dearest partner of greatness” (1.5.11). The speech that follows, in which life “Signifying nothing.” (5.5.31), suggests that her death has drained even the last shared meaning from his world.
checklist: Replaces ’doesn’t care’ with a precise argued point
Notes the staging: they never meet and the death is reported
Offers 2 readings of “hereafter”
Compares with Act 1 using a precise quotation
Links to the “Tomorrow” speech or another moment
questions.explanation: Moving up the levels means explaining, then exploring.

units.title: Planning a whole-play essay
units.summary: For a whole-play essay, write a thesis, then choose 5 moments in order, each with a quotation, a method and a point. On Eduqas, spend about 40 minutes: 5 planning, 30 writing, 5 checking, with no context needed.

questions.prompt: How many marks is the Eduqas Shakespeare essay worth?
options: 20 plus 5 for AO4
30 plus 4
36 plus 4
questions.explanation: 20 for AO1 and AO2, equally weighted, plus 5 for accuracy.

questions.prompt: True or false? (Eduqas essay)

statements.s: No context is needed or rewarded.
You should refer to characters and events from across the play.
You are advised to spend about 40 minutes on it.
You must base the essay on the printed extract.

questions.explanation: The essay is on the whole play; the extract has its own question.

questions.prompt: Put this 40-minute plan in order.
items: About 5 minutes planning
About 30 minutes writing
About 5 minutes checking spelling, punctuation and names
questions.explanation: The checking time protects the 5 AO4 marks.

questions.prompt: You are planning: How does Shakespeare present loyalty and betrayal? Match each moment to its quotation.
pairs: “No more that Thane of Cawdor shall deceive / Our bosom interest.” (1.2.73-74)
“He was a gentleman on whom I built / An absolute trust.” (1.4.15-16)
“This tyrant, whose sole name blisters our tongues, / Was once thought honest:” (4.3.14-15)
questions.explanation: A plan built on a clear path through the play keeps the essay focused.

questions.prompt: Which thesis is strongest for: How does Shakespeare present loyalty and betrayal?
options: Shakespeare shows betrayal spreading from 1 traitor to a whole kingdom, so that by Act 4 loyalty itself must be tested before it can be trusted.
In this essay I will write about loyalty.
Loyalty and betrayal are in Macbeth.
Macbeth betrays Duncan.
questions.explanation: It answers the question and gives the essay a direction to follow.

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth’s line after the murder: “I am ___ to think what I have done;” (2.2.66)
questions.explanation: A short, plain line that shows fear turning into guilt.

questions.prompt: Which order of paragraphs builds the strongest argument for an essay on loyalty and betrayal?
options: Through the play: Cawdor (1.2), Duncan’s trust (1.4), Macbeth’s double trust (1.7), Banquo’s silence (3.1), Malcolm’s test (4.3)
All Act 4 moments first
Random order
Alphabetical by character
questions.explanation: A chronological path often shows development most clearly.

questions.prompt: Eduqas examiners in 2023 found weaker answers ran short of time on the essay. Why?
options: They wrote about Act 3
They used too few quotations
They planned for too long
They spent too long on the extract question, which is worth fewer marks
questions.explanation: Watch the clock: about 20 minutes on the extract, about 40 on the essay.
questions.misconception: Spending too long on the lower-mark extract question.

questions.prompt: Which opening avoids “unnecessary preamble”?
options: Shakespeare presents betrayal as a disease that spreads from one traitor to a whole kingdom.
Macbeth is a play by William Shakespeare, the famous playwright, written in Jacobean times about the eponymous hero.
Loyalty is important to everyone.
In this essay I am going to write about loyalty and betrayal in the play Macbeth.
questions.explanation: Start with your argument, not with facts the examiner already knows.

questions.prompt: Write a thesis and a 5-paragraph plan for the Eduqas-style essay: How does Shakespeare present loyalty and betrayal in Macbeth? Give a moment, a quotation, a method and a point for each paragraph. (8 marks)
questions.model:
Thesis: Shakespeare shows betrayal spreading from a single traitor to a whole kingdom, until loyalty must be tested before it can be trusted.
1. 1.2: Cawdor’s treason. “No more that Thane of Cawdor shall deceive / Our bosom interest.” (1.2.73-74) Method: dramatic irony, as the title passes to the next traitor. Point: betrayal is punished, but its pattern continues.
2. 1.7: “He’s here in double trust:” (1.7.12) Method: soliloquy listing duties. Point: Macbeth knows exactly which bonds he will break.
3. 3.1: Banquo’s suspicion, “I fear, / Thou play’dst most foully for’t;” (3.1.2-3) Method: soliloquy. Point: loyalty silenced by fear.
4. 4.3: Malcolm’s test, “This tyrant, whose sole name blisters our tongues, / Was once thought honest:” (4.3.14-15) Method: deception used for good. Point: trust must now be earned.
5. 5.2: “Those he commands move only in command, / Nothing in love:” (5.2.22-23) Method: an outside view. Point: the betrayer is himself abandoned.
Conclusion: loyalty returns with Malcolm, but only after Scotland learns to test it.
checklist: Clear thesis that answers the question
5 moments ordered to build an argument across the play
Each paragraph has a quotation, a method and a point
Includes Act 3 or Act 4
No context, as Eduqas does not assess it
Ends with a judgement
questions.explanation: A detailed plan like this takes about 5 minutes and keeps every paragraph on the question.
